A second study tested six cursor enhancement techniques across positions. The best combination adjusted acceleration and distance response together with cursor enlargement. It significantly improved performance wherever the user stood. That is a practical recipe for walk-around large-display interfaces.
arxiv-2511-02226:
Mercè Roig and nine co-authors explain a puzzling observation in a one-atom-thick superconductor. Monolayer iron selenide grown on strontium titanate has two iron atoms per unit cell that crystal symmetry says should behave identically. Yet experiments found the gap differing between the two sublattices, with an unusual imbalance between particles and holes. The team traces the effect to the substrate underneath the film.

Beyond breaking inversion symmetry, the substrate also breaks the nematic kind, and that second breaking is the key. Two mechanisms could produce the asymmetry; the authors argue for a nodeless d-wave gap shaped by the symmetry-breaking substrate. Their scanning tunnelling measurements across nematic domain walls found the sublattice effect clearly enhanced, as predicted. The effect also involves odd-frequency pairing, giving an experimental realisation of that unusual correlation.
arxiv-2511-02326:
Ji-Hao Wang and six colleagues in the CLQCD Collaboration report the most precise calculation yet of two numbers that describe how the nucleon responds to scalar and tensor probes. These charges, computed in lattice quantum chromodynamics, feed into searches for new physics in neutron and nuclear decays. The calculation uses a recently proposed blending method that estimates the all-to-all fermion propagator accurately, plus a new operator capturing the main excited-state contamination.

Fifteen lattice ensembles were used, spanning five lattice spacings and several volumes, three of them at the physical pion mass. The tensor charge came out at about 1.03 and the scalar charge at about 1.11, in units where the quoted values carry a full accounting of systematic uncertainties from the continuum limit, finite volume, chiral extrapolation, excited states, and renormalisation. The error budget is presented in unusual detail, including fit sensitivity to chosen windows.
arxiv-2511-02526:
Marc Schneider and Walter Fichter offered a method for guiding many interceptor missiles against many targets at once, but Schneider later withdrew the submission from arXiv. The withdrawal notice states that later checks showed the proposed method does not generalise beyond the specific scenario considered in the manuscript. The simulation results in the paper should therefore be read as limited to that scenario, not as evidence for the method in general.

As submitted, the work had replaced direct assignment of interceptors to targets with virtual targets. These were predicted trajectory distributions produced by a normalizing-flow model, with each interceptor steered first by zero-effort-miss guidance and then by proportional navigation. Monte Carlo simulations had reported interception gains that grew when interceptors outnumbered targets, the gains the later checks failed to support beyond the tested setup.
arxiv-2511-02626:
Renfei Dang, Peng Hu, Zhejian Lai, Changjiang Gao, Min Zhang, and Shujian Huang investigate a side effect of teaching language models new facts: they start hallucinating about old ones. Fine-tuning on fresh knowledge provokes confident errors on previously mastered material, but how the damage spreads was unclear. The team built a controlled dataset mixing biography material with reasoning tasks, and analysed failures by knowledge type and task type.

Hallucinations hit not only tasks involving the new knowledge but propagated to unrelated evaluations. The strongest driver was not how much new material was added overall, but whether one whole knowledge type was unfamiliar: that pattern reliably raised hallucination rates. Interpretability analysis found the mechanism: learning new knowledge weakens attention to key entities in a question, leaving the model leaning on surrounding context. Mixing a little known knowledge back into late training restored the attention pattern and cut the hallucinations substantially.
arxiv-2511-02826:
Harshith Padigela and thirteen colleagues introduce PLUTO-4, a family of foundation models for pathology images. Such models, trained on huge slide collections, transfer well to many diagnostic tasks. The 2025 release extends their earlier PLUTO line to frontier scale with two vision transformer designs, one compact and one very large.

Both were pretrained with a self-supervised method derived from DINOv2. The training corpus held over half a million whole slide images from more than 137,000 patients at over fifty sites, spanning sixty disease types. On public and internal tests, the family set new marks in tile classification, segmentation, and slide-level diagnosis. The large model improved skin pathology diagnosis by 11 percent. The small one trades a little power for fast, practical deployment.
arxiv-2511-02926:
The Euclid space telescope's first quick data release includes a hunt for bright galaxies seen when the universe was young. N. Allen, P. Oesch, and the Euclid Collaboration forecast and report first finds in a 2025 paper. Galaxies at redshift above six are scarce in older surveys because those covered tiny areas. Euclid's deep fields will span a hundred times more sky, down to faint limits.

Simulations show that signal cuts plus full spectral fitting recover over 76 percent of true early galaxies with under 10 percent contamination from nearer fakes. The team expects more than one hundred thousand such galaxies in the final data, and perhaps over one hundred beyond redshift twelve. Two ultra-bright candidates already found in the northern field support the more generous forecast model.
arxiv-2511-03326:
Sanjay Mishra offers a self-contained guide to simplicial homology, a tool that counts holes in shapes built from simple blocks. Starting from oriented blocks and free groups of chains, the guide defines boundary rules by an alternating sum. A short proof shows that taking a boundary twice always gives zero, the hinge fact of the whole theory.

Cycles and boundaries then appear as the kernel and image of those rules, and their quotient forms the homology groups. Worked low-dimensional cases show each matrix step, from building boundary tables to naming generators. Readers gain a concrete feel for how groups detect joined parts, loops, and voids. The guide suits students meeting algebraic topology through hands-on computation.
arxiv-2511-03726:
Davide Bincoletto, Korbinian Stein, Jonas Motyl, and Jakob S Kottmann train machine learning models that guess good quantum circuit settings for new molecules, not just ones they saw in training. Variational eigensolvers, a leading route to electronic structure on quantum hardware, stall on slow per-molecule tuning of circuit parameters. Most learned predictors so far serve one molecule or one molecule at many bond lengths.

Using a well-studied circuit design on hydrogenic systems, the team tests strategies built for transfer across molecules. Predictions hold up on systems much larger than any in the training set, a strong form of generalization. Transferable warm starts could cut the tuning bill that now limits quantum chemistry on near-term devices.
arxiv-2511-20426:
Bandyopadhyay and colleagues overlap video generation steps to double the frame rate. Their 2025 paper speeds up block-causal video models without retraining. Such models denoise video block by block in sequence. Small models at 1.3 billion parameters reach only sixteen frames per second. Large 14-billion models crawl at four and a half. Users must trade responsiveness against quality.

The key insight is that later blocks can start early. A future block need not wait for a fully denoised predecessor. Partially cleaned context is enough to begin its own denoising. Blocks then proceed in parallel like a cascade. Five graphics processors exploit that time parallelism. The small model accelerated from sixteen to thirty frames per second. The large model jumped from four and a half to twelve and a half. Evaluations found no significant quality loss from the switch. The trick also removes a 200-millisecond cache overhead in interactive use.
arxiv-2511-20826:
Nicholas Pellegrino, David Szczecina, and Paul Fieguth expose in 2025 a quirk of newborn neural networks: before seeing any data, a freshly initialised network already plays favourites. It assigns near-total probability to a few classes and roughly zero to the rest, an Initial Guessing Bias. In one demonstration a single class absorbs all the probability mass, averaging near 1 while every other class sits near 0.

Early training fits the data's coarse structure, and the loss function steers it. Standard cross-entropy pushes back hard where the model is most wrong, so it can correct the bias. But two losses designed to resist label errors, Blurry loss and Piecewise-Zero loss, mute gradients when predicted probabilities are low. Under initial bias, that muting can leave them unable to steer training; Blurry loss even pushes away from the labelled class in one region. The authors warn that loss design and initialisation bias interact.
arxiv-2511-21026:
Marwa Ennaceur builds in 2025 a spectral theory for Hom-Lie Banach algebras, algebras whose bracket is twisted by a map alpha. The paper introduces almost periodic elements and bounded derivations twisted by alpha, then proves a Bohr-Fourier spectral decomposition for them under compactness assumptions. The surprise is algebraic. The almost periodic and ergodic parts are not just complementary subspaces but closed subalgebras. Both are invariant under alpha and stable under the twisted bracket, so dynamics can be restricted to them.

Constructions follow, including the first Hom-Banach-Malcev algebras built from operators and semigroups. The showcase is a twisted Weyl algebra read through the metaplectic representation. There, a non-commuting twist stretches the Bohr spectrum from a cyclic group into a two-dimensional lattice, proving the twist can reshape the spectrum itself. Three example classes, from bilateral shifts to UHF C-star algebras, verify the theory's hypotheses.
arxiv-2511-21126:
Causal discovery tries to recover the diagram of causes among variables from data, hard once effects bend non-linearly. Xiaozhu Zhang, Nir Keret, Ali Shojaie, and Armeen Taeb attack causal additive models in 2025, where each variable is a non-linear function of its parents plus Gaussian noise. They expand each function in basis functions and write the learning problem as a convex mixed-integer program, solvable to a set optimality gap. Background knowledge, such as banned edges, drops in naturally.

The team proves the estimator recovers the true graph consistently, as the number of variables grows with sample size. An early-stopping rule, derived from error bounds, lets the solver quit early without losing that guarantee. In synthetic tests it posted the lowest structural Hamming distance, the count of wrong and missed edges, across all four noise settings tried. Real data agreed, with better graph recovery than rival approaches.
arxiv-2511-21226:
Mathieu Hoyrup, a researcher in computability and logic, asks in 2025 how a set of strings can be built when every position follows only its own local rule. A language here means a fixed-length family of strings, like all binary strings containing exactly one 1. Hoyrup introduces a way to measure how much the positions must communicate while the string is being produced.

He captures that communication pattern as a simplicial complex, a geometric object whose faces record which groups of positions share information. The central problem becomes naming exactly which complexes can generate a given language. Hoyrup develops the theory step by step and tests it on a range of concrete languages. The results link a practical question about distributed production to combinatorial topology, the study of shapes built from simple pieces.
arxiv-2511-21326:
Sukanta Dutta estimates in 2025 how well an electron-proton collider could measure lepton flavour violation, a smoking gun for physics beyond the Standard Model. The Standard Model forbids an electron turning into a muon; many extensions allow it, rarely. Dutta studies the process where an electron-proton collision yields a muon plus a jet, described by dimension-six effective operators.

The analysis targets the Large Hadron-electron Collider at 1.3 teraelectronvolts, with data up to about one inverse attobarn. With operator coefficients set to one and a new-physics scale of 10 teraelectronvolts, signal cross sections land near a ten-thousandth of a picobarn, against a background of 0.27 picobarns from W-boson production. Dutta applies cut-based estimates and the optimal observables method, which extracts the most from kinematic distributions. He quantifies how polarising the electron beam sharpens the reach, mapping five-sigma discovery contours for coefficient pairs.
arxiv-2511-21526:
Alexandra Carpentier, Christophe Giraud, and Nicolas Verzelen close a gap in the theory of finding hidden communities in networks, in 2025. The stochastic block model plants groups of nodes with denser internal links, and the question is when an efficient algorithm can recover them. With few communities, the Kesten-Stigum threshold marks the exact cliff. With many communities, more than the square root of network size, recent work proposed a new, lower threshold.

Carpentier and her coauthors prove the conjecture from their own earlier paper. Above the proposed threshold, recovery succeeds in every density regime by counting carefully chosen motifs, small subgraph patterns with the right structure. Their earlier result showed low-degree polynomial methods fail below the threshold. Together, the two papers complete the map of where computation hits its barrier for community recovery in the many-communities regime, settling where feasible algorithms must stop.
arxiv-2511-21626:
Mathew Vanherreweghe, Michael Freedman, and Keith Adams find the same hidden geometry inside neural networks at every zoom level, in 2025. Freedman and Mulligan had shown that shallow networks trained on synthetic three-dimensional tasks spontaneously develop Kolmogorov–Arnold geometry, a textured pattern in how their internal functions organize, named for a 1957 representation theorem. Whether the pattern survives realistic, high-dimensional data was unknown.

Vanherreweghe and his coauthors extend the analysis to MNIST digit classification, 784-dimensional inputs handled by two-layer perceptrons. The geometry emerges during training and appears at every spatial scale examined, from local 7-pixel neighborhoods up to the full 28-by-28 image. It extends across the input space, even between well-separated pixels. Two training procedures produce the same qualitative pattern, one standard and one with spatial augmentation. The result suggests this organized structure is a general feature of how networks learn, not an artifact of toy problems.
arxiv-2511-21726:
Yicong Zheng and five coauthors argue that language models should search raw memory instead of compressing it, in 2025. Long-term memory systems usually squeeze past conversations into summaries, but compression loses information and bakes in designer bias. A fixed compressor cannot suit every kind of data.

Their system, SUMER, trains an agent with reinforcement learning to use search tools over uncompressed conversation history, gathering evidence before answering. Built on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SUMER was tested on LoCoMo, a benchmark for long-conversation understanding. It beat every compression-based rival and the full-context baseline, setting a new state of the art with a 43 percent gain over the previous best. The conclusion is pointed: nearly doubling judge-rated accuracy came from simple goal-directed search, not cleverer compression. Searching only for what the question needs preserves details that summaries throw away.
arxiv-2511-21826:
Azatov and colleagues propose a new way for the early universe to change phase, the way water turns to steam but for the vacuum of space itself. The universe may sit in a false vacuum, stable-looking because quantum tunnelling out of it is extremely slow. Their proposed mechanism involves boson stars, dense clumps of a lightweight field.

When such a dense star grows too heavy it collapses under its own weight. The collapse concentrates the field at its core past the barrier separating the false vacuum from the true one. If the true-vacuum region at the core grows larger than a critical bubble size, it expands and converts the surrounding space, triggering a full phase transition. Simulations confirmed the effect for small-radius bubbles. The point is unsettling: a vacuum stable against tunnelling could still be destroyed astrophysically.
arxiv-2511-22126:
Sette, a mathematician, adds a new construction to interpolation theory for metric spaces. Classical interpolation, developed by Peetre for normed spaces, builds intermediate spaces between two given ones, letting analysts transfer operator bounds from extremes to everything between. Extending that idea beyond linear spaces is delicate, and Sette's earlier work produced metric analogues of the classical K and J methods. The new J_M-prime method instead builds the interpolated space from approximating sequences inside the intersection of the two spaces.

Concretely, sequences in the intersection, measured with a J_M metric. Are completed relative to the union space, giving a well-defined interpolated metric space with controllable relationships between its J_M and K_M metrics. Lipschitz continuity of operators is preserved as expected. The author deliberately leaves comparisons with the earlier methods and with classical functors open, positioning the construction for nonlinear analysis and Wasserstein-type spaces.
arxiv-2511-22226:
Meulemans, Nasser, Wołczyk, and colleagues rebuild multi-agent learning theory around a simple embarrassment. Standard reinforcement learning treats the agent as separate from a stationary world. In a society of learners the world contains other agents modeling you while you model them. Their framework of embedded universal predictive intelligence makes Bayesian agents predict their actions alongside their perceptions, extending the AIXI theory of universal intelligence to agents embedded in the universe they inhabit.

Self-prediction, they show, lets agents reason about others running similar algorithms, producing new game-theoretic solution concepts and forms of cooperation unreachable by classical decoupled agents. Idealized agents starting from a Solomonoff prior can form consistent mutual predictions and achieve infinite-order theory of mind, each modeling the others modeling them without regress. They offer it as a gold standard for practical embedded multi-agent learning.
arxiv-2511-22726:
Friesen and colleagues hunt software's repeat offenders: methods that keep attracting bug fixes. Defining ExtremelyBuggy methods as those involved in more than one bug fix, they study over 1.25 million methods from 98 Java projects. These methods are a tiny fraction yet account for a disproportionate share of bugs.  From birth they are distinguishable: significantly larger, more complex, less readable, and less maintainable than singly-buggy or clean methods.

Distinguishable, however, is not predictable. Evaluating five machine learning models, the authors find early prediction of ExtremelyBuggy methods remains unreliable, defeated by class imbalance, project differences, and bugs emerging through later evolution rather than the original code. A manual analysis of 265 methods finds recurring smells, confusing control flow, fragile error handling, misused variables, and risky roles such as core logic and external resource handling. Evolution-aware code representations, they argue, are needed over static metrics.
arxiv-2511-22826:
Chen and colleagues ask: when sight, sound, and text disagree, which does a multimodal model believe? Today's multimodal models are trained almost entirely on data where all modalities agree, so their behaviour under contradiction is untested and potentially unsafe in robotics and medical diagnostics. They built MMA-Bench, videos and tasks deliberately misaligning audio-visual pairs or adding misleading text, with paired questions whose answers differ by modality.

Probing open and closed models with black-box and white-box techniques, they found current systems struggle badly under misaligned pairs and misleading text, taking shortcuts instead of reasoning across modalities. Their remedy is modality alignment tuning, teaching the model when to prioritise, leverage, or ignore specific modality cues. Across extensive experiments the tuned models showed stronger multimodal grounding. They offer both diagnostic tools and a training path toward models whose cross-modal reasoning can be trusted when channels conflict.
arxiv-2511-23226:
Barnoff and Bright attack a combinatorics puzzle dating to 1971. The puzzle asks how long a staircase path on the lattice, stepping only north or east, can run before some k of its points are forced onto a straight line. Theory guarantees collinear points eventually appear, but the known bounds are astronomically loose. So the thresholds are known only for tiny cases, four steps for three collinear points and 97 for six.

Encoding the search as a satisfiability problem, they enumerate every maximal avoiding path, up to symmetry, for all k up to six. This confirms the earlier thresholds and catalogues how many distinct longest paths exist in each case. For seven collinear points they found an avoiding path of 327 steps, beating the previous record of 260 steps set by Shallit. This pushes the threshold's lower bound to 328, though the exact value for seven remains open.
arxiv-2511-23326:
Qidan and colleagues design dynamic resource management for an indoor optical wireless network. Infrared lasers under eye-safety limits serve many users at once through non-orthogonal multiple access, stacking users' messages in the power domain. A blind interference alignment precoder coordinates the multiple optical access points, but grouping users well and splitting power fairly form a max-min fractional optimization that is notoriously hard to solve directly.

Their answer is two dynamic algorithms. One forms user groups with help from a radio-frequency side channel, where users exchange binary variables to build distance-based weights. The other allocates power optimally to each group afterward. In simulations the dynamic scheme converged to the optimum solution and beat counterpart schemes on sum rate, fairness between weak and strong users, and energy efficiency. It still guarantees each user's traffic demand regardless of channel strength.
arxiv-2511-23426:
Fraija and colleagues rebuild the standard model of gamma-ray burst afterglows by letting the microphysical parameters vary with time instead of holding them fixed. These parameters set how a relativistic shock splits its energy between accelerated particles and the magnetic field. And the team derives light curves and closure relations for synchrotron self-Compton emission from the external reverse shock in both uniform and stellar-wind surroundings in the analysis.

Covering thick-shell and thin-shell regimes, they show time-varying parameters can imitate the plateau phases seen in afterglows and produce decay slopes steeper than high-latitude emission alone allows. Directly changing how bursts get interpreted. Fitting the model with Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations to Fermi-LAT catalog bursts and the very-high-energy bursts 190114C and 221009A. They find uniform media favored for thick shells and wind profiles for thin shells, informing progenitor environments.
arxiv-2512-00126:
Protein inverse folding means designing an amino acid sequence that folds into a chosen three-dimensional shape. Jin Han, Tianfan Fu, and Wu-Jun Li present RadDiff for this problem in a 2025 study. The task is a basic step in computational protein engineering.

Existing methods either generate sequences without outside knowledge or lean on protein language models. RadDiff combines retrieval with a denoising diffusion process, pulling in helpful external information while it designs. Better inverse folding tools help researchers design new proteins for medicine and industry, from enzymes to candidate drugs. Retrieval brings proven sequence patterns into the design loop instead of starting from nothing. That habit mirrors how engineers reuse known parts.
arxiv-2512-00226:
Three-dimensional scene understanding is a key skill for AI assistants that operate in the real world. Zirui Wang and Tao Zhang present DenseScan in 2025, work aimed at richer data for that field. Current datasets give geometry and object instances but lack detailed semantic labels.

DenseScan advances scene understanding through dense two-dimensional annotation, adding the rich labels that visual-language tasks need. Better annotations let models connect words to parts of a scene, not just whole objects. Such data could improve robots and assistants that must describe, find, and manipulate things in cluttered rooms. Dense annotation is expensive, which is exactly why a dataset built around it stands out.
arxiv-2512-00326:
Loneliness harms student health, but surveys capture it only after the fact and only when students answer honestly. Qianjie Wu and co-authors predict university students' loneliness scores from smartphone sensing data in 2025. Passive sensing records behavioral signals continuously, without asking anything of the student.

The study looks for behavioral indicators of loneliness in that sensing data. Real-time behavioral context could catch rising loneliness earlier than retrospective self-reports. The work also raises care questions universities must handle well, since sensing data is intimate even when students consent to share it. Smartphone sensing is passive, so students are not asked to keep diaries or wear devices. Prediction, not just description, is the goal the authors set for the data.
arxiv-2512-00526:
Nearby cycles are a tool for studying how a family of geometric spaces degenerates. Pascal Boyer describes filtrations of the perverse sheaf of nearby cycles in the strict semi-stable situation in 2025. The filtrations come from the stratification of the special fiber.

Boyer determines which extensions given by these filtrations split and which do not. Such details control deep invariants in arithmetic geometry, including those behind the local Langlands program and Weil conjectures. The work is technical algebraic geometry, sharpening a machine that number theorists rely on to study degenerating families. Semi-stable reduction is the tame case of degeneration, which is why it is studied first. Perverse sheaves are the coefficient systems that make such filtrations meaningful.
arxiv-2512-00926:
Shulan Li, Jian-Pin Wu, and Xian-Hui Ge build a cosmology model without a beginning singularity in a 2025 paper. In the standard picture, the universe starts from a point of infinite density. Non-singular models try to avoid that breakdown, often by matching the cosmos to a regular black hole, one whose center stays finite.

Their model uses a modified Oppenheimer-Snyder framework, a classic way to join a collapsing or expanding interior to an outside spacetime. They study its dynamics with dust alone and with a scalar field added. They also compare it with two other non-singular models and with standard cosmology. Comparisons show which features are generic.
arxiv-2512-01126:
Jishnu Goswami and Frithjof Karsch compare lattice QCD calculations with collider data in a 2025 physics paper. Their subject is net-baryon number cumulants, measures of how the net count of baryons fluctuates in hot nuclear matter. Fluctuations can signal the change from hadrons to quark-gluon plasma.

The authors compute ratios of higher order cumulants along the pseudo-critical line, where that change occurs in theory. They compare them with STAR measurements from the RHIC beam energy scan program, taken along the freeze-out line where particles stop interacting. Early agreement for one key ratio is reported, with details across collision energies.
arxiv-2512-01226:
Faust, Robinson, and Sottile study graphs that repeat in a grid with no end. Each such graph has an operator, a rule that acts on waves over it. The waves form a shape called the Bloch variety. Points where that shape pinches are called critical points.

The count of those points is the focus here. That count is a step toward a big claim about spectral edges. Past work capped the count by a shape volume tied to the graph. The team shows the cap is not tight when some points drift far off. Their result sharpens how the count can be found.
arxiv-2512-01326:
Omar Farooq Khan Suri and John McCrae study attacks that hide bad orders in prompts. A prompt attack tricks a language model into doing a harmful task. The model just follows words, so sly words can bend it. Wide use of these models makes the risk real.

They review a defense called JATMO. It trains a plain base model to do one task only. A model locked to one task has less room to obey stray orders. The study weighs how well that lock works. It also notes what the lock costs in range and ease of use.
arxiv-2512-01426:
Yiyang Ma and co-authors improve high-resolution image making with diffusion models. Big pre-trained models often fail when asked for images larger than their training size. Layouts collapse and fine texture turns muddy. Past fixes stack complex steps to guide the large output.

The team's appendix text lays out a simpler path. It uses the base-size pass to guide the large pass in a lean way. Clean high-resolution output matters for art, ads, and design tools. A lean fix that keeps layout and texture would be easy for many teams to adopt.
arxiv-2512-02026:
Ultra-short pulse lasers can carve metal and glass with great care, a plus for greener factories. But a flawed part found too late wastes the work. Luis Correas-Naranjo and four co-authors use machine learning in 2025 to watch laser micromachining and catch bad parts early.

Their system is built to work no matter how the stock was prepared first, a common source of change on real shop floors. Early detection guards both the fine quality and the green case for the tool. The study ties learning methods to the daily craft of keeping a high-end process on track.
arxiv-2512-02326:
Some tools split a signal the way a prism splits light, but with math tuned to curves called orthogonal polynomials. Such tools are known as chromatic derivatives. Aleksandar Ignjatović returns in 2025 to his 2009 work on them. He grows it, and he fixes parts of it.

The tools rest on sets of curves that stay orthogonal under set weights. From them come ways to expand a signal and spaces where those expansions live. A clean record counts in this field, since later work builds on the printed forms. Chromatic tools give a second kit for signal work, shaped for uneven samples and curve-based tasks.
arxiv-2512-02626:
S. J. S. de Rooij and B. Hunyadi adapt seizure detection models so they can move between patients or datasets. Transfer learning reuses what a model learned on one task to do better on a related one. Their method uses a tensor kernel machine, a compact model suited to structured brain signal data.

The design borrows an idea from the adaptive support vector machine. Knowledge passes through regularization, which keeps the new model close to the old one where that helps. Efficient transfer matters in epilepsy care, where labeled data per patient is scarce and fast personalization can improve alarm accuracy. Small gains per case add up fast when a ward must screen many new cases each week of the year.
arxiv-2512-02726:
Md Abdul Kadir and three co-authors test language models as fraud hunters in accounting ledgers. Auditors run journal entry tests to flag odd records in tax related books. Rule based tests raise floods of false alarms and miss subtle irregularities.

The team's AuditCopilot investigates whether large language models can serve as anomaly detectors for double entry bookkeeping. A model that reads entries in context might catch patterns rules miss. Smarter screening could focus human auditors on the riskiest records, cutting cost while raising the chance of catching real fraud early. Fewer false alarms means staff time goes to the books that hide real risk, not to noise in the logs.
arxiv-2512-03026:
Saeid Jamshidi and four co-authors propose continuous ethical checking for large language models. Moral consistency means keeping ethically coherent reasoning across varied contexts. Existing alignment frameworks use static datasets and after the fact evaluations, which reveal little about how reasoning evolves.

Ethical behavior can drift as contexts change or time passes, and one time tests miss that drift. The Moral Consistency Pipeline evaluates models continuously instead. Ongoing checks suit deployed systems in support, education, and advice roles, where a slow ethical slide could harm users before anyone notices. Checks that run all the time catch the slow slip. One big test, run once at launch, will miss it by the time the harm shows in use by real folks.
arxiv-2512-03226:
How galaxies move apart from smooth expansion shows gravity at work. C. E. Ross and a large team present a catalog for that study in this 2025 work. It is part of the DESI first data release peculiar velocity survey.

The catalog uses the Fundamental Plane, a relation among galaxy size, brightness, and internal speeds. It covers nearby galaxies with redshifts below a tenth. The authors call it the largest single set of its kind. Such data help measure how fast cosmic structures grow and test dark energy at low redshift. Peculiar velocity data from the plane add an independent route to galaxy distances.
arxiv-2512-03826:
X-ray spectroscopy in a laboratory, rather than at a giant synchrotron, needs instruments that are precise and flexible at once. Simone Manti and colleagues describe upgrades to the VOXES spectrometer in a 2025 applied physics preprint. The instrument, built at the Frascati national laboratories in Italy, uses curved mosaic crystals in a Von Hamos arrangement to study samples with X-ray emission and absorption.

Recent work added an energy-dispersive fluorescence line built around a silicon pin-diode sensor, enabling flux monitoring and simultaneous measurements in both modes. A dedicated holder for liquid samples joined the setup. A Y-shaped support makes the spectrometer ready for a transmission layout, bringing laboratory absorption studies within reach. The authors argue these upgrades widen what the table-top platform can do. Automation and versatility both improve, strengthening its role for high-resolution spectroscopy on extended and dilute samples.
arxiv-2512-03926:
Software verification tools face a trade-off. Push quantifier reasoning hard and proofs finish more often but slowly. Hold back and the tool stays fast but demands more human hints. Alexander Y. Bai, Chris Hawblitzel, and Andrea Lattuada give developers a dial for that trade-off in a 2025 preprint.

Their mechanism controls which quantified facts are available inside each verification context, down to the level of a module, a function, or a single proof. Library authors can ship preset automation levels, and users can adjust them further for local needs. The team implemented the idea in Verus, a Rust-based verifier, and tested it on several open codebases. The experiments chart the automation-versus-performance curve directly. Selective quantifier management, they show, lets developers pick the right level of automation for each part of a system instead of accepting one global compromise.
arxiv-2512-04026:
Markov numbers appear in solutions to a famous Diophantine equation and have fascinated number theorists for a century. Esther Banaian studies a generalised family, the k-Markov numbers, in a 2025 number theory preprint. Setting the parameter k to zero recovers the classical numbers, while positive values deform the defining equation and generate new sequences.

A central mystery is the unicity conjecture, which says every Markov number is the largest entry of exactly one solution triple. It remains open, but Aigner proposed weaker statements, proved using cluster algebra methods. Banaian shows the same weaker conjectures hold across the whole generalised family, for every k. The proof extends the cluster-algebraic techniques that settled the classical case. The result tightens the analogy between ordinary and generalised Markov numbers, while full unicity stays out of reach.
arxiv-2512-04126:
A grainy infrared clip from 2024, appearing to show a missile striking a glowing orb and bouncing off, spread widely online. Mauricio Barbi gives the footage a physicist's audit in a 2025 preprint on popular physics. Working with classical mechanics, fluid dynamics, and the geometry of the imaging system, he asks what the video can and cannot support.

Barbi examines momentum transfer, how the debris behaves, and the optical distortions a gimballed camera can invent. A balloon-like object, he concludes, remains the most conservative explanation, fully compatible with known physics. He is careful in both directions: modern physics is admittedly incomplete, so anomalies should not be dismissed as impossible on principle. But extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence, and this single unverified video, lacking calibrated multi-sensor data, does not supply it. The paper models how to hold both thoughts at once.
arxiv-2512-04226:
Matrix multiplication kernels live or die by their tuning parameters, and the usual way to find good ones is expensive trial and error. Ryan Swann and a large team offer an analytical alternative in a 2025 preprint on GPU computing. Their tritonBLAS model predicts near-optimal configurations from first principles, with no runtime autotuning at all.

The model reasons explicitly about cache hierarchy, the placement of code and data, matrix shapes, and algorithmic blocking behaviour. On top of it, the authors built a lightweight matrix multiplication framework entirely within Triton. Across a diverse set of problem sizes on modern GPUs, tritonBLAS matched over ninety-five percent of autotuned performance. The tuning time, meanwhile, dropped to zero. The authors pitch it as a ready substitute for empirical tuning in production computing and machine learning, where deterministic behaviour is worth real money.
arxiv-2512-04326:
Sebastián Espinosa, Rene Mendez, Jorge Silva, and Marcos Orchard review how well astronomers can pin down the place and brightness of a point of light in the sky. Such measures drive star positions, motions, and fluxes across modern astronomy. Early practice used rough centering rules of thumb. Newer work builds exact chance models at the level of single pixels. Their 2025 review traces that shift and weighs its payoff.

The review gathers the key works that set hard limits on accuracy, such as the Cramér-Rao bound. It also grades the estimators in daily use, from maximum likelihood to least squares and its weighted form. The bound proves reachable only in certain signal ranges, and real tools drift from it elsewhere. By mapping where each tool stands, the review gives observers a clear guide for squeezing the most from array detectors.
arxiv-2512-04526:
D. Y. Zhong and G. Q. Wang recast the study of dissipative nonlinear waves in the language of contact geometry. Their test case is the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, a standard model for systems that gain and lose energy as patterns form. Contact geometry tracks quantities that plain Hamiltonian tools cannot hold when friction enters. Their 2025 arXiv paper stretches a least-constraint theorem to complex fields and ties it to probability measures.

From that frame, a dissipative Hamilton-Jacobi equation governs how the action functional evolves. Classic transforms and a traveling-wave view then yield exact solutions built from elliptic functions. The solutions slide from periodic wave trains, called periodons, to lone solitons. A universal switching line splits the regimes, and the change between them is a first-order transition with hysteresis. The conserved contact potential emerges as the key quantity steering pattern choice in lossy media.
arxiv-2512-05026:
Pat Lank and Fei Peng prove a generation result in algebraic geometry for a broad class of spaces called stacks. They work in positive characteristic — the arithmetic setting where a prime number counts as zero. Their central tool is the Frobenius map, which raises quantities to a prime power. They ask whether pushing sheaves forward along that map, again and again, produces enough building blocks to assemble every well-behaved sheaf.

The authors first set up a notion of F-finiteness suited to stacks, then show that for a wide family of them, enough Frobenius pushforwards generate the full derived category of coherent sheaves. The theorem generalizes an earlier result by several other authors for simpler spaces and, along the way, recovers it by an independent route. Results of this kind underpin how geometers break complicated spaces into understandable pieces.
arxiv-2512-05426:
Andrei Stan presents two abstract methods for trapping the solution of a fixed point equation between a lower and an upper solution. The method of lower and upper solutions is a classic existence strategy: trap a solution between two ordered guesses and let the ordering do the rest. Stan's part is to state the machinery in abstract form, covering cases beyond the differential equations where the technique is usually taught.

The first method works when the nonlinear operator splits into a linear map composed with a nonlinear one. The second applies when the operator obeys an inequality of Harnack type, a comparison principle borrowed from the theory of positive solutions. An example goes with each method, showing the abstract conditions at work. For analysts, the paper packages two existence arguments into reusable form, ready to be checked rather than rebuilt for each new equation.
arxiv-2512-05526:
Michele Caprio, Shireen Manchingal, and Fabio Cuzzolin teach classifiers to say how unsure they are — and to refuse when unsure enough. Their two methods represent a prediction not as one probability distribution but as a set of them, or an interval of evidential distributions. That separates the uncertainty that more data could cure from the randomness that nothing cures. Trained with ordinary backpropagation and a loss drawn from evidence theory, the models avoid overfitting their training data by construction.

When either kind of uncertainty passes a threshold, the classifier abstains and flags the reason; within bounds, it returns a set of labels with robust guarantees. Across image benchmarks and their shifted counterparts, the methods match competitive accuracy, detect out-of-distribution inputs at state-of-the-art levels, and give tight prediction regions that widen reliably as inputs drift. A small ensemble, they show, already stabilizes the estimates.
arxiv-2512-05626:
Farhana Farooq and Danish Rafiq work on speeding up simulations of power grid networks. Modern grids are so large that the math behind stability studies has very many dimensions. Full simulations after a fault are slow and heavy. The usual fix shrinks the model by projecting it onto a flat, linear set of directions. But the swinging motion of generators is strongly curved, so flat approximations compress poorly and can miss what matters during fast faults.

Their 2025 paper builds the reduced model on a quadratic manifold instead. A standard linear basis from proper orthogonal decomposition is kept, and a learned quadratic correction is added to cut the rebuilding error. The team tests the method on benchmark grid models of growing size and complexity. They also give the full numerical recipe for building such a manifold, with code. Faster faithful models mean more stability checks can be run.
arxiv-2512-05926:
Wenyan Luo and Dustin Mixon bring optimal transport to a fairness flavored clustering problem. Ordinary k-means splits data into groups of whatever sizes the geometry dictates. Balanced k-means insists the groups come out even, a demand that arises in load balancing, fair assignment, and experimental design. Their algorithm, BalLOT, alternates steps, solving each assignment as an optimal transport problem under the balance constraint.

Theory comes first. For generic data, each step of the algorithm yields whole, integral assignments rather than fractional smears. A landscape analysis shows when it recovers planted clusters, exactly or partially, under a random ball model. The authors also give initialization schemes that recover the planted clusters in a single step. Numerical experiments line up with the theorems. A transport based method with proofs turns a practical chore into understood machinery.
arxiv-2512-06126:
A. Bocchieri, J. Zak, and D. Turrini release ExoNAMD, a tool for grading how dynamically stirred up a planetary system is, using a clue observers increasingly measure: the tilt between a planet's orbit and its star's spin. Multiplanetary systems are natural laboratories. Their excitation records past collisions and scattering. The angular momentum deficit compresses excitation into one number.

The advance is folding the spin orbit angle itself into the metric. The angle aware version describes the state better than relative tilts alone. With PLATO and Roman about to multiply the census, target choice matters. A fast, principled ranking of dynamical histories helps aim those instruments. Ranking histories is triage for the coming flood.
arxiv-2512-06726:
Shuo Li and eleven co authors study entropy, a measure of a model's uncertainty, in the task of pointing at what a phrase describes in an image. Multimodal models fine tuned with reinforcement learning have gained from tricks that control entropy in reasoning tasks. Whether the same holds for perception tasks like visual grounding, and how entropy behaves there, was largely unexplored.

The team first maps how entropy acts during grounding, set against its role in reasoning. Grounding rewards being sure about one spot; reasoning rewards keeping options open longer. From that contrast they build ECVGPO, an algorithm that regulates entropy openly, balancing exploration against commitment in a way a user can read. Across several benchmarks and model families the method improved grounding scores broadly. The work gives perception training a control knob that reasoning research had already learned to use.
arxiv-2512-06926:
Salma Albelali and Moataz Ahmed test how fragile a popular forecasting model is when its input data changes shape or quality. Their model, a bidirectional LSTM, reads sequences both forward and backward to predict what comes next in a time series. The authors vary two things in controlled experiments: how long each input sequence runs, and how much random noise is mixed in.

Three real-world data sets, sampled at different rates, run through a clean, repeatable pipeline the team built. Longer sequences raised the risk of the model memorizing its training data and of information leaking across splits. Noise dragged accuracy down at every sampling rate. Together, the two problems hurt stability most of all. Faster-sampled data resisted better yet still failed when both struck. The lesson is that data choices, not just model design, decide whether forecasts can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-07026:
Sergii Voloshyn solves a model used to mimic the hot, dense heart of quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons. The model centers on the Polyakov loop, a quantity that signals whether quarks are confined or free. Voloshyn's version keeps the exact contribution of static quarks, at finite temperature and with an imbalance between matter and antimatter. In a limit where the numbers of colors and flavors both grow large together.

In that limit a mean-field treatment becomes exact, and the model collapses to a deformed matrix model that can be solved on paper. Voloshyn computes the free energy and its derivatives, the loop's expected value, and the density of baryons, then maps the phase diagram in detail. The three-phase pattern known from one-dimensional studies survives at nonzero coupling, with clear differences from the simpler symmetry case treated before.
arxiv-2512-07926:
Arvind Agarwal, Lisa Amini, Sameep Mehta, Horst Samulowitz, and Kavitha Srinivas wrote this 2025 position paper on enterprise data. Running a company's data estate is a monumental, many-layered job. Architecture, integration, quality, and governance each demand constant care.

AI assistants today help individual roles with slices of that stack. Engineers and stewards use them to navigate and configure single components. Full automation of the whole estate remains far beyond that piecemeal help. The authors argue the moment for a paradigm shift has arrived. Agents should manage the entire data lifecycle, not isolated operations. Stage by stage, they examine how the modern stack could run itself. The end users of such estates would include AI systems themselves. Mounting pressures and fresh capabilities both push toward that future. Open questions and research gaps are flagged honestly throughout. The paper aims to spark debate and joint work, not to declare victory.
arxiv-2512-09226:
Cosmas Kravaris writes a pure mathematics paper about the geometry of the symmetric group, the group of all rearrangements of n objects. He studies its Cayley graph, the network built from two chosen moves: one long cycle through all the objects and one swap of the first two. The question is how faithfully that network can be placed inside a simple distance space called L1.

Kravaris shows the placement can be done with bounded distortion, answering a question posed by Ostrovskii. Combined with an earlier theorem of Kassabov, this gives the first family of groups that embeds nicely into L1 for one small generating set but not for another. One consequence is that these graphs cannot hide expander networks inside them. They also serve as new test cases in the Ribe program, which links the geometry of groups with the behavior of functions on them.
arxiv-2512-09726:
Paweł Lisiak, Maciej Łebek, and Miłosz Panfil study how density spreads in a gas of particles that touches a much larger reservoir. For weakly coupled integrable systems, the usual answer is plain diffusion. The authors show that the picture changes when motion is studied on top of long lived states that are not thermal. For states that are not symmetric under a flip of direction, a different equation takes over.

That equation is the Burgers equation, a standard model of flow with a nonlinear push. The authors compute its diffusion constant and its advective coefficient using a variant of a classic approximation method. Their formulas agree well with computer simulations of a simplified model of random two body collisions. The result rests only on a few broad assumptions, such as Galilean invariance and weak coupling between the gas and the reservoir.
arxiv-2512-10126:
S. Shajidul Haque, Ghadir Jafari, and Bret Underwood ask what is truly quantum about the seeds of cosmic structure. Perturbations from inflation, the universe's early expansion, carry striking quantum features: entanglement and enormous circuit complexity. Yet every observation so far matches what classic random variables would produce. The authors measure the gap using quantum magic, a resource measure tied to Wigner negativity. Magic is what a quantum state needs to be hard to mimic with classical machines and useful for universal quantum computation.

They show inflationary perturbations are continuous variable stabilizer states with no magic. Despite their quantum origin, they can be run fast by classic algorithms. Any magic from primordial non Gaussianity is suppressed twice: by the small nonlinearity of the early universe and by the extreme squeezing of the perturbations themselves. The picture that emerges is a high complexity, low magic regime.
arxiv-2512-10226:
Shuhan Tan leads a team teaching self driving cars to reason in a latent language instead of English. Vision language action models often explain themselves in words before acting, but text is a clumsy medium for driving futures. Their model, LCDrive, reasons by interleaving two kinds of tokens. Action proposal tokens use the same vocabulary as the driving commands themselves. World model tokens, grounded in a learned latent world model, express what would happen if an action were taken. Thinking and deciding thus share one action aligned space.

Training starts cold, supervised by real future rollouts of each scene, so proposals and predicted outcomes learn from ground truth. Closed loop reinforcement learning then strengthens the reasoning interactively. On a large end to end driving benchmark, the latent reasoner inferred faster, drove better trajectories, and gained more from reinforcement learning than both silent and text reasoning baselines.
arxiv-2512-10426:
N Mangala and co-authors design a privacy-protecting layout for healthcare systems that mix bedside devices, edge computers, and the cloud. Wearables and connected medical devices now feed remote monitoring and emergency care, but the data is deeply personal. And fast response in a crisis cannot come at the cost of leaking it.

Their design spreads tasks across device, edge, and cloud layers by how urgent and lasting each job is. Differential privacy noise is added inside several learning models, and a hybrid noise scheme with an adaptive budget gave the best balance between accuracy and protection. While blockchain records keep the traffic traceable and tamper-proof. Edge handling cut emergency delays sharply, and inference and rebuilding attacks became measurably harder.
arxiv-2512-10526:
Nils Siemonsen and William East follow an instability that strikes spinning objects with an ergoregion but no horizon. Such spacetimes are known to be linearly unstable, yet what happens once the growth turns nonlinear was largely unexplored. The authors evolve a massless vector field on a rapidly spinning boson star in full general relativity to find out.

The instability feeds on itself: backreaction makes the star more tightly bound, which speeds the growth, until a black hole forms. Along the way, fine features develop and nonlinear gravity drives a direct turbulent cascade in both the unstable mode and the emitted radiation. The gravitational wave signal comes in bursts of rising strength, resembling the echoes discussed in other contexts, right up to the collapse. The study gives the first full picture of how this instability ends.
arxiv-2512-10726:
Jonah Nagura, Mykyta Onizhuk, and Giulia Galli explain why diamond quantum sensors go deaf near the surface. Nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond are superb nanoscale sensors, but the closer one sits to the surface, the faster surface noise, both magnetic and electric, scrambles its quantum state. Where that noise comes from, and exactly how it bites, had stayed murky.

The team combined atomistic surface models built with density functional theory and decoherence calculations by cluster correlation expansion. They mapped how the echo lifetime depends on crystal orientation, surface treatment, and the density of unpaired surface electrons, and found the depth where surface effects stop mattering. A key ratio, sensor depth against the spacing of surface electrons, governs whether the noise flickers fast or sits quasi-static. Only when surface spins were allowed to hop along the surface did the calculations match measured lifetimes.
arxiv-2512-11426:
Shuowei Cai, Yansong Ning, and Hao Liu design multi agent language model systems that respect real budgets for cost and response time. Such systems now power web search, social analytics, and customer support, where expense decides whether deployment is practical. Prior work shaped communication patterns or picked models in isolation, rarely optimising under explicit token and latency limits, and often designed the wiring before choosing the models.

Their AgentBalance framework reverses that order: backbones first, topology second. It builds a pool of candidate models, selects from it, and matches roles to suitable backbones, creating a deliberately mixed team. Then it learns agent representations and synthesises a communication topology that accounts for latency. Across benchmarks with fourteen candidate backbones, the method gained clear performance under matched budgets and produced strong trade off curves. It also plugs into existing systems and generalises to models it never saw during design.
arxiv-2512-11526:
Joel Ekstrand, Zahra Taghiyarrenani, and Slawomir Nowaczyk teach forecasting models to treat anomalies with care: some shocks change the future and must be heeded, while others are blips to ignore. Standard forecasters cannot tell the difference, so they either chase noise or sleep through real shifts. Their setup, Co-TSFA, learns the distinction through contrastive training.

Two kinds of added data manufacture cases: changes confined to the input, modelling irrelevant shocks, and changes carried into the output, modelling relevant ones. A latent alignment loss ties how much the internal picture moves to how much the forecast moves, enforcing calm under irrelevant disturbance, and a readiness to react to real change. Tests on traffic and electricity benchmarks plus a real cash demand data set bettered forecasting under anomalous settings without sacrificing scores on normal data. Code is provided for release.
arxiv-2512-11626:
Leonardo García-Heveling studies a fresh way to tell time in cosmology. The cosmic volume function marks time by the volume of space up to each event, as a swap for the older cosmic time function. A useful time label must vary smoothly, or the math built on it breaks.

García-Heveling proves that in many cases of interest the volume function is smooth in the needed sense, with a steady first derivative. That fact splits the space time metric into clean space and time parts. It also yields a matched Riemannian metric by a Wick rotation trick. Extra results and cases round out the picture for both the time and volume functions.
arxiv-2512-11826:
Weihong Xu and co-authors built FSL-HDnn, a silicon chip that learns new classes from a few examples right on the device. Edge gadgets often cannot phone home for training, and normal learning chips burn too much power. Their chip, made in a 40 nanometer process, joins feature extraction and few shot learning in one pipeline.

A weight clustering trick shrinks the feature extractor. The classifier uses hyperdimensional computing, which learns in a single pass with no gradient steps. Early exit and batched training boost speed further. On a 10 way, 5 shot task the chip used 6 millijoules per image and trained at 28 images per second. Training lag fell by 2 to 20.9 times versus rival chips.
arxiv-2512-12326:
J Alexander Curtis and Nasir U Eisty review how AI is changing penetration testing in a 2025 paper. Penetration testing probes a system's defenses by acting like an attacker, and the work is slow and manual. The authors survey 58 peer-reviewed studies from major academic databases.

Reinforcement learning led the field, as the focus of 77 percent of the works. Most studies target finding and exploiting flaws, where AI can automate repeat tasks and sharpen attack plans. Real tools include the European Space Agency's PenBox. Gaps remain in recon and post-exploitation phases, and large language model uses are still little studied, marking a clear path for future work.
arxiv-2512-12826:
Matei Drilea and co-authors study beams made by 3D printing with continuous carbon fiber inside them. Carbon fiber is strong, and it also changes its electrical response when bent. That dual role lets a beam act as both a structure and its own strain sensor.

The team shows that a large bending load applied first can raise the sensor response for good. They link the gain to small local breaks in the fibers. They also print a conductive filament around the fibers, which cuts noise and improves the contact. Together, the two steps point to printed parts that can sense load with high sensitivity.
arxiv-2512-13026:
I. A. Seit-Dzhelil and A. Yu. Shvets study a non-ideal system that couples a tank of liquid with an electric motor. Non-ideal here means the motor's power limits feed back on the motion, so the liquid and the drive shape each other. Delays in that feedback are their focus.

They consider two models that approximate the delay and ask how it changes the system's limit sets, the patterns motion settles into. They compute the main traits of steady regimes, both regular and chaotic. They also trace how orderly motion gives way to chaos. A route called generalized intermittency, driven by the delay, is shown to occur in this system.
arxiv-2512-13526:
Asa Cooper Stickland and co-authors stress-test delayed monitoring for AI coding agents. Such agents work on real code, at times with access to private data or security-critical files. A delayed monitor reviews acts after the fact, adding no runtime lag, but must still catch sabotage before harm is fixed in place.

The team frames monitor design as a game between a blue team that builds monitors and a red team that builds sabotaging agents. They built five software settings based on work inside an AI firm. Their combined monitor reached a 6% false negative rate at a 1% false positive rate on a held-out test setting. They then model how that rate maps to risk at deployment.
arxiv-2512-13626:
Dev Prakash Jha and Raju K. George study control of heat-like equations that carry memory of the past. To stop such a system for good, both the state and the stored memory must reach zero at the end time. If memory remains, the motion can restart after control stops.

They assume the memory kernel is a finite sum of exponentials, which lets them rewrite the problem as a coupled parabolic and ordinary system. They define a Memory Geometric Control Condition: the moving control region must visit every point in space. Under that term, they prove an observability bound and gain null controllability. They also note why a full necessity proof stays out of reach with memory effects.
arxiv-2512-13826:
Dylan Bissuel and a large team present a reproducible container solution for materials science codes and workflows. Computational materials work needs software environments that others can rebuild exactly. Their approach pairs the GNU Guix package manager with the Apptainer container system for fully declarative, reproducible setups.

The system can host complete frameworks with workflow managers such as AiiDA and Ewoks, deployed on clusters. Examples include AiiDA workflows for making data sets and path-integral molecular dynamics from ab initio runs. Other cases cover training machine-learning interatomic potentials and Ewoks analysis of X-ray diffraction data at synchrotrons. The authors present the environment as a reliable base for data-driven materials research.
arxiv-2512-14026:
Yibing Fu and co-authors present CITab, a self-supervised framework that learns from medical images and tabular data across different cohorts. Combining scans with tables has helped clinical decision-making, and self-supervised pretraining can use large unlabeled data sets. Past methods were often limited to one cohort because their tabular modeling was too rigid for varied table structures.

CITab uses column headers as semantic cues, so knowledge can transfer across tables with different columns. A prototype-guided mixture-of-linear module specializes tabular features and handles that variety. Tests on Alzheimer's disease diagnosis covered three public cohorts with 4,461 subjects in total. CITab beat state-of-the-art approaches, supporting scalable cross-tabular multimodal learning for medicine.
arxiv-2512-14526:
Debendra Meher, Nikhil Avula, and Sundaram Balasubramanian chase a long-missing computer model of boron oxide glass. Experiments say much of the glass is built from six-membered boroxol rings, yet ordinary simulations rarely form enough of them. The team trained a machine-learned atomic potential to near quantum accuracy and cooled the virtual melt unusually slowly.

Slow cooling pushed more than thirty percent of boron atoms into rings. One technical choice proved decisive: the network describing each atom's surroundings needed a wide enough view, or pressure and ring counts went wrong. The lowest-energy glasses sat near seventy-five percent rings, close to what experiments suggest for the real material.
arxiv-2512-14726:
Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from pre-collected data, with no live interaction with the environment. Decision transformers brought sequence modeling to that task, but they struggle with long-horizon credit assignment and complex links between states and actions.

The quantum decision transformer, QDT, answers with an architecture that adds quantum-inspired mechanisms, drawing on entanglement and interference as computational motifs. The synergy is meant to represent long-range dependencies more richly than a plain transformer can. If it performs as hoped, offline agents could learn better policies from fixed logs in settings like robotics, games, and operations.
arxiv-2512-14826:
Stephan Foldes and Russ Woodroofe prove a neat result about lattices, the ordered grids of math where elements can be joined and met. They work with lattices that carry a rank graded by a bounded span of real numbers. An antichain cutset is a set of pairwise unranked elements that every path from bottom to top must cross.

Their theorem says any such cutset is a level set, a slice at one height, for a grading built to fit it. The result holds in the rank supersolvable case they study. It then applies to three classic settings: the measurable Boolean lattice, the continuous partition lattice, and continuous projective geometry. In each, a fresh grading can be chosen so the cutset sits exactly on one level.
arxiv-2512-14926:
George-Andrei Dima and two coauthors work to close a language gap in AI that can see and talk. Their focus is Romanian, a language with few multimodal training resources. Progress in such languages is a step toward making generative AI useful to more of the world.

The team translated the Flickr30K image dataset into Romanian and extended it for visual question answering with help from open language models. They then fine tuned vision language models from three families, LLaMA 3.2, LLaVA 1.6, and Qwen2, using the efficient LoRA method. The tuned models answered Romanian questions about images better and even improved at tasks they were not trained on, like writing Romanian captions. The best, a seven billion parameter Qwen2 model, gained 2.29 percent on question answering and 4.45 percent on captioning, and made far fewer grammar errors.
arxiv-2512-15126:
Yupeng Zhu and three coauthors animate a single still image into controllable 3D motion, without a full 3D production pipeline. Classic 3D animation is slow, expert, and costly. Recent AI tools either keep those costs or switch to video synthesis, which gives up true 3D control and interaction.

Their system, 3DProxyImg, splits the job in two. A coarse 3D estimate acts as a structural carrier that handles geometry and motion control. Learned image space priors then supply fine appearance and new views. This 2D-3D aligned proxy gives control close to classical pipelines, with no need for exact geometry or heavy optimization, and it extends to background animation. In tests it ran on low power platforms and beat video based methods on identity preservation, consistency, and precise interactive control.
arxiv-2512-15426:
Cecilia Cavaterra and co authors prove solutions exist for a relaxed tumor growth model in a 2025 math paper. The model pairs a Cahn Hilliard equation, which tracks how tumor and healthy phases separate, with a nutrient equation. Its mobility degenerates and its potential is singular, which makes the math delicate.

The system also includes terms for cell growth, nutrient use, and chemotaxis, the pull of cells toward chemical signals. The authors add an elliptic regularization set by a parameter delta and prove a weak solution exists for the relaxed system. Letting delta go to zero then gives a weak solution for the original tumor model.
arxiv-2512-16026:
L C Gonzalez-Morales, I Perez Castillo, and J I Jimenez-Aquino study heat and disorder in a physics paper posted on arXiv during 2025. Their system is a charged particle jittering in a fluid, held by a spring-like trap, and pushed by crossing electric and magnetic fields. The fluid has memory, so friction arrives with a delay, described by a generalized Langevin equation.

Solving the motion exactly, the authors compute how the particle's position and velocity spread over time. From that they derive the entropy produced along each random path. For two driving setups, a direct time-varying force and a dragged trap center, they prove the entropy obeys a detailed fluctuation theorem. Such theorems link tiny random events to the second law of thermodynamics.
arxiv-2512-16426:
Andrey I Bondarev recalculates atomic fingerprints in an arXiv paper posted in 2025. The hyperfine structure of an atom's spectrum, tiny splittings from the nucleus's magnetism, is summarized by constants called A. For singly ionized thulium, early measurements clashed with theory, and newer experiments showed two of the old measured values were simply wrong.

Bondarev computes the A constants for several low-lying levels of Tm II using the configuration interaction method, with random-phase corrections included. His results agree well with the corrected experimental data. He also predicts values for states that have never been measured, giving spectroscopists targets to test. Reliable hyperfine data for thulium matter for atomic physics and for reading the element's lines in stellar spectra.
arxiv-2512-16726:
Alexandru Ciobanu and coauthors find a way to lower the interaction order in hard search problems such as 3-SAT, where each rule links three choices at once. In physics terms the task is to find the lowest energy state of a spin system with three-way links.

Past fixes cut the order by adding extra units, but those units slow the search badly at scale. The new route uses renormalization ideas to build a two-way system that keeps the same free energy. The extra units act freely once the main ones are fixed, so they can be traced out step by step. The team shows the ground state hunt then costs the same as in the raw form.
arxiv-2512-16826:
Arslan Amin and coauthors test YOLOv8 models for reading license plates, a core task for traffic systems and vehicle watch tools. Past methods often miss real-time accuracy when scenes vary in light, angle, and plate style.

Two data sets covered plate finding and character reading. YOLOv8 Nano hit 0.964 precision and 0.918 mAP50 on plate finding, while YOLOv8 Small hit 0.92 precision and 0.91 mAP50 on characters. A custom step orders found characters by their sideways position to form the plate string. The paired pipeline, Nano for plates and Small for characters, keeps compute low, suiting edge devices in smart traffic setups.
arxiv-2512-16926:
Oren Bell and coauthors address scheduling for ROS 2, the robot software frame, on a single processor. Real robot apps form branching task graphs, not simple chains, and past scheduling work leaned on chain models with ad hoc timing math.

The team shows ROS 2 apps can be viewed as forests of trees, mapping them to classic real-time DAG task models. Using the events executor with a custom queue and LIFO message delivery, they run fixed-priority and EDF schedulers for full graphs. The setup yields the same schedules as a standard DAG scheduler, even without direct access to precedence data. That match closes a gap between scheduling theory and ROS 2 practice.
arxiv-2512-17026:
Óscar Carrión-González, Sylvestre Lacour, and Mathias Nowak propose adding a fifth 8-meter telescope, UT5, to the Very Large Telescope Interferometer in Chile. The white paper targets exoplanets seen in reflected starlight, a hard direct-imaging prize.

UT5 would add four new baselines of about 200 meters aimed northwest. Longer baselines shrink the inner working angle and sharpen contrast, the two traits that decide whether a mature planet can be split from its star glare. The authors frame the upgrade as an optimization of the whole array for planet hunting, offered to the ESO Expanding Horizons call for 2040s astronomy.
arxiv-2512-17626:
Tijn De Wringer and three co-authors cut the wait for peering inside an exoplanet from days to minutes. Guessing a planet's core and mantle from its mass and size means running a slow physics model thousands of times inside a Bayesian search. That cost has kept interior studies one planet at a time.

Their stand-in model, a blend called polynomial chaos-Kriging, learns the physics model's behavior from just a few hundred runs, then answers in its place inside the search loop. The swap speeds inference about 320-fold, and the stand-in tracks the true model with R-squared above 0.99 in most cases. A check on 1,000 fake planets confirmed the error bars stay honest. Population-wide interior surveys are now within reach.
arxiv-2512-18526:
Leonardo Bohac studies what can be learned from a quantum memory you may read but never touch directly. The interface is U-QRAM, a fixed interaction that performs coherent random-access reads against a truth-table basis. The memory may sit in any state, even one entangled with a hidden reference. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, proves a sharp limit on such read-only access.

For any protocol with finitely many reads, however clever the steps between them, the accessible output depends on the memory only through its diagonal in the truth-table basis. Coherences between truth tables are simply invisible. Every test of memory hypotheses thus reduces to standard state discrimination, governed by Helstrom theory. Three examples illustrate the result, including one with best possible success of three quarters.
arxiv-2512-19026:
Connor Kilrain and five co-authors propose a sharper test for image generators that personalize output to one subject, such as a pet. Most scores reward overall likeness and miss small identity marks, like a spot on the head. Their protocol, Finer-Personalization Rank, scores identity as a retrieval task instead.

Each generated image is used as a query against a gallery of similar real photos labeled by identity. Strong scores mean the fine details survived generation. Tests span bird species, car models, and animal re-identification sets. The protocol caught identity drift in popular methods that looser scores missed, giving builders a stricter check.
arxiv-2512-19226:
Shubham Dey and Sean Raymond test whether the seven planets of TRAPPIST-1 could keep moons. The system packs its planets tightly, so each planet's gravity well is squeezed by its neighbors. N-body simulations follow test moons around each planet, from the Roche limit outward toward the prograde stability edge.

Moons stayed stable out to about forty to forty-five percent of the Hill radius for every planet. Neighbor pulls were weak alone but shrank the stable zone together, most for the innermost and middle planets they name. Simple tidal decay math then caps the largest moon that could survive for billions of years at a tiny fraction of Earth's mass.
arxiv-2512-19326:
Philipp Schneider and Julian Werthmann compare two distributed computing models that shard a graph across many machines. In massively parallel computation, machines hold pieces of the input with small memory each. In the node-capacitated clique, every graph node is a machine that knows its neighbors but may trade only a few words per round.

The strongly sublinear memory regime had no known simulation results between the models. The authors give techniques that simulate one in the other with only constant round overhead, under set restrictions. They also prove impossibility results for other settings, showing the limits are real, not a lack of cleverness. Parameter ranges, problem families, and graph classes all matter.
arxiv-2512-19526:
Li Puyin, Tiange Xiang, Ella Mao, and Shirley Wei built QuantiPhy, a benchmark that asks vision-language models for numbers, not adjectives. A general agent must judge size, speed, and acceleration from video, yet most tests grade only wordy plausibility. More than three thousand video-text cases carry exact numerical ground truth.

Each task hands the model one true property as a prior and asks it to estimate another at a set moment, under standard prompts and scoring. Leading models were tested across the set. A steady gap opened between answers that sound right and numbers that are right. Side analyses probe background noise, false priors, and other failure drivers.
arxiv-2512-19726:
Carlos Purves tackles a deployment problem for reinforcement learning: smart visual policies usually live on a server, so every decision waits on a network round trip. His MiniConv approach splits the policy in two. A tiny on-device encoder, written as OpenGL fragment-shader passes so it runs on almost any embedded graphics chip, compresses each camera observation into a compact feature tensor for transmission.

Only that small tensor crosses the network to the remote policy head, cutting bandwidth, decision latency, and server load per request. Benchmarks span a Jetson Nano, a Raspberry Pi 4B, and a Pi Zero 2 W, measuring learning quality, behavior under sustained load, and latency under shaped bandwidth. Final learning performance stayed broadly comparable to unsplit policies, with modest trade-offs in average return, and the code is open source.
arxiv-2512-20326:
Felix Huber works on Quantum Max Cut, a quantum analogue of the classic Max Cut problem tied to the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model. He asks how well the optimum can be bounded from below using a famous graph invariant. The invariant is the Lovász theta function, applied to the complement of the graph.

Huber proves a lower bound in which a graph with many edges gains a correction term that shrinks as the theta value grows. A simple product state achieves the bound. A relaxed version replaces theta with the maximum degree, making it handy for quantum many-body systems. He also strengthens earlier results for triangle-free graphs using ideas of Carlson and Shearer.
arxiv-2512-20426:
Junjie Chen and co-authors expose a structural clash inside quantum sensing. Quantum metrology gains precision by letting a signal imprint coherently on a probe. Error correction protects that probe from noise, but correction works by distinguishing errors, while sensing needs signal and noise responses to stay indistinguishable along the signal direction.

The authors quantify the clash with trade-offs between code distance and quantum Fisher information for several code families.
