A late report from Lisbon shows the summit's ripples reaching quiet waters. Cannon could gauge how the news played in a capital outside the fight. Readers get that outside view at the moment of decision. The document rounds out the Portugal thread. It proves that in 1945 no European post, however calm, stood apart from the settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d926:
The United States delegation offered this memorandum at Babelsberg on July 25, 1945. It covers removals from Germany of property owned by citizens of Allied or neutral nations. The paper states that such ownership should not block a removals program.

Owners from Allied nations would file statements of their German property with the Control Council. Removed property would stay theirs where practical. Where not, Reichsmark accounts based on council valuations would be set up and paid off in foreign exchange. Neutral owners would get Reichsmark deposits as payment. The editors note the paper was circulated but never discussed, and Byrnes withdrew it on August 1.
frus-1969-76v17-d126: A 1969-1976 FRUS message from the government on China. The opening to Beijing. This document preserves that message. Later readers can locate it. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
galsworthy-silver-spoon-1926:
John Galsworthy published The Silver Spoon in 1926, part of his second Forsyte trilogy, A Modern Comedy. The story now centers on Fleur Forsyte, Soames's daughter, and her husband Michael Mont. Galsworthy set the action in the restless England of the 1920s.

Fleur, born with the silver spoon of the title, hunts for excitement and status in fashionable London. A libel case, a trip related to America, and clashes with her aging father test her marriage. Soames watches the new generation with worry and grudging love. The novel satirizes the smart set while keeping sympathy for its flawed people.
gao-gaoreports-b-295526: A March 2005 protest docket, B-295526, with thin metadata — this GAO ruling is all that survives as the record. The claims were tested on what the file showed. The docket got its hearing despite the gaps. The gaps did not stop the review.
gao-gaoreports-b-296526: Integrate took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-296626: Firetech Automatic Sprinkler took its September 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298426: Crown Title Corporation took its September 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Title deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298626: Lockheed Martin Aeronautics took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The giant said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Even the biggest defense names bow to bid law.
gao-gaoreports-b-299526: Medical Matrix took its June 2007 contract fight to GAO — two case numbers, one health deal — and the combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards; the call weighs each claim. Medical contracts get the same fair-bid treatment as any federal buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-300826: NIH's conference food spending got a fiscal ruling in March 2005, and GAO decides whether the catering was legal. The decision reads the money law. The ruling separates the allowable from the wasteful. The law had the final word. The catering was judged.
gao-gaoreports-b-308026: The labor board's contract spending got a fiscal slap in this September 2006 GAO ruling, which finds an improper obligation for severable services. The decision reads the money law. The ruling voids the illegal spending. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-311126: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by B-311126.2, B-311126.3, B-311126.4, Savannah River Alliance, LLC. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-526: Immigration phone lines needed cleaner deals in 2005, and GAO's report says the call-center pacts had to improve. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the callers deserved honest contracts. The callers deserved honest contracts. The pacts had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-626: Disability aid programs got a GAO once-over in 2005, and the report says the patchwork needed a modern rethink. The findings demand the reckoning. The report warns that the disabled deserved coherent aid. The disabled deserved coherent aid. The patchwork had to be rethought.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-726: FAA airline oversight needed systems integration in 2005, and GAO's report says the safety approach required further weaving into oversight. The findings demand the integration. The report warns that the flying public deserved proven oversight. The approach had to be integrated.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-926: Army modular transformation costs needed better estimates in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were needed to improve cost oversight. The findings demand the math. The report warns that the reorganization billions deserved honest counting. The estimates had to improve. The reorganization billions deserved honest counting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-126: Other countries' Social Security lessons got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says foreign experiences could inform U.S. reform. The findings look abroad. The report warns that the retirees deserved proven ideas. The lessons had to be learned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-26: Special education transitions needed guidance in 2006, and GAO's report says Education should provide more help for smooth state transitions. The findings demand the support. The report warns that the disabled students deserved seamless changes. The guidance had to be provided.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-326: Nursing homes housing sex offenders got a GAO look in 2006, and the report shares information on residents registered for crimes. The findings deliver the data. The report warns that the frail residents deserved to know. The information had to be shared.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-426: Broadband was spreading but hard to measure in 2006, and GAO's report says deployment was extensive, though assessing it was difficult. The findings balance the good news and the fog. The report warns that the digital divide needed honest mapping. The assessment had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-826: Evacuating hospitals in disasters needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says limitations in federal evacuation assistance should be addressed. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the patients who could not walk needed a way out. The assistance had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1126: Were buses and trains truly open to riders with disabilities? GAO's 2007 report says nobody could really tell — thin data and weak enforcement tools left the question hanging. The findings describe a civil-rights promise running on honor system: rules on the books, little proof on the ground.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-126: Depot repair money needed clearer tracking in 2007, and GAO's report says Congress deserved more consistent funding data. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the fix-it shops' budgets should not be a mystery. The data had to be dependable.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-26: The IRS could collect more with better procedures in 2007, and GAO's report says procedural changes could enhance tax collections. The findings target the process. The report warns that the tax gap was partly a paperwork gap. The procedures had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-26: This 2007 GAO report takes Social Security reform past the usual old-age talk to the benefits paid for injury and to dependents. Plans that trim the program ripple hard through checks for hurt workers and their kin. The report maps those ripple lines — the trade-offs Congress would face if it touched the program's most tender promises.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-326: The Government Accountability Office dug into financial Audit: American Battle Monuments Commission's Financial Statements for Fiscal Years 2007 and 2006 in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-426: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at defense Management: Overarching Organizational Framework Needed to Guide and Oversee Energy Reduction Efforts for Military Operations. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
glasgow-romantic-comedians-1926:
Ellen Glasgow published The Romantic Comedians in 1926, her sharpest comedy of Southern manners. Glasgow set it in Richmond, renamed Queenborough, among the aging gentry she knew so well. She once described the book as a comedy about people who refuse to grow old gracefully.

Judge Gamaliel Honeywell, a widower of sixty-five, shocks his family by marrying a pretty young woman of twenty-three. The marriage collapses in farce and pathos, while his grown children pursue their own late romances. Glasgow mocks Southern gallantry with unusual lightness of touch. Under the comedy sits a serious theme: the danger of living inside romantic illusions. It remains one of her most entertaining novels.
guiraldes-don-segundo-sombra-1926:
Ricardo Guiraldes published Don Segundo Sombra in 1926, an Argentine novel told by a boy who becomes a gaucho. The narrator leaves a dull town life to ride with Don Segundo, a quiet and skilled horseman. On the pampas they herd cattle, break horses, and face storms and fights. The boy learns the gaucho code by watching his mentor.

Don Segundo speaks little, yet his example teaches courage, patience, and loyalty. At the end, the boy inherits land and must leave the roaming life. The farewell is sad and dignified. The novel is a beloved portrait of a fading way of life in Argentina.
hemingway-sun-also-rises-1926:
Ernest Hemingway published The Sun Also Rises in 1926, his novel of Jake Barnes and the expatriates of Paris. The Lost Generation's founding document follows drifting expatriates from Paris cafés to the Pamplona fiesta. Hemingway drew the cast from his own circle, and the roman à clef gossip only fed the book's fame.

Jake, wounded in the war, loves Brett Ashley, who drifts through men she cannot settle with in Paris and Spain. The fishing at Burguete gives a brief peace before the fiesta's bullfights, wine, and brawls take over in Pamplona. Romero, the young bullfighter, restores a code of grace under pressure that the expatriates admire and nearly corrupt by contact. Hemingway's cut, plain sentences and dialogue that implies oceans made a style a generation copied. The book defined how America writes about war's aftermath and expatriate drift.
hemingway-torrents-of-spring-1926:
Ernest Hemingway wrote The Torrents of Spring in about ten days in late 1925. He published it in 1926. The comic novella parodies Sherwood Anderson, the older writer who had helped launch Hemingway's career and whose gentle style Hemingway had outgrown.

Two Michigan factory workers wander through a fog of borrowed literary manners, courting waitresses and discussing books they half understand. Hemingway stuffs the tale with fake footnotes and long apologies to the reader. The joke had a business purpose: it broke his contract with Anderson's publisher and freed him for a new house. The parody ended a famous mentorship. Read today, it is Hemingway's only long piece of pure mischief.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol9-1926:
The ninth volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law came out in 1926, carrying the story toward its author's own time. Holdsworth had begun the history as a young Oxford scholar; by now it was the standard work in its field. Few single-author histories in any subject match its scale.

Volume 9 deals with the later nineteenth century, above all the Judicature Acts that fused the old separate courts into one Supreme Court. Holdsworth explains how law and equity, split for centuries, were at last administered together. The modern court system of England takes its shape in these pages. Nine volumes in, the history approaches its close with the law made new. The set as a whole remains the last word on English legal history for most readers.
holmes-science-of-mind-1926:
Ernest Holmes built a movement on The Science of Mind, whose first edition appeared in 1926. The thick textbook lays out a full course of lessons in what Holmes called Science of Mind and Spirit. Mind, in his teaching, responds to thought as law, and prayer becomes a treatment: a clear statement that heals.

Holmes drew on New Thought, scripture, and philosophy to frame Religious Science as both church and method. Lessons move from first principles to daily practice for health, supply, and peace. The 1926 text launched the Religious Science movement, and its churches still study this founding course.
hughes-weary-blues-1926:
Langston Hughes published The Weary Blues in 1926, his first book of poems. Hughes was a young Black writer linked to the Harlem Renaissance. The poems draw on blues and jazz, with their rhythms, refrains, and plain speech. Harlem streets, clubs, and workers fill the pages.

Some poems sing of joy and music late into the night. Others speak of weariness, low pay, and dreams put off. Hughes writes in voices close to the people he describes. The title poem shows a piano player swaying as he sings of having nobody in the world. The book announced a major new voice in American poetry.
hurston-eatonville-anthology-1926:
Zora Neale Hurston grew up in Eatonville, Florida, one of the first all-Black towns in the United States. The Eatonville Anthology, published in the Messenger in 1926, gathers fourteen short sketches of her neighbors there. Hurston wrote them with the eye of both a storyteller and a trained student of folklore.

Each sketch gives a quick, vivid portrait of a local character. Their talk, tricks, jokes, and troubles fill the pages with town life. Hurston treats the townsfolk with warmth and respect, never as mere curiosities. The anthology was early proof of the gift she later showed in her novels and in her folklore collecting across the South.
hurston-sweat-1926:
Sweat, a short story by Zora Neale Hurston, appeared in the magazine Fire in 1926. Its heroine is Delia Jones, a washerwoman in a Florida town. Delia has worked for years to buy her own house, while her lazy husband Sykes torments her and flaunts his mistress.

Sykes, knowing Delia fears snakes, brings home a rattlesnake to drive her out. The cruelty builds until the snake turns on its keeper. Hurston writes the tale largely in Black Southern speech, handled with care and music. Sweat became one of the best-known stories of the Harlem Renaissance and a lasting study of labor, pride, and revenge.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-26:
Volume 26 of the Jesuit Relations came out in 1898 as part of Reuben Gold Thwaites's vast edition of reports from New France. Jesuit priests in Canada sent these yearly accounts back to France in the 1600s. They wrote about their missions among Native nations in the St. Lawrence valley and the lands beyond, in what the edition calls Lower Canada.

Inside are letters and journals on travel, hunger, sickness, language study, and the slow work of winning converts. The priests also recorded Native customs, councils, and wars with a close eye, even when their judgments were harsh. Historians still mine these pages as a first-hand record of early Canada and its first peoples.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maarssen-joseph:
Joseph ben Jacob Maarssen, a Dutch scholar and publisher of Amsterdam, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He came from a family of printers and lived across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. His work joined publishing to translation. Much of it served readers of Judeo-German.

The article lists his books one by one. He translated a Dutch account of the Amsterdam uprising of 1696, which his own father had witnessed. With Moses Bendin he compiled model letters in Judeo-German, with a glossary of foreign words. He also turned Ben Sira's wisdom and seven tales of Boccaccio into Judeo-German from the Dutch. Another work gave specimens of business notes and the law on commercial bills. The entry shows a publisher feeding a growing market for practical books in the Jewish vernacular.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malcha-10326:
Malcha, a Russian town in the government of Grodno, is given a short entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A Jewish community existed there by 1583. That year rumors spread that Jews had killed a Christian laborer. The community invited the district constable to investigate the matter in person.

The article explains how the accusation was answered. No evidence supported the rumor, and the Jews filed a formal protest against its spreading. By 1903 the town held about three thousand people, half of them Jews. Among them were 291 artisans. Ninety Jewish children learned in the town's heders, and forty more in its two Talmud Torahs. Charities included a sick-visiting society and a free-loan fund. The entry preserves a small community's brush with a blood libel and its quiet institutions three centuries later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marks-marcus-m-:
Marcus M. Marks, an American merchant, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Schenectady, New York, on March 18, 1858, he started in business at Passaic in 1877. He later entered his father's wholesale clothing firm, David Marks and Sons. By 1904 he stood near the top of the clothing trade.

The article is a catalogue of trade offices. Marks presided over the Clothiers' Association of New York and the National Association of Clothiers. He also chaired the clothing trade's hospital charity auxiliary. Beyond the trade he directed the Educational Alliance and sat on the National Civic Federation's conciliation committee. He was organizing credit cooperation across several trades, aiming at a central clearing-house for trade information. His articles on labor and conciliation appeared in trade journals. The entry portrays a merchant whose real work was organizing his industry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mccaul-alexande:
Alexander McCaul was an English Christian missionary. He spent his life arguing with Judaism and defending Jews, and Joseph Jacobs profiles him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Dublin on May 16, 1799, was educated at Trinity College, and was sent as a missionary to Poland in 1821. He stayed ten years at Warsaw, learned Hebrew and German, and won the ear of princes. He died at London on November 13, 1863, a professor of Hebrew and rabbinical literature at King's College.

His fame came from “The Old Paths.” That long attack on Jewish legalism was issued weekly from 1837 and was translated into several languages, Hebrew among them. A Hebrew answer, “Paths of Truth,” followed in 1847. Yet the same man wrote vigorously against the blood accusation. He also refused the Anglican bishopric of Jerusalem, saying it should be held by a Jew by birth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mesquita-moses-:
Moses Gomez de Mesquita, born in 1688, was haham, or chief rabbi, of the Spanish and Portuguese Jews of England. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote his short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He took the office in 1744, succeeding Isaac Nieto, and held it until his death on May 8, 1751.

The article records two marriages that mark his years in office. In 1747 he solemnized the second marriage of his predecessor, Isaac Nieto. Two years later he married his own daughter to Moses Cohen Dazevedo Ferme, who himself became haham in 1760. A brief bibliography points to Gaster's history of the Bevis Marks congregation and the catalogue of the Anglo-Jewish Historical Exhibition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mikwa-ot-baths-:
Miḳwa'ot is the Mishnah treatise on ritual baths, the pools used for purification after leprosy and other conditions named in Leviticus. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The bath had to hold at least forty seahs of water, about 268 liters, enough to cover the whole body at once.

The water could come from a spring, a river, or rainfall, but never from a vessel, and the treatise exists to pin down such rules exactly. It runs ten chapters and seventy-one paragraphs, opening with six grades of water ranked by cleansing power. The article also notes the treatise's wandering place in the order Tohorot across different editions of the Mishnah and Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-mokiah:
Mordecai Mokiaḥ of Eisenstadt, born in Alsace about 1650, was the would-be Messiah. He kept Shabbethai Ẓebi's movement alive after its messiah's death. Gotthard Deutsch recounts him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When Ẓebi died in 1676, Mordecai preached that he had only withdrawn to heaven. He would return within three years to finish his task.

Ascetic, eloquent, and commanding in person, he won crowds of followers. Italian cabalists called him to Italy about 1678. There he began to announce himself as the Messiah outright. Fear of the Inquisition, perhaps, drove him out. He preached through Austria, Germany, and Poland. Then he settled in Hungary and lived quietly until 1729. His son became an eminent Talmudist, a steadier fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morse-leopold-1:
Leopold Morse was a Boston merchant who served five terms in the United States Congress. Cyrus Adler's Jewish Encyclopedia entry traces him from Wachenheim in Rhenish Bavaria, where he was born on August 15, 1831. He emigrated in 1849, sold clothing in New Bedford, and settled in Boston in 1851.

In Boston, Morse built a large and successful clothing business. Voters in a district with a supposed Republican majority sent him, a Democrat, to the House of Representatives five times. He also sat as a delegate at the Democratic conventions of 1872 and 1876. The entry closes with his charity work. He founded the Boston Home for Infirm Hebrews and Orphanage, the first Jewish institution of its kind in New England.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munz-minz-moses:
Moses Münz was a Hungarian rabbi born in Podolia about 1750 and called to the chief rabbinate of Alt-Ofen in 1790. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He had won a great name as a Talmudic scholar at Brody, on Ezekiel Landau's recommendation. Questions reached him from all over the Austrian monarchy.

Münz fought Mordecai Benet over phylacteries with double straps, proving them lawful. His harder test was Aaron Chorin, the reforming rabbi whose book he first approved and defended as free of heresy. Pressed by the Orthodox, he summoned Chorin to judgment, then failed to appear and refused to join the sentence. He condemned Reform in an unsigned letter, and Chorin recanted under his threat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-narol-moses-113:
Moses Narol was a Galician rabbi and physician who ended as rabbi of Metz. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He had held both callings at Narol until the Cossack rising of 1648 drove him to Germany. His son Tobias Cohn became a noted physician.

Narol wrote sermons on the Pentateuch and on the Five Scrolls, printed as the two parts of his Birkot Tob. He also composed a prayer on the misfortunes of Poland in 1643, with commentary. Works on medicine and mathematics came from the same hand. He died at Metz in 1659, an exile of the 1648 rising.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehemiah-ha-koh:
Nehemiah ha-Kohen was a Polish cabalist caught in a messiah scandal. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Polish Jews sent him east in 1666. At Gallipoli he was to judge Shabbethai Zebi's claim. Zebi was then held there as a claimed Messiah.

After long debate, Nehemiah called Zebi an impostor. Zebi's men then plotted in secret to kill him. Nehemiah fled, crying that he would embrace Islam. A turban was set on his head at once. He told the sultan what he knew of Zebi. Home again, he shocked all by praising Zebi as Messiah. He even claimed the forerunner's role for himself. Polish communities cast him out for it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nicodemus-nakdi:
Nicodemus ben Gorion was Jerusalem's richest peace-party leader. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived there in the first century C.E. During the revolt under Vespasian, he backed Rome. His true name, says tradition, was Buna.

On a pilgrimage he hired twelve cisterns for the people. He pledged their owner twelve hundred talents of silver. His name is explained as a pun in the Talmud. With Kalba Sabbua and Ben Zizit, he stockpiled food. The three friends swayed Bar Giora against the Zealots. In revenge the Zealots burned their vast stores of provisions. That loss, in the war on Titus, hastened Jerusalem's hunger. His wealth could not shield the city he loved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunes-torres-da:
David Nuñes-Torres was a ḥakam and an editor. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Amsterdam was probably the city of his birth. He died at The Hague in the year 1728. Two Amsterdam societies first heard his preaching.

Praise attended him as Talmudist and as preacher. The Hague then called him as its ḥakam. Its Spanish-Portuguese community was his charge there. His library was large for a private man's. Auction scattered it the August after his death. Its printed catalogue is still cited by scholars. Six Portuguese sermons of his appeared in 1690. He issued the Hebrew Bible in 1700. New editions of two great codes bear his hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-abrah:
Abraham Oppenheim was a chief of the flock at Worms. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms, in Germany. He died at Heidelberg on December 2, 1692. His father was Simon Wolf Oppenheim of Worms.

Men called him Abraham zur Kanne, for his fine house. Its sign was a can, or jug, in German speech. He owned six houses in the Jews' street at Worms. He won great favor with the German princes of his day. He served them as a shtadlan, one who pleads for Jews. In 1689 the town of Worms was laid waste. He fled with his flock to Heidelberg, where he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ovruch-ovrutch-:
Ovruch is a district town in Volhynia, in Russia. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1629 just three houses there were owned by Jews. Yet a fair sized Jewish group must have lived there. In that year a synagogue was built in the town.

In 1896 the Jews of Ovruch numbered 4,177 souls. The whole town held 9,845 souls in that count. So Jews made up close to half the town's folk. They held three houses of prayer and one poor house. In the whole district, Jews numbered near 20,750 souls. Small trades in the small towns lay in Jewish hands. That held for most such trades in the district, the piece says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-passover-sacrif:
The Passover sacrifice was the lamb offered on the night before the Exodus. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its blood on the doorposts marked Israelite homes for safety.

The article sets out the full Temple ritual for later years. Each family group offered one lamb or kid, a male without blemish. Priests passed cups of its blood hand to hand to the altar. The people came in three groups while Levites sang the Hallel. At home the lamb was roasted whole and eaten that night.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perez-12026:
Perez was a Marano family of Cordova and Seville. Four writers shared this article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were Isidore Singer, Meyer Kayserling, M. Franco, and Gotthard Deutsch. The Inquisition hunted some members of the family. Others found safety in Turkish lands.

One Aaron Perez became chief rabbi at Jerba. His Bible commentary was printed at Leghorn in 1806. Antonio Perez, a rich merchant, escaped Spain in 1487. His kin were not so lucky at Saragossa. Three of them were burned there as Jewish heretics. Other branches wrote sermons and law in the east.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prag-jacob-1232:
Jacob Prag was a teacher of Hebrew and a rabbi at Liverpool. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Danzig in 1816. He learned at the rabbinical school at Libau. At eighteen he took his first post. He died at Liverpool in 1881.

Prag next served as rabbi at Shoenek in Prussian Poland. He was then called to the Old Hebrew Congregation at Liverpool. He held that pulpit until his death. Soon after settling, he became Hebrew master of a school there. He also held the Hebrew chair at Queen's College, Liverpool. Few men joined pulpit and classroom as he did.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-ix-surn:
Ptolemy, surnamed Euergetes the Second, was king of Egypt. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He reigned from 146 to 117 B.C. When Ptolemy Philometor died, this brother moved at once. He tried to throw down the widow, Cleopatra. She kept the throne against him for a time.

A Jewish general, Onias, led the queen's army then. Josephus tells of Jews held captive in Alexandria. He tells of their rescue from death as well. On the strength of Third Maccabees, men lay those acts on Ptolemy the Fourth. The writers place them here, with this later king. Jews were hit for politics, not for faith, they stress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rado-anton-orig:
Anton Radó was a Hungarian poet and author born at Moor in 1862. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of the grammarian Adolf Roder. He studied old and new tongues at Budapest. He took up work for the papers in 1880. In 1883 he took his doctorate with a learned book.

That book told the history of translation in Hungary. Radó then went to Italy for more study. He won his name as a translator of great works. Tasso's epic stands among the works he rendered. The entry lists his versions and his own poems. It shows a scholar who served two tongues at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ree-anton-12626:
Anton Ree was a German teacher born at Hamburg on November 16, 1815. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died on January 13, 1891. He was educated at Kiel.

The article says he joined the Hamburg Jewish free school in 1838. In 1848 he became its director. He opened the school to Christian pupils as well. By 1869 they outnumbered the Jewish pupils there. He wrote two early works on ethics and duty. After his only daughter died young, he founded a scholarship. It served Christian and other non-Jewish pupils in her memory. The entry honors a teacher who widened his school's doors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosanes-12826:
Rosanes is the name of a Jewish family that first came from Rosas, a seaport in Spain. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote the family entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Members moved to Portugal in the late fifteenth century, and later settled in Turkey, Austria, and Russia.

The entry profiles the family's leading rabbis one by one, across several centuries. Abraham Rosanes the Elder was a Turkish Talmud scholar in the seventeenth century. Another Abraham served as chief rabbi of Constantinople in the eighteenth century. Later members include a Minsk preacher and a Bulgarian scholar who wrote about his 1867 trip to Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubo-ernst-trau:
Ernst Traugott Rubo was a German jurist born at Berlin on July 8, 1834. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his law degree at Heidelberg in 1857 and joined the bar in 1859.

Rubo became a judge in Berlin in 1861, then taught at its university. He rose there from privat-docent to professor of law. His books treat defamation and the forcing of witnesses to testify in court. He also helped draft the military law code of the German empire. His essays appeared in leading journals of criminal law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salgo-jakob-130:
Jakob Salgó was a Hungarian psychiatrist born at Pesth in 1849. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1874 and trained at Göttingen.

Salgó headed a Vienna sanitarium from 1880 to 1882 as chief physician. In 1884 he became head physician at Budapest's State Insane Asylum. He sat on Hungary's state sanitary council and medico-legal council as well. His books urge reform of psychiatry and map the brain states behind psychoses. A Hungarian handbook of psychiatry from his hand appeared in 1890.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-sir-marc:
Sir Marcus Samuel, an English financier, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind, published in 1906. Samuel was born in London in 1853. He was the senior partner of Samuel, Samuel & Co. That shipping firm, based at Yokohama, stood high in Japan. In 1898 it placed the Japanese loan.

In 1891 Samuel was elected alderman for Portsoken Ward. He was knighted in May 1898. He held the manor at the Mote, near Maidstone. He also served as a justice of the peace for Kent. In 1903 he was made a baronet. That honor closed his year of office as lord mayor of London. The entry marks his rise from shipping to the top of city government.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saul-abba-13226:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Abba Saul. He was a tanna of the third generation. Abba Saul seems to have been a pupil of Rabbi Akiba. He lived in the middle of the second century. The Abba in his name is a title only. His trade is said to have been burying the dead.

Abba Saul read Scripture with a moral eye. He taught that man must imitate God in charity and kindness. Two of his sayings survive: discord in the school breeds general corruption, and morality is greater than learning. He studied the Temple service with great care. He also made his own collection of mishnayot. It differed from other collections in many points. Judah ha-Nasi, the Mishnah's editor, drew on it at times. Parts of it live on inside the present Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schulklopfer-13:
Cyrus Adler and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Schulklopfer. The name belonged to a medieval synagogue beadle. His job was to call the congregation to services. The Minhagim of Jacob Levi describes his rounds. He summoned worshipers every day except the Ninth of Ab. His knocks followed a set pattern.

At Neustadt the beadle struck four times on each door. He gave one blow, paused, gave two more, then a fourth. Rabbi Israel Isserlein traced the pattern to a verse in Exodus. The Hebrew letters of its first word add up to one, two, and one. In the Rhine province the beadle struck only three times. Christians called such officials campanatores, or bell-strikers. The article shows how a small custom carried a verse inside it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sennacherib-ass:
Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 B.C. as son and heir of Sargon. Emil G. Hirsch and Louis H. Gray wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His name means that the god Sin increased the brethren. His reign mixed constant war with grand building and art.

Soon after taking the throne, Sennacherib crushed a Babylonian revolt. He then beat tribes along the Euphrates and marched west toward Tyre and Egypt. Cities paid tribute, and Ascalon fell to his army. For Bible readers, he matters most as the Assyrian king who pressed on Judah in Hezekiah's day. The entry sets that clash in a wider empire at war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sibbechai-13626: Sibbechai was a captain under King David who came from a town near Bethlehem. Emil G. Hirsch and E. I. Nathans wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He won fame by overcoming a Philistine giant in battle. Samuel and Chronicles both record that victory. He is listed among David's thirty valiant followers in Chronicles. He may be the same man as Mebunnai, named in Samuel's list of heroes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sosa-sossa-sous: De Sosa was envoy of King John III of Portugal to Pope Paul III. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. While at Rome he pressed a cause for the Maranos. They sought relief from the severity of the Inquisition. They urged the pope to send a nuncio to Portugal. The pope at first opposed the plan, then gave way. De Sosa's blunt letters home are quoted in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-alfred-14:
Alfred Stern was a German historian born at Göttingen on November 22, 1846. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. His father, Moriz Abraham Stern, taught mathematics at Göttingen. Alfred studied at Heidelberg and Berlin after his home gymnasium. He worked as an assistant archivist at Carlsruhe in 1869.

In 1873 Stern became professor at the University of Bern. He held that post until 1887. He then took the chair of general history at Zurich's polytechnic. His books cover Milton and the English revolution in depth. He also wrote a life of Mirabeau in two volumes. His history of Europe after 1815 appeared in 1894. The entry records a career spent on European political history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-susanna-the-his:
The History of Susanna is a short book of the Apocrypha. Crawford Howell Toy wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Some manuscripts title it The Judgment of Daniel. Greek copies survive in two main versions. Theodotion's version stands behind most English translations today.

In most Greek manuscripts the tale opens the Book of Daniel. Jerome placed it at Daniel's end instead. He noted it is absent from the Hebrew Bible. Early Christians accepted it as canonical for centuries. Catholics still regard it as scripture today. Origen said the Jews had hidden the book away. The story tells of Susanna, pious wife of rich Joacim. Two elder judges spy on her in her garden. The entry weighs the text's versions and standing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tammuz-14226:
Tammuz is the fourth month of the Hebrew religious year. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It is the tenth month of the civil year. Its twenty-nine days span parts of June and July. The month carries both a feast memory and a fast.

Late in the Second Temple age, its fourteenth day was festive. It marked a Pharisee victory over the Sadducees in law. The seventeenth day is a public fast day. It recalls the breaching of Jerusalem's walls by Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah dates that breach to the ninth day instead. Titus breached the walls on the seventeenth, fixing the date. Tradition adds four more calamities to that day. Moses broke the tablets of the Law then. Three weeks of mourning open with the fast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-aryeh-j:
Aryeh Judah Löb Te'omim was a rabbi and scholar of Poland. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He is also called Zunz or Zinz in sources. He lived at Pinczow and later at Plotzk. His life spanned the 1600s and 1700s.

Te'omim wrote sermons on the weekly Torah portions. A compendium of Maimonides' divorce laws followed in 1812. His Passover rules book appeared at Warsaw in 1817. Responsa compendia came out in 1827 and 1849. He commented on the whole treatise Bezah as well. Other works cover slaughter law and the Yoreh De'ah. A Pentateuch commentary and a Haggadah round out the list. His name, meaning twins, matched a doubled output. The entry catalogs a code writer of many volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-todros-of-cavai: Todros of Cavaillon, also called Tauros, was a French physician of the late fourteenth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Carmoly placed his work around 1375. His treatise, Sha'are ha-Harkabot, is a sort of drug handbook. It was written partly in Hebrew and partly in Latin. Carmoly claimed the elders made him rabbi of Cavaillon. The entry notes that he gave no proof for that claim. Todros may be the Maestro Toros who directed Avignon's community in 1440.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trop-14526: Trop is the Judaeo-German term for tropes, the short musical cadences of Scripture reading. Joseph Jacobs and Francis L. Cohen wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Church plain-song calls such cadences distinctions. The tropes give the traditional sung reading of the Hebrew accents. They shape how the Hebrew Scriptures are chanted in synagogue. The entry points readers to the fuller article on accents in Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valabregue-mard:
Mardochée-Georges Valabrègue was a French general born at Carpentras in 1852. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He trained at the Ecole Polytechnique and the artillery school. After reaching captain, he studied at the war college. Staff duty in Paris followed his graduation in 1880.

He commanded an artillery battery from 1884. Two years later he served General Boulanger, then war minister. He rose to lieutenant-colonel in 1898 and colonel in 1902. As colonel he headed the military artillery school. In 1904 he became chief of cabinet at the War Ministry. Brigadier-general rank came in 1905 with new commands. He also received the Legion of Honor that period.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-jacob-1482:
Jacob Weil was a German teacher and writer on Jewish rights. He was born at Frankfort in 1792. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Frankfort on November 18, 1864. His first work drew fragments from Talmud and rabbis. He taught at Frankfort's Jewish school, the Philanthropin.

From 1818 to 1845 Weil ran his own school institute. In 1816 he voiced hope for Jewish emancipation. He then answered attacks by professors Rühs and Fries. His pamphlet defended Jewish claims to German citizenship. He helped found a group promoting crafts among Jews. He backed Gabriel Riesser and wrote his life story. His essays filled the Frankfort press for years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilenkin-gregor:
Gregory Wilenkin was a Russian government official. Cyrus Adler wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tsarskoye Selo on February 22, 1864. His family held landed estates for two centuries. An ancestor, Blema Wilenkin, endowed houses at Minsk and Jerusalem. Her Minsk house still serves as a study hall.

Wilenkin studied law at Dorpat and St. Petersburg. In 1887 he entered the Ministry of Public Instruction. The ministry sent him to England on a study mission. He examined Oxford and Cambridge and Paris schools. France honored his report on its schools. Finance minister Witte then recruited him in 1895. He became assistant financial agent in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wormser-andre-a:
Andre Alphonse Wormser (born 1851) was a French composer of operas and ballets. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Paris, he trained at the Paris stage music school. His teachers were Bazin and Marmontel, both famed men. In 1875 he won the Prix de Rome for his work.

That prize marked him as a star of his class. He wrote a great store of stage and piano works. The list holds overtures, light operas, and farces. It holds ballets for the Paris stage as well. Two full operas stand at the head of the list. One played at Aix-la-Chapelle in the year 1887. The second, named Rivoli, played at Paris in 1896. The short entry rests on a music word book of 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeitlin-william:
William Zeitlin was a Russian scholar and maker of book lists. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Homel in the Moghilef state, he lived in the 1800s. His fame rests on one great work of his long life.

That work is the Kiryat Sefer, a list of Hebrew books. It lists new Hebrew books from the age of Mendelssohn. That age runs to the year 1890 in the scope of the list. The work took him twenty years of his life to make. He drew on two great lists made by men before him. He toured the book towns of Wilna and Warsaw for facts. He toured great school towns of Europe for more facts. The list holds notes on the lives of the scribes as well.
journal-of-discourses-vol-26:
Volume Twenty-Six, from 1886, closes the Journal of Discourses for good. Twenty-six volumes span thirty-two years of Tabernacle and frontier preaching. Hundreds of sermons end here, in the set's final gathered book.

The founding generation's voice falls silent as this volume shuts. Apostles who crossed the plains now preach to grandchildren in Zion. Their record covers doctrine, war, law, farming, and the soul's fate. No new faith of the age left so full a firsthand record. Scholars still mine the Journal as Mormonism's great primary source today. Its last pages close an era that print alone could preserve.
kafka-das-schloss-1926:
Franz Kafka left The Castle unfinished at his death in 1924, and it was published in German in 1926. The text here is that first German edition, from Kurt Wolff. No English translation of the book is in the public domain. Its hero, known only as K., arrives in a snowbound village claiming the Castle has hired him as a land surveyor.

The Castle's officials never confirm his post, and every effort to reach them snares him deeper. Clerks, letters, and village rules form a maze with no center in sight. K. fights on with stubborn, comic energy against pure fog. The novel became the classic image of life under faceless power. Its cold absurdity still defines the word Kafkaesque.
lawrence-plumed-serpent-1926:
The Plumed Serpent, published in 1926, is Lawrence's Mexican novel and the most argued-over of all his books. Kate Leslie, an Irish widow of forty traveling in Mexico, is drawn into a movement reviving the cult of Quetzalcoatl, the plumed serpent god.

Its leaders, Don Ramon and Don Cipriano, preach a new-old religion of blood and ritual against church and revolution alike. Kate resists and yields by turns, and the novel never settles whether the cult saves or devours her. Lawrence wrote it out of his own Mexican journeys and longings. The result is powerful, disturbing, and impossible to ignore.
levy-bruhl-how-natives-think-1926:
Lucien Levy-Bruhl, a French philosopher, argued in this famous work that native peoples think in a fundamentally different way from modern Europeans. The authorized English translation by Lilian A. Clare appeared in 1926 and spread his thesis widely.

Levy-Bruhl claimed that collective representations, the beliefs a group shares, bend individual thought toward what he called participation mystique. In that mode, a person can feel one with an ancestor, an animal, or a sacred object. Critics attacked the idea as unfair to native reason, and Levy-Bruhl softened it late in life. The debate it started shaped anthropology for decades.
livy-history-rome-books-9-26:
Livy wrote his monumental History of Rome under Augustus, narrating the republic's rise. D. Spillan and Cyrus Edmonds translated this stretch, covering Books 9 through 26. The Second Punic War dominates the later books here.

Early books here cover Rome's wars with the Samnites and Pyrrhus. Then Hannibal crosses the Alps, wins at Cannae, and nearly breaks Rome. Livy tells the story as patriotic epic, full of speeches and omens. Rome's recovery after Cannae becomes his great theme of resilience. This volume completes the library's main Livy set. Ancient history rarely reads at this scale or with this sweep.
llull-blanquerna-peers-1926:
Blanquerna is the great romance of Ramon Llull, the Catalan thinker of the thirteenth century. E. Allison Peers translated it into English in 1926. Its hero, Blanquerna, climbs step by step through the estates of the world: marriage, the religious life, the bishopric, the papacy, and at last the hermit's cell.

Along the road Llull sets out his whole vision of a reformed Christian world, taught by reason and his famous Art of finding truth. The famous Book of the Lover and the Beloved blooms inside the tale. Blanquerna is part novel, part plan for the church and the schools. It shows medieval Catalonia dreaming of a wiser age.
malinowski-crime-custom-1926:
In 1926 Malinowski returned to the Trobriand Islands in print with a short book on law and custom. Crime and Custom in Savage Society asks how order holds in a land with no courts, police, or written laws. It grew from the same field work as his Argonauts.

Malinowski argues that law lives in daily duty, not in force from above. He shows that custom binds because people depend on each other and fear shame before their neighbors. Gifts, feasts, and duties form a web that no one can lightly break. The book founded the study of law in anthropology and still starts debates about rules without rulers.
malinowski-myth-in-primitive-psychology-:
Malinowski based this short 1926 book on his fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands, where he had lived in a village and learned the language. It states his functionalist view of myth in its clearest form.

A myth, Malinowski argues, is not a bad attempt at science or history. It is a charter: a sacred story that justifies present customs, ranks, and land claims by grounding them in the age of origins. He shows Trobrianders using tales of ancestors to settle real disputes. The book helped move anthropology from the armchair to the field, and its argument still frames debates about myth.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-2-1926:
Jalal al-Din Rumi, the Persian poet of the 1200s, wrote the Mathnawi, a long poem of Sufi teaching told through stories. R. A. Nicholson spent years turning it into English. His second volume, printed in 1926, gives the English text of the poem's first two books.

Rumi teaches through tales of kings, lovers, merchants, fools, and saints, and each story turns toward a lesson on God and the soul. The tales pile up, short and long, comic and grave, and each one points past itself to truths about prayer, love, and the self. Nicholson's version became the standard English Mathnawi for students of Persian verse.
mcbride-symmes-theory-concentric-spheres:
James McBride, a friend and backer of Symmes in Ohio, gave the hollow earth scheme its first full book in 1826. Symmes had put his claim in short forms, and it drew much scorn. McBride set out to give it a learned, full dress case.

He lays out the spheres within spheres, the polar holes, and the seas and lands inside. He draws on maths, star lore, and the tales of north sea men for his proof. The book is the chief shield of the scheme in its first, bold years.
mirrlees-lud-in-the-mist-1926:
Hope Mirrlees set a prim town by the edge of faerie in Lud-in-the-Mist, her novel of 1926. The town bans all talk of fairy fruit and the wild hills. Yet the fruit slips in. Sons and girls stray, and old rites stir in the calm streets.

The tale blends law, lore, and quiet dread. Mirrlees writes with grace and sly wit. She asks what a town loses when it shuts out awe. The book was long hard to find. Now chief tale-smiths rank it at the top. Mayor Chanticleer, stiff and prim at first, must face his own past. His slow change gives the wild lore a warm, sad human core.
morgan-theory-gene-1926:
Thomas Hunt Morgan led the famous 'fly room' at Columbia, where tiny fruit flies remade biology. His Theory of the Gene, published in 1926, sums up what those flies had taught. Morgan had once doubted Mendel; the flies changed his mind.

Morgan shows that genes sit in a line on chromosomes, like beads on a string. Crossed flies reveal how traits link, swap, and map to fixed places. That mapping let scientists chart heredity with real precision. Morgan won a Nobel Prize, and his book stands as the classic statement of gene theory. Diagrams of fly crosses make the argument easy to follow.
openalex-w1487331926:
Pablo Smircich, Fabiola Holetz, José Sotelo-Silveira, and co-authors wrote this study. It appeared in BMC Genomics in the year 2015. The subject is Trypanosoma cruzi, the Chagas disease parasite. Such parasites barely control genes at transcription, they note. Control after transcription shapes most gene changes instead.

The team used RNA sequencing and ribosome profiling together. They compared non-infective and infective life stages. Transcript levels stayed largely steady between the stages. Translation levels dropped for a large share of genes. Virulence factor translation rose in the infective form. The authors conclude that control of translation drives this change. The paper is open access and free for all to read. Its teams worked in Brazil and in Uruguay, the author notes show.
openalex-w2030126026:
Diego Jarquin, Jose Crossa, Xavier Lacaze and colleagues built a model to predict wheat yield from genes and weather. Their paper appeared in Theoretical and Applied Genetics in 2014. Genes affect traits differently in different environments. Breeders call this gene-by-environment interaction. Modern tools now produce huge gene and weather datasets.

Their reaction norm model uses both kinds of data. It includes main effects of genes and environment. It also includes how the two interact. The model raised prediction accuracy for grain yield. Gains held across environments and within them. Better prediction helps breeders pick lines before field trials end. The method suits other crops with rich data too.
openalex-w2066642526:
D. K. Tiwari, Nabanita Dasgupta-Schubert, Luis Manuel Villasenor Cendejas and colleagues tested carbon nanotubes on maize seedlings. Their paper appeared in Applied Nanoscience in 2014. Tiny carbon tubes had boosted sprouting in some plants. Results were uneven between studies. Factory-made tubes of known quality offered a cleaner test.

At low doses, the tubes improved seedling growth. At higher doses, growth was depressed instead. Better water delivery explained much of the benefit. The tubes also changed mineral nutrient flow to seedlings. Effects differed by nutrient type and tube dose. Two forces competed: water inflow and nutrient holding. The authors discuss what this means for nano-agriculture. Careful dosing is essential for any farm use.
openalex-w2099600826:
Georges Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration measured Higgs boson production through its decay into two photons. Their paper appeared in Physical Review D in 2014. The two-photon channel is rare but very clean. It gives a sharp signal above background noise. Data came from two LHC energy runs.

The team counted Higgs decays in the photon channel. They compared counts with standard model predictions. Overall production matched the prediction within errors. They also split results by production route. Each route agreed with expectations within wide uncertainties. A new photon calibration improved the mass precision. No clear deviation from the standard model appeared. The measurement confirms the Higgs picture further.
openalex-w2101094926:
Roderick Escombe, David Moore, Robert Gilman and colleagues measured how infectious TB patients with HIV are. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2008. Classic knowledge came from 1950s guinea pig studies. Those studies exposed animals to ward air. The team recreated that model in Lima, Peru.

They used gene fingerprinting to match infections to patients. That let them trace which patient infected which animal. Patients also had HIV alongside tuberculosis. The question was whether HIV changes infectiousness. Ward air exposure ran over long periods. Molecular matching gave a patient-level picture of spread. Such data help hospitals judge isolation needs. They also refine models of TB transmission.
openalex-w2113626726:
Juan Carlos Motamayor, Philippe Lachenaud, Jay Wallace da Silva e Mota and colleagues reclassified the cacao tree using gene data. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2008. Cacao seed collections guide chocolate breeding work. Many collected samples were wrongly labelled, though. Links between wild and farmed trees were poorly understood.

The team checked over a thousand cacao samples. Fine DNA markers covered the species' range widely. Wrongly labelled samples were dropped before the checks. Grouping by gene patterns found ten clusters. Tradition had recognised only two groups before. Each cluster ties to a place of origin. A new scheme for cacao was proposed. Breeders can now use the collections with more trust.
openalex-w2130143426:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this search in the Journal of High Energy Physics in 2014. They looked for direct production of three kinds of proposed supersymmetric particles: charginos, neutralinos, and sleptons. The sign they sought was two leptons plus missing sideways momentum, which hints at unseen particles escaping the detector.

The team used proton collision data recorded by ATLAS at the Large Hadron Collider. They found no clear excess beyond what the standard model predicts. Instead, they set limits on the masses these particles could have under several simple model setups. The results were also read against broader versions of the minimal supersymmetric standard model.
openalex-w2150408626:
Arnaldo Dubín, Mario Pozo, Christian Casabella, and colleagues published this study in Critical Care in 2009. In septic shock, doctors raise blood pressure with the drug norepinephrine. The team asked whether pushing pressure higher also improves flow in the tiniest vessels, where oxygen actually reaches tissue.

Twenty ventilated patients were studied as their pressure target rose in steps. Heart output and vessel resistance rose with the higher doses, as expected. Oxygen delivery, oxygen use, and lactate levels stayed unchanged. Direct imaging under the tongue showed tiny-vessel flow and the share of working capillaries also stayed flat. Raising the pressure number, the study concludes, did not improve microcirculatory flow.
openalex-w2153034426:
Teresa To, Sanja Stanojevic, Ginette Moores, and colleagues published this study in BMC Public Health in 2012. They estimated the global burden of asthma in adults from the World Health Survey. Asthma drives disability and health costs worldwide, yet comparable adult figures across many countries were scarce.

The survey covered more than one hundred seventy-eight thousand adults in seventy countries. About four in a hundred reported doctor-diagnosed or treated asthma, and about nine reported recent wheezing. Rates varied as much as twenty-one fold between countries, with Australia highest. Among people with treated asthma, almost a quarter still smoked, and one in five had never received treatment at all.
openalex-w2260781726:
Gissela Borrego-Soto, Rocío Ortiz-López, and Augusto Rojas-Martínez published this review in Genetics and Molecular Biology in 2015. They discuss radiation-induced DNA injury in breast cancer care. Radiotherapy helps many patients, yet some suffer worse side effects, possibly because their DNA repair machinery is weaker.

Ionizing radiation breaks DNA, most dangerously as double-strand breaks. Cells answer with repair systems, and flaws in those systems also drive inherited breast and ovarian cancer through BRCA gene mutations. Milder variants may shape risk in ordinary cases too. The review covers damage and repair mechanisms, the genes involved, and tests designed or in development to spot patients with raised radiosensitivity before treatment.
openalex-w2482115826: Anthony M. Reilly, Richard Ian Cooper, and Claire S. Adjiman lead the long author list on this 2016 report in Acta Crystallographica Section B. Its title announces the sixth blind test of methods that predict organic crystal structures. The preserved sample holds only the title pages and author affiliations, with no readable abstract or results. Nothing more about its targets, methods, or findings can be stated from the evidence kept here.
openalex-w2792366526:
Carlos Rosales reviewed the neutrophil's many faces in Frontiers in Physiology in 2018. Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells in human blood. Bone marrow releases about a hundred billion of them daily, and most live only a day. They patrol for microbes and kill them by eating, by poison release, and by casting DNA traps.

Recent research shows neutrophils do far more than kill germs. They release cytokines and other signals that steer inflammation and shape wider immune responses. They help resolve inflammation too, not just start it. This versatility raises the question in the paper's title: one flexible cell type, or several distinct ones? Rosales surveys the evidence for neutrophil subpopulations and changing states. The answer matters for treating diseases where neutrophils drive damage.
openalex-w2811473826:
Crystian B. Oliveira, Christopher G. Maher, and Rafael Z. Pinto lead this 2018 overview of low back pain rules in the European Spine Journal. Non-specific low back pain fills primary care waiting rooms everywhere. Dozens of guidelines tell doctors how to diagnose and treat it. The team updated their 2010 overview to see what current guidelines say, and what changed.

They found fifteen clinical practice guidelines from 2008 to 2017. For diagnosis, the rules agree: check history and examine for red flags and nerve involvement. Imaging is discouraged unless serious disease is suspected, and psychosocial factors deserve assessment. For acute pain, they advise reassurance, staying active, and short courses of anti-inflammatory drugs. Chronic pain adds exercise therapy, antidepressants, and psychosocial interventions. The overview lets clinicians see the consensus, and guideline writers see the gaps.
openalex-w2929552226:
Gianpiero Manes, Gregorios Paspatis, Lars Aabakken, and colleagues wrote this clinical guideline for the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, published in Endoscopy in 2019. It covers stones in the common bile duct and how doctors should find and remove them using endoscopy, a scope passed into the digestive tract.

The guideline advises offering stone removal to all patients with these stones who are fit enough for the procedure, whether or not they have symptoms. It names liver function tests and an ultrasound scan of the belly as the first diagnostic steps. Combined, those tests show how likely a patient is to have bile duct stones. Each advice point is graded by strength and by the quality of evidence behind it.
openalex-w2985579226:
Leticia Arregui, Marcela Ayala, Ximena Gómez-Gil, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Microbial Cell Factories. It covers laccases, enzymes made by fungi and other organisms, and their promise for cleaning polluted water. Cities and industry keep adding foreign chemicals to water, harming ecosystems and health.

Laccases attack a broad range of compounds and can break down pollutants found in factory and hospital wastewater. Trials with crude or purified enzyme show real potential for water treatment. Large-scale use is held back by the harsh mix, salt levels, and acidity of real waste streams, which can damage the enzyme. The review maps the enzymes' structure and function and the knowledge still needed for wider use.
openalex-w3010629926:
Christian Lieven, Moritz Beber, Brett Olivier, and colleagues described this software in a letter to Nature Biotechnology in 2020. The tool, called MEMOTE, runs standard tests on genome-scale metabolic models. Such models map the full chemistry of a cell and can include thousands of substances and reactions.

Model quality varies widely between collections, the authors show. Models from modern automated pipelines are internally consistent, while an older collection proved inconsistent in up to half its entries. Key gene-to-reaction rules are also often missing. MEMOTE checks these points in a uniform way and scores each model. Shared testing should raise the trust researchers can place in metabolic models.
openalex-w3027520426:
S. Abdollahi, F. Acero, M. Ackermann, and colleagues of the Fermi team published this catalog in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series in 2020. It is the fourth source catalog from the Large Area Telescope aboard the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. Gamma rays are the most energetic form of light.

The catalog rests on the mission's first eight years of science data and is the deepest yet in its energy range. It doubles the exposure of the third catalog and adds several analysis improvements, including a fresher model of our own galaxy's glow. Each listed source is a gamma-ray emitter in the sky, from pulsars to distant galaxies. Astronomers use the catalog as a map for follow-up study.
openalex-w3133277826:
Nikolaos Kyriakidis, Andrés López-Cortés, Jorge Vásconez-González, and colleagues wrote this review in npj Vaccines in 2021. It surveys vaccine strategies against SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19, focusing on candidates that had reached final phase three trials. By early January 2021 the pandemic had killed more than one point eight million people.

Most leading candidates aim to raise antibodies that block the viral spike protein and stop it latching onto human cells. Growing evidence on the role of T cells pushed some designs to favor cellular immunity as well. Others use whole killed or weakened virus to draw a broader response. The review compares these platforms, their trial designs, and their early results for readers judging a crowded field.
openalex-w4206133226:
Rainer Bussmann, Narel Paniagua-Zambrana, Inayat Ur Rahman, and colleagues catalogued the food plants and fungi of Georgia. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine in 2021. Georgia sits in the Caucasus biodiversity hotspot, and farming there is at least six thousand years old. The team asked how plant use in home gardens and wild gathering compares with nearby regions.

Between 2013 and 2019 they interviewed more than three hundred eighty people across the country, in their homes and gardens. The interviews, held in many local languages, recorded nearly twenty thousand uses. In all they documented four hundred seventy-four kinds of food plants and fungi. The survey shows deep local knowledge, alongside early signs of knowledge loss.
openalex-w4220969226:
Nsikak Benson, Omowumi Agboola, Omowunmi Fred-Ahmadu, and colleagues review micro- and nanoplastics in water life, in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2022. These tiny plastic particles now appear in rivers, lakes, beaches, and oceans, even near the poles. Wastewater plants can pass them into freshwaters instead of removing them. Their amount in aquatic systems is projected to keep climbing for decades.

The review covers how common these particles are, how they move through food webs, and how toxic they prove to water organisms. Small size lets them enter the bodies of tiny animals at the food web's base. From there they can pass upward to fish and beyond. The authors gather scattered findings into one assessment for researchers and regulators.
openalex-w4411251826:
Asahi Hirata, Miho Sumiyoshi, Hazuki Fujita, and colleagues hunt for rare signalling molecules in Streptomyces bacteria. Their paper appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2025. One strain makes two antibiotics, lankacidin and lankamycin. Small butenolide signals switch that production on.

The team tested more than a hundred other Streptomyces strains for the same signals. Almost none could restart antibiotic output in a signal-less mutant strain. Only one known producer strain succeeded. A related signal from another species also failed, even at high doses. A slightly altered signal molecule proved inactive too. The pattern and the chemistry show these signals are rare and highly specific to each strain.
openalex-w7125123226:
Chinenye Iguh, Edith Nwandiko, Asya Azad, and colleagues study sleep apnoea and hidden heart disease risk in obese adults. Their study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. It is an international cross-sectional study. Obesity alone affects nearly a quarter of adults worldwide.

Obstructive sleep apnoea repeatedly blocks the airway during sleep. The broken sleep and oxygen dips strain fat tissue and metabolism. Both conditions share pathways toward heart disease. The study examines whether apnoea marks higher risk of subclinical ischemic heart disease. That is heart damage present before symptoms appear. Finding such a link would argue for screening obese patients with apnoea early, while prevention can still change outcomes.
openalex-w7125428726:
Yu Zheng, Yanhui Zhao, and Shunji Takahashi review enzymes that borrow charged transfer RNAs to build natural products. Their review appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2026. Charged tRNAs normally feed amino acids into protein synthesis. Some microbes instead use them as building blocks for other molecules.

The review opens with the making of ascamycin, an antibiotic nucleoside. A key enzyme there was found with an AI-guided prediction approach. The authors then model several enzyme families with modern structure prediction. They detail how each family catalyses its reaction. These enzymes expand the known uses of tRNA in chemistry. Understanding them opens routes to engineered antibiotics and other valuable compounds.
openalex-w7204124426:

Refractory depression fails to improve after at least two different antidepressant treatments. The authors searched two databases for the last ten years of work and selected fourteen studies, including clinical trials and case reports.

The therapy showed high effectiveness, especially for patients with severe symptoms or additional psychiatric conditions, and it is treated in the literature as a first-line option for this group. Its antidepressant action is linked to brain chemistry changes, improved neural plasticity, and growth factors, though the mechanism is not fully understood. Possible adverse effects demand careful use, the authors stress.

Elise Gabrieli Wisniewsky Trevisan led a Portuguese-language narrative review, published in Brazil in 2026, on how cycling affects the nervous, hormonal, and immune systems. Cycling is widely practiced as sport, leisure, and transport. Searching three databases for 2015 to mid-2026 publications and screening to fifty-nine papers, the team synthesized evidence across the three regulation and defense systems.

Regular, adapted cycling favored mood, well-being, and executive functions, they report. Moderate to hard efforts produce acute cortisol and testosterone responses, while training softens the hormonal response to the same effort. Regular practice links to better immune surveillance and lower population infection risk, though high loads with poor recovery, sleep, or fueling can raise vulnerability. Temporary white cell changes after effort should not alone be read as immune suppression.

Bruno Jose Smek and João Edmilson Fabrini released a Portuguese-language paper in Brazil in 2026 on rural settlers, politics, and republican ideals outside channels. Focusing on agrarian reform settlements in western Paraná, the authors investigate how settlers' experiences and living standards shape their political engagement and their conditional appreciation of republican ideals. Their politics, the study notes, shows up in forms that follow the settlers' own needs and conveniences rather than party or routines.

By examining the history of land struggles and the role of movements such as the MST. The landless workers' movement, the paper offers a detailed analysis of the dynamics between politics and agrarian reform in Brazil. It contributes to understanding how participation works where institutions are thin.

Bianca Magro Cardoso, Giani Petri, and Ricardo Tombesi Macedo test whether Scratch can strengthen math thinking in high school. Scratch is a free block-based coding tool created at MIT, built for learning by making. The team combined a literature review with hands-on classroom work at a state school in Rio Grande do Sul.

Students first played a math logic game built in Scratch, then wrote their own code and deepened the ideas behind it. The authors report that the tool supported learning, sharpened logical reasoning, and made lessons livelier and easier to enter. Their study offers teachers a worked example of coding used not as a separate subject, but as a way into mathematics itself.
openalex-w7206190426: Veronica da Silveira Leite leads a team of eight authors in an overview of systematic reviews on preventing anxiety disorders, published in 2026 in the journal Research, Society and Development. The available sample gives the title, authors, and journal only, without an abstract. The work's stated scope is interventions meant to prevent the first onset of anxiety disorders and to prevent relapse after recovery.
openalex-w7211884526:
Hyusnaia Kenia de Medeiros Santos leads a team studying the school inclusion of a student with autism at a public school in Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil. Laws have widened access for autistic students into ordinary classrooms, yet real inclusion still runs into teacher training, school organization, curriculum adaptation, and weak support networks. The authors follow one case at a state school in Parnamirim, reading the accounts of a teacher, a family member, and a psychopedagogue.

Through those three voices, the study traces how the student was identified, what interventions followed, and how support was maintained over time. The case shows inclusion as daily work shared among school, family, and specialists, not a placement decision made once. For teachers facing the same situation, the value lies in seeing the obstacles named plainly and the practices that grew around one real student.
openalex-w7213423026:
Kaline Sousa dos Santos leads a review on physiotherapy for motor growth in children with autism. Their 2026 review searched health databases in March 2026. Five studies from 2021 to 2026, freely available, made the final sample.

Approaches studied included motor physiotherapy, psychomotor work, structured exercise, and sensory integration. Water therapy and horse-based therapy also appeared. Benefits included better coordination, balance, posture control, and motor planning. Daily life function improved as well, the authors report. They conclude that physiotherapy plays a central part in motor development for these children, supporting greater autonomy and social inclusion over time.
openalex-w7213968826:
Aniely de Souza dos Santos leads a team on play and the development of neurodivergent children. Their 2026 literature review gathers papers and documents from digital platforms. Neurodiversity is treated as natural variation in brain function, and early childhood schooling is the setting.

Play, when planned with intent, supports cognitive, emotional, and social growth, the results indicate. It encourages communication and peer interaction, strengthens bonds, and promotes emotional self-regulation. Schools and educators should treat play as real pedagogy, the authors argue, not as a pause from it. In inclusive settings above all, play belongs inside educational practice in a significant, deliberate way.
openalex-w7218493526:
Caroline Barros Cordeiro, Taiana Renata Siqueira, and Paloma Tainá França Cardoso Nogueira ran a 2026 systematic review on Pilates as therapy for abdominal diastasis. Diastasis is the separation of the belly's paired muscles along the midline, weakening trunk function and stability. Pilates trains strengthening, control, and stabilization of the trunk muscles, a plausible match. Searching five databases, they included primary studies from 2015 to 2025 and kept four after screening.

Three of the four studies observed a reduction in the gap between the muscles, while one, carried out during pregnancy, found none. Improvements in abdominal strength and endurance and reduced lower back pain also appeared. Pilates looks effective for narrowing the separation in most of the small evidence base. It can be considered an applicable physiotherapy resource, the authors conclude, though the studies differ enough to limit generalization.
openalex-w7220739326:
In 2026, Luanna Rodrigues de Oliveira and André Manoel Correia dos Santos wrote on functional nutrition against the exposome in adolescence, the total of exposures taken in over a life. Adolescence is a window when the body is highly plastic and the reproductive axis restarts, so food and metabolic factors can interact with pubertal maturation. Their review covers hormone disruptors, gut microbiota, gene switching, and bioactive food compounds.

Xenoestrogens, foreign compounds that mimic estrogen, take center stage, above all zearalenone, a fungal toxin in cereals and products, which binds estrogen receptors. Such disruptors can meet hormonal, metabolic, and neuroendocrine paths of maturing, with gut microbes and epigenetic changes taking part. Parts of food might tune the body's clearance of toxins, its antioxidant response, and metabolic pathways. But current evidence cannot show that steps through food neutralize or prevent these effects; clinical and population studies are still needed.
pero-tafur-travels-letts-1926:
Pero Tafur was a Castilian knight who roamed the late medieval world. His Travels and Adventures cover the years 1435 to 1439 abroad. Malcolm Letts put the old Spanish account into English in 1926.

Tafur visits Constantinople, the Holy Land, Egypt, and the courts of Italy. He notes ships, relics, markets, and the manners of each great city. His eye is curious, shrewd, and often frankly amused by strangers. Few books show the 1400s through one traveler's eyes so well. Readers rank it among the most fun travel works of its century by far. Tafur's voice stays fresh, bold, and plainly human throughout.
plaw-119-1-2026: Private Law 119-1, approved on March 26, 2026, concerns one Marine and the Medal of Honor. The law lets the President award that medal to James Capers, Jr., setting aside the normal time limits for such awards. The honor is for acts of valor as a member of the Marine Corps in the Vietnam War. The acts took place from March 31 through April 3, 1967, and Capers had earlier won the Silver Star for them.
plaw-119-100-2026: Public Law 119-100 is Lulu's Law, approved on June 26, 2026 by the 119th Congress. The law deals with the wireless emergency alert system, which sends warnings to mobile phones. Within one hundred eighty days, the Federal Communications Commission must issue an order on alerts. The order must state that a shark attack is an event for which an alert message may be sent.
plaw-119-101-2026:
