pmc-13293426:
Qianyao Yuan and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study, scans and tissue traits of a rare lung cancer that mixes two cell types. Adenosquamous carcinoma holds both glandular and squamous parts, acts aggressively, and is hard to spot before surgery.

Scans and records covered 27 patients with the mixed cancer, plus 40 each with pure glandular or pure squamous cancer, matched by age, sex, and smoking. Mixed tumors sat more toward the lung edge than squamous ones and spread to lymph nodes more often. Against glandular ones, they were larger and more often solid. A combined scan-plus-tissue model split the types best, aiding pre-surgery calls.
pmc-13293726:
Chadi Bourimi and co-authors untangle, in a 2026 case report, repeated urethral bleeding during sex in a 39-year-old man with no injury or fracture. Bleeding during erection usually hints at a torn penis cover or urethra, neither of which fit here.

The man was using outside testosterone. A scope showed a small focal defect in the urethra lining, and dynamic MRI found a 4 mm blood pocket with early leak from a tiny branch of a deep penile artery. With bleeding stopped on its own and the patient stable, doctors chose watchful care. Healing was complete at three months with good function.
pmc-13293926:
Xiaowei Li and coauthors survey 4,456 college students from five universities in Sichuan Province for a 2026 study on short video addiction and resilience. Mean age was 20.34 years, and 52.1% were female. Students rated video addiction, belief in a just world, meaning in life, and resilience, and the team tested chain pathways between them.

Heavier addiction predicted lower resilience. Three indirect paths mattered: through just-world belief alone, through meaning alone, and through belief then meaning in order. Together indirect paths made up 62.5% of the total link. Meaning in life was the closest correlate of resilience, which points to layered campus support.
pmc-13294126:
Yingling Luo and Tao Quan chart passing networks by pitch zone at the UEFA Women's Euro 2025 in a 2026 social network analysis. The field was split into 48 zones, and six network measures were compared by match outcome, tournament stage, score state, and match half. Four situational lenses show how space use shifts under pressure.

Winning sides built stronger bridging links and used the flanks more. As play moved from groups to knockouts, hubs shifted from the defensive third toward midfield, with steadier circulation up front. Trailing teams crowded central zones but lost local structure, while second halves showed weaker connectivity overall. Drills on wide link play follow from the patterns.
pmc-13294226:
Wang Tao and colleagues frame diabetic nerve damage as an energy failure in a 2026 review. Long nerve fibers in the common stocking-glove pattern need heavy energy supply, and high blood sugar alone no longer explains their decay. Glucose, fat, and amino acid handling all go off balance, starving both neurons and their Schwann support cells.

Anatomy, energy pathways, and fiber-support teamwork are integrated into one account of how supply and demand drift apart. Fixing a single pathway is unlikely to stop or reverse damage, the authors argue. Restoring overall energy balance in both cell types offers the stronger path to preserving nerve function.
pmc-13294426:
Marco Finocchiaro and coauthors catalog staph germs on healthy eyes in a 2026 typing study. Eye swabs from 49 adults aged 18 to 77 gave 120 germ samples. Of these, 68 proved to be staph by mass tests and gene tests. Drug strength, clone prints, and key genes were charted across three staph types.

One type, Staphylococcus aureus, made up 74% of staph finds in the reported share. Shield rates ran high for three common drugs. Close to half the strains shrugged off many drugs at once. Clone prints were highly mixed, with one clone at times shared across adults. Healthy eyes can hold drug-tough germs.
pmc-13300026:
Sixteen seasons of United States influenza hospital data form the basis of a 2026 analysis by Hayden D. Hedman. Working with FluSurv-NET records from 2009–2010 through 2024–2025, Hedman split the timeline into pre-pandemic, disruption, and recovery phases. The aim was to measure how burden, seasonal timing, and racial gaps changed across the COVID-19 years.

Peak weekly hospitalization rates nearly doubled after the pandemic, rising from 5.1 to 11.1 per 100,000 people. Seasonal peaks also arrived earlier, and yearly patterns grew far more regular. Black patients faced rates roughly twice those of White patients in every phase. Forecasting and anomaly tools both flagged recent seasons as departures from pre-pandemic expectations.
pmc-13300926:
A cheap index built from two routine blood values may flag completely blocked heart arteries, Yan Li and colleagues report in a 2026 retrospective study. They reviewed 1,157 coronary angiography patients treated at Beijing Chaoyang Hospital between January 2024 and January 2026. The triglyceride–glucose index, a stand-in for insulin resistance, was compared between 317 patients with chronic total occlusion and 840 without.

Patients with a blocked artery averaged a TyG index of 8.98 against 8.79 in the others. Each step up in the index raised occlusion odds, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.377 overall. The link held across age, sex, and health subgroups, bending rather than running straight in dose-response curves.
pmc-13301126:
Life at the edge of survival invents unusual chemistry, and Daniela Giordano introduces a 2026 special issue of Marine Drugs devoted to bioactive molecules from extreme environments. The editorial frames the third edition of a series running since 2019, set against a MarinLit catalogue now listing 44,710 marine compounds.

Hydrothermal vents, briny basins, polar seas, and the deep ocean push organisms toward novel defenses and signals with drug, cosmetic, and industrial promise. The issue gathers eleven contributions, eight original studies and three reviews, spanning those harsh habitats. Giordano's overview threads the papers together and points readers toward the work closest to their own questions, while noting how much remains unexplored.
pmc-13302026:
Operating early on a squeezed cervical cord paid off for most patients in a 2026 Italian case series by Michele Incerti and colleagues. Fifty-one people had neck spine surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy at the Policlinico di Monza between 2020 and 2023. Three quarters started with mild cord scores, and recovery was tracked with neurological scales and the SF-36 survey.

At follow-up, sixty-five percent had recovered fully, twenty-nine percent improved, and the rest held steady, with nobody worse. A mild starting score independently predicted complete recovery in adjusted analysis. Quality-of-life gains showed in mood, social life, pain, and general health, strongest in mild cases. Complications were few, at 5.8 percent, and limited to passing swallowing trouble.
pmc-13302426:
Curved magnetic fields could let MRI scanners image just the region that matters, Emre Kopanoglu and colleagues propose in a 2026 methods study. Nonlinear gradients encode space along two directions at once, so standard slice pulses can excite rounded sub-volumes directly. The team worked out the smallest field of view a study must encode and tested a Z2 harmonic field in simulations and phantom scans.

Against one-dimensional slice selection, scan time fell while tissue heating, measured as SAR, stayed unchanged. Against two-dimensional selective pulses, the method won on SAR, echo time, and scan time together. Faster reduced-volume imaging without exotic pulses is the practical promise for SAR-limited sequences.
pmc-13303626:
Ling Wang and co-authors offer a 2026 critical review proposing city fountains that grow microalgae to capture carbon. Algae systems can store carbon dioxide and yield useful biomass, but costly, energy-hungry reactor designs limit their spread.

Retrofitting existing fountains would reuse public infrastructure in busy places, cutting setup costs. Fountain-style growing methods may raise biomass output, while visible displays could teach passersby about carbon and prompt greener habits. The review weighs gains for developers, city governments, and residents, and draws on work in suspended cultures, building-mounted reactors, and landscape design. A shared plan for wider city use is laid out.
pmc-13303726:
Wei Zhang and Jianlou Yang report a 2026 randomized trial of planned exercise for mental health in Chinese college students. Stress, anxiety, and low mood are common in this group, but strong trial proof for structured programs has been scarce.

A total of 120 students with mild to moderate symptoms were split among team sports, solo aerobic exercise, and a waitlist group. Both active groups trained three times weekly for eight weeks in hour-long supervised sessions. Depression and anxiety scores fell sharply in both exercise groups and held at one-month follow-up. Resilience rose as well, and team and solo formats worked about equally well.
pmc-13303926:
Hongzhan Ju and co-authors study gadolinium doping in permalloy films for spin electronics in a 2026 physics report. Permalloy damps magnetic motion very weakly, which saves power but limits fast-switching devices that need stronger braking.

Films pairing platinum with permalloy-gadolinium mixes were made by sputtering and probed with spin-torque resonance tests. Adding gadolinium raised damping step by step, peaking at a mid-level dose with more than double the pure value. Charge-to-spin conversion also improved sharply, reaching its best level at a higher dose. Rare earth tuning thus gives device designers two useful dials at once.
pmc-13305326:
Berthe Sabine Mapoko Esson and co-authors present a 2026 case of sudden limb blood loss in a patient with Kaposi's sarcoma, a vessel-born tumor. Blocked limb arteries in cancer patients are usually blamed on body-wide clotting effects of the tumor.

The 51-year-old man had purple skin patches and nodules on both legs for six months and a matching mouth lesion. New HIV treatment had just started. His left leg developed dry gangrene that worsened over time. Because this tumor grows from vessel lining cells, the authors ask whether it can harm limb arteries directly rather than through general clotting.
pmc-13305526:
Kuo-Cheng Lu leads a 2026 review of body-clock disruption and melatonin in chronic kidney disease. The kidney runs its own daily clock guiding filtering, salt handling, and blood pressure rhythm, and kidney failure steadily breaks that timing.

Built-up toxins, oxidative stress, and inflammation suppress clock genes while night melatonin output fades, removing a key repair signal. Melatonin pathways that fight oxidation, calm inflammation, and limit scarring are traced in detail. Nightly supplements improved sleep in dialysis patients in early studies, but proof that they slow kidney decline is still missing.
pmc-13305726:
Braulio Mark Valencia set out a 2026 protocol for mapping what is known about genetic testing in everyday primary care. Rather than testing a treatment, the plan describes how a Campbell evidence and gap map will be built and judged.

Steps cover a systematic search for studies, a visual summary of where evidence clusters, and a clear account of empty areas that need new work. The finished map is meant to help researchers, clinicians and policymakers judge the current landscape at a glance. It should also guide choices about bringing genomic tools into routine front-line care.
pmc-13306026:
Rumbidzai Mugwira tried to recover phosphorus from bay mud dredged at Malmfjärden, Kalmar, in a 2026 early-stage study. The goal was strong phosphorus release with as little metal contamination as possible.

Single washes used citric acid, sulphuric acid, sodium hydroxide or EDTA at two strengths, with acidity also varied in some runs. Stronger mixes and more acidic settings usually pulled out more in the reported results, and sulphuric acid at pH 1 freed the most phosphorus at 46.4% of content. EDTA also performed well, and a two-step wash was tested to balance yield against purity.
pmc-13306126:
Yazhen Zhang proposed a recovery framework after bleeding inside the brain in a 2026 synthesis linking bone, tea and exercise signals. Brain bleeding stroke has few preventive options and a hard recovery path, so the authors seek shared routes that protect vessels.

Tea chemicals, notably EGCG, and exercise products such as lactate and short-chain fatty acids act on common stress and inflammation pathways in the evidence reviewed. Gut microbe shifts toward calming profiles may further steady vessel walls and brain blood flow. Patient education sits inside the plan, aiming to turn daily habits into part of rehabilitation.
pmc-13307826:
Lauren R Finka and co-authors survey in 2026 how cat shelters across the United Kingdom and Ireland assess cats and adopters, manage behaviour, and decide new homes. Their study, part two of a sector wide pair, drew 393 replies from staff and volunteers who do that daily work.

Replies showed that checks on cats and on would be adopters were routine, and that results guided care and homing choices for each cat. How standard or fair those checks were stayed unclear, and practice varied a lot from place to place. Some habits carried a risk of poor welfare for cats. The authors flag clear spots where shared, kinder methods could lift outcomes for cats and staff alike.
pmc-13308326:
Christopher Chadwick and co-authors study in 2026 how flu vaccine know how has been shared between makers, and what helps such sharing succeed for pandemic readiness. They mixed surveys and talks with 24 makers and global experts, plus written records, and charted 18 sharing cases in depth.

Of those cases, 15 transfers finished and 13 led to an approved vaccine for use in people. Past sharing skill, private firm control, and direct two party deals all tracked with faster finish and approval times. State backing for local making and buying ranked as the top aid. Know how also spilled into COVID-19 and routine shots, which widened the gain.
pmc-13308726:
Jie Yang and co-authors run in 2026 a randomised trial of esketamine, given as a single push or as a slow drip, to ward off low mood after caesarean birth. In all, 503 women with no low mood before birth were split among push, drip, and salt water control groups for the test.

At six weeks, low mood struck 9.15 percent of the push group versus 19.33 percent of the control group in the trial. The drip group sat close to the push group, with no firm gap between the two drug routes. Push dosing brought less dizziness and sickness during surgery than drip dosing did overall. Both routes worked alike, so the simpler push may win on comfort.
pmc-13308926:
Nandita Gawande and co-authors give a 2026 account of a rare face case of Schweninger-Buzzi anetoderma, a skin state where elastic tissue fades and loose sacs form. The usual form dots the trunk and upper arms with no symptoms, and face spread is scarce in past reports.

Their patient, a woman aged 36 years, had a soft cheek lump for three years that bulged when she tipped her face left. No drug, hurt, or swelling came before it, and no kin shared the mark in her tale. Naming face anetoderma for what it is can spare needless tests and calm fears about looks, which weigh most on young women.
pmc-13309526:
Sieun Jeon and co-authors present a 2026 study of a soft robot material that reads, stores, and acts on light-based commands. Most soft robots move when told, while the thinking stays in outside electronics. Here, liquid crystal networks joined with silk protein fold command storage, coded display, and movement into one soft body.

Light patterns written into the material can be hidden, shown, and then used to drive shape change without a separate controller. Tests show the platform holding coded images and bending on cue from stored commands. The authors frame the design as a step toward soft machines that process information in their own material. Engineers working on gentle robots and smart materials are the main audience.
pmc-13310726:
Roma Patel and co-editors open a 2026 collection on gene based causes of diabetes. Doctors once treated diabetes as one illness, yet patients with the same blood sugar can differ in the body paths that drive harm. Faults may sit in insulin cells, fat tissue, immune control, or gene switches that turn traits on and off.

Studies in the set span groups in China, India, Pakistan, Qatar, Russia, Sri Lanka, Brazil, and Latin America. Work covers immune signals, gene switches, and gut health, plus tests in diabetic mice. One line links three genes to both immune control and gut function. Together the set pushes care toward types defined by cause.
pmc-13310826:
Venkata Avinash Addanki and co-authors study tiny leaf blister mites on rose family plants in a 2026 paper. Mites that feed on apple, pear, and rowan trees were long seen as one wide ranging pest. New proof hints at hidden species tied to single hosts, which body measures alone may miss.

Gene data from two markers and measures of 28 body traits were joined in one test. Family trees showed strong host based splits, with up to seven deep lines. Apple mites stood apart in body form, while pear and rowan mites overlapped and looked cryptic. Pest control should treat the group as host tied species.
pmc-13310926:
Karen Gambina reports a 2026 case of a triple immune side effect after cancer immunotherapy. A woman aged 77 years got a PD-1 blocking drug for bladder cancer and then grew weak with drooping lids and slurred speech. Tests pointed to joint harm of heart muscle, skeletal muscle, and nerve muscle signaling at once.

Strong steroids, a second immune calming drug, and antibody infusions cleared her symptoms. Blood cell profiling before, during, and after care showed memory killer cells surged at flare. A worn effector cell subset tracked disease activity and shrank with steroids. Cell tracking may guide care for rare immune harms.
pmc-13311826:
Lisa Büttgen and colleagues offer a 2026 systematic review of traits that might show how resilient a chicken is to short shocks such as germs or heat. A resilient bird dips briefly, then bounces back.

The search, run with AI-assisted screening, settled on 33 relevant studies. Most were small or mid-size trials, and most used immune challenges or heat stress as the test shock. Studied traits centered on production measures and immune or disease signs, with about half also tracking genes. Behavior traits were barely studied. The review maps a young field that breeding programs hope to use.
pmc-13311926:
Ji-Won Park and colleagues, in 2026, report a study on a low-weight beta-glucan from the fungus Aureobasidium pullulans against colon cancer cells. Beta-glucans have many body effects, but their anti-cancer routes were unclear.

Treated SW480 colon cancer cells lost viability in a dose and time pattern, with half-maximal doses falling as exposure lengthened. Death signs included active caspases, lost mitochondrial voltage, and freed cytochrome c, marking the intrinsic death path. Blocking caspases rescued cells only partly, so other death routes also ran. Self-eating markers rose too, and a key survival pathway quieted. The compound attacks on several fronts at once.
pmc-13312026:
Aleksander Lühr Hansen and co-authors ask, in a 2026 Danish study, whether the root cause behind a person's type 2 diabetes changes how the disease looks and what harm follows. They sorted 7,867 newly diagnosed adults from a national cohort by whether genes, low birthweight, or lifestyle seemed the main driver.

Groups formed by genes alone differed from the rest: those classed as intrauterine or lifestyle cases had lower insulin sensitivity, higher triglycerides, and more inflammation at diagnosis. Over ten years, major cardiovascular events struck 14.8 percent of the intrauterine group, 13.2 percent of the lifestyle group, and 11.5 percent of the genetic group. The split suggests that cause-based grouping could sharpen risk prediction and care.
pmc-13312126:
Dae Kwan Ko and Federica Brandizzi present a 2026 protocol for running the NEEDLE gene discovery pipeline in plant species that lack a model organism's resources. Finding the transcription factors that switch key genes on or off is central to understanding gene regulation, yet non-model plants have few ready tools for the job.

The protocol covers setting up the computing environment, preparing data, running the analysis, and reading the outputs. NEEDLE chains together RNA sequencing processing, co-expression network analysis, a tree-based network inference method, and promoter conservation checks to rank candidate regulators. The walkthrough uses sorghum stem development, with 11 samples, as its example. The authors note that six or more meaningful samples generally give stable networks, and that the pipeline transfers to other species with suitable data.
pmc-13312526:
Christina Darwish and colleagues report a 2026 case of a patient diagnosed with two B-cell cancers at the same time: Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Blinatumomab, a bispecific T-cell engager aimed at CD19, is approved for the acute leukemia but had barely been explored as treatment for the chronic one.

Given as consolidation therapy for the acute disease, the drug cleared the patient's measurable residual disease. Follow-up checks showed the chronic leukemia clone had been eradicated as well, leaving both diseases in deep remission. The authors note the acute leukemia masked whether the chronic clone would ever have needed treatment on its own. They present the case as evidence that CD19-directed immune therapy can reach across both conditions when they collide in one patient.
pmc-13312826:
Wen-Li Deng and co-authors test, in a 2026 prospective study, whether fine-grained retinal function testing beats the standard letter chart at catching early gains from treatment for diabetic macular oedema. This swelling of the central retina is a leading cause of vision loss, and first-line anti-VEGF injections can improve the retina in ways a coarse acuity score misses.

Fifty-eight patients received conbercept injections and were checked the day before, a day after, and a month after treatment with acuity, retinal imaging, and microperimetry, which maps sensitivity point by point. Microperimetry showed far larger effect sizes and detected improvement within a day. Among 26 patients whose acuity never changed, it still revealed clear functional gains at one month. Starting fixation measures and a triglyceride-glucose index helped predict who would benefit, information the authors say can guide expectations.
pmc-13313226:
Marta Tkachuk and Nataliya Matiytsiv review the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster as a test animal for organophosphate poisoning in work published in 2026. These chemicals cause fast nerve toxicity, stress damage, DNA harm, and slow nerve decay by blocking an enzyme called neuropathy target esterase.

The review covers three kinds of fly tests. Plain flies get the chemicals in food or vapor, and staff score survival, movement, climbing, and enzyme and stress markers. DNA harm is checked with the SMART test and the comet assay. A mutant fly called swiss cheese, whose gene matches the human PNPLA6 gene, models the slow nerve disease apart from the fast nerve effects. Together the tests sort hazards and help find guards against both harm paths.
pmc-13314426:
Giorgia Corli and a large team test the heart harm of a synthetic stimulant in animals in a study from 2026. The drug, 4,4 prime-DMAR, belongs to the aminorex class, acts like amphetamine, and has shown up in poisonings and deaths in adults and teens.

The drug comes in two mirror forms, cis and trans, with unlike effects in the body. The team gave the cis form alone and mixed with the trans form to living animals and tracked heart and breathing action. Such stimulants can speed the heart, strain breathing, and trigger sudden cardiac death, yet lab study of those harms is thin. By splitting the two forms, the work shows which shape drives the acute heart risk, data that can guide care of poisoned patients and drug policy.
pmc-13315426:
Andrea K. Blanchard and co-authors used national survey data in 2026 to track fairness in mother and newborn care in urban India over two decades. They pooled household surveys from 2002 to 2008 and family health surveys run from 2015 to 2021, covering about 200,000 births. Groups were compared by wealth, at public and private care sources.

Coverage of pregnancy, birth, and after-birth care rose a lot, and newborn survival improved to a lesser degree. The team used several inequality measures to judge whether gaps by wealth narrowed, and how the National Urban Health Mission era, begun in 2013, lines up with those shifts.
pmc-13315826:
Yazan Mohsen and colleagues study in 2026 whether recorded sleep apnea marks a distinct group among atrial fibrillation patients treated with ablation. Blocked breathing in sleep is common with this rhythm disorder and may shape both its form and the chance of return after vein isolation treatment.

The main registry held 2,559 first ablation patients treated from late 2021 to mid 2025, with a nested active group of 666 patients given week-long rhythm checks. Documented apnea appeared in 10.5 percent of the registry group and about 10.1 percent of the active subset. Outcomes centered on repeat ablation or shock treatment at the same center.
pmc-13316126:
Arndt Schmidt and colleagues test in 2026 a simpler way to count plant and arthropod interactions from environmental DNA on single flowers and leaves. DNA sampling finds which species are present with ease, but judging how abundant each is remains weak, and replicate filtering methods are slow and costly.

Skipping filtration, the team extracted DNA directly from individual flowers and leaves and compared isolation methods with a standard filtration protocol. Simple precipitation was enough to recover community-level arthropod DNA from single flowers. Using how often a species appears across replicates as a stand-in for abundance could make semi-quantitative monitoring practical. Less lab work per sample means more sites can be checked.
pmc-13316226:
Galit Karpov and colleagues followed teenagers in 2026 to see how emotion processing develops differently in anxiety and mood disorders shaped by childhood adversity. Anxiety and depression peak in onset during adolescence, when frontal brain systems mature, and poor emotion regulation is a shared symptom that adversity worsens.

Youth aged 10 to 17 years, 65 with internalizing disorders and 74 comparison peers, did an emotional working memory task and a rethinking task during scans at start and one year later. Mixed models tracked group and age differences in frontal activity. Disorder youth showed altered development in the left ventral anterior insula. Age shaped some of these paths as the teens grew.
pmc-13316626:
Philip J Batterham and co-authors evaluated, in a 2026 mixed methods study, what helps a one-session digital mental health program, called Helipad, take root in workplaces. The program aims to guide staff toward proper help, and the team drew lessons from a cluster trial.

Interviews with 16 people and survey data from 344 staff showed Helipad beat plain written education on appeal, fit, and ease of use. Workplaces that pushed harder, with extra emails, meetings, and delivery through learning systems, got more staff to join. Ratings held across workplace types. Users praised the wide content but flagged a hard problem: reaching staff who feel no need for support. Leader backing and paid time to finish were key tips.
pmc-13320026:
Huada Tang and co-authors map brain lesions in a rare energy failure illness in a 2026 study of scans from a Beijing hospital. In MELAS, spells that mimic strokes leave swelling in the outer brain layer that can fade again, yet how those patches spread and where they stop was unclear. Records and scans from more than a decade of care were pooled to trace the pattern.

A total of 61 scans from 55 patients were split by fine brain maps, and a math split found eight patch families. Patches favored the back side lobes and tracked with maps of cell link density. Spread looked free inside a zone but held back at zone edges, as if borders fence the harm. The map may help doctors read new spells in this illness.
pmc-13320326:
Murilo Augusto Ferreira and co-authors tell of a single patient seen in 2026 whose rare fat cancer of the sperm cord mimicked a trapped groin hernia. A 55 year old man with a past hernia repair came in with a stuck scrotal mass that looked like the hernia had come back and jammed. Such fat cancers grow slowly and painlessly, so they are often read as far more common groin lumps.

A first surgery found no hernia at all, and scans then pointed to a fatty growth. Wide removal with the testicle on that side gave tissue proof of the cancer. Full removal with clear edges is the gold path for this tumor, and long watch must follow since return is a real risk even years later.
pmc-13320426:
Aragaw Zemene Sendekie and co-authors test fungi that live on seaweed off Kenya for germ killing power in a 2026 study. Sea living fungi are a rich but barely tapped well of new drug leads. Fungi were grown from red and green algae at one coastal site and screened against tough drug proof germs that sicken people.

From 330 fungal strains first sorted by shape, nine active strains were named by gene reads. Extracts in two solvents killed germs across wide zones in dish tests and at low doses in broth, and scope views showed torn germ walls that point to a membrane attack. Extracts also broke up germ films, though most cuts were modest. Two lead extracts held a broad mix of active compounds on chemical scans.
pmc-13323026:
Tianhui Niu and co-authors profile gene changes in a rare cervical cancer tied to Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, in a 2026 single-patient study. Gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma is aggressive and unrelated to HPV, and its appearance in this inherited syndrome is exceptionally rare.

Targeted sequencing and tissue staining covered one well-described patient with stage IB3 disease. Testing found an inherited STK11 change plus tumour changes in KRAS and ERBB3, and strong staining for Claudin18.2 and MUC6 confirmed the gastric character, while p16 stayed negative. Claudin18.2 gives a proven target from gastric cancer care, and ERBB signals offer another lead. The authors propose routine molecular profiling for this cancer type.
pmc-13323226:
Shanshan Han and co-authors build a survival model for breast cancer that joins immune and inflammation signs, in a 2026 single-centre study of 503 surgically treated patients from 2020 to 2025. Recurrence risk varies widely, and standard clinical factors miss part of the immune picture.

Stromal immune cell levels in tissue and a blood-based inflammation index defined three immune types, from favourable to poor. During follow-up, 107 patients had a disease-free survival event in the cohort records. A random survival forest beat Cox and boosting models on accuracy across five years in their comparisons. Staining for CD8 and CD163 supported the grouping, and nodal stage carried the largest weight in the forest model.
pmc-13325126:
Supanit Chungyampin and colleagues make magnetic alginate beads that carry a copper catalyst in a 2026 materials study. The beads let a liquid-phase reaction run and then be fished out with a magnet for reuse.

Beads formed by gelation trapped copper on titanium dioxide plus magnetite inside a sodium alginate shell. Raising magnetite content changed swelling, density, and how well the cargo stayed inside. A mid-level recipe balanced strength against access to the catalyst. In acetic acid hydrogenation, the best bead made 18.69 mg per liter of ethanol, while too little copper starved the reaction and too much clumped. Reuse slowly lowered output, likely from fouling and copper loss.
pmc-13325326:
Ioannis Panagopoulos and colleagues scan fusion genes across sites in high-grade serous ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. These cancers cause most ovarian cancer deaths, and fused genes can flag targets or predict behavior.

RNA sequencing from several tumor sites in each patient showed wide variation between cancers. Most fusions were one-offs, unique to a single tumor, rather than shared events. Protein kinases appeared among fusion partners far more often than chance suggests. Several kinase fusions kept their working catalytic parts intact, which may leave them druggable. Fusion patterns also widened the known reach of DNA repair faults in these tumors. The diversity complicates any one-size marker plan.
pmc-13325726:
Zeen Feng and Yalin Sun report a ten-year result after laser surgery for a misplaced urinary opening in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 50-year-old woman, had doubled kidney drainage systems on both sides and an ectopic ureterocele.

The cyst-like swelling caused repeat urinary infections and urgent leaks. A thulium laser cut through the urethra opened the ureterocele with little heat spread. Ten years on, the upper kidney cortex had thickened from 0.52 cm to 1.14 cm on imaging. Swelling of the kidney had cleared, and symptoms never returned. No second operation was needed. The case backs laser incision as a kidney-sparing fix for adults.
pmc-13325826:
Wendi Guo and co-authors map the cell network behind vessel invasion in endometrial cancer in a 2026 study. Lymphovascular space invasion predicts spread and poor outcomes in the endometrioid type, yet its team mechanics were unclear.

Single-cell sequencing covered three invasion-positive tumors, two negative ones, and two healthy samples. Positive tumors held a restless epithelial subset marked by low oxygen, partial transition traits, and progesterone resistance. Support cells and macrophages jointly rebuilt the matrix and grew new vessels. Signals through LGALS9 quieted T cells inside the niche. Nine genes in cancer cells tied to prognosis were named. The invasion front paired oxygen-starved tumor cells with PD-L1 rich immune cells.
pmc-13328026:
Laura Hertner and co-authors argue for measuring social suffering apart from depression in a 2026 study of displaced Syrians in Lebanon. Standard screens capture illness symptoms, but much burden grows from injustice, poverty, and broken social worlds. They used survey data from 1,228 Syrians gathered in late 2023, comparing a new feeling broken or destroyed scale with a standard depression questionnaire.

The new scale held together well, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.822 in its first Lebanese use, and it correlated only moderately with depression scores, at 0.56 in their sample, marking it as a related but distinct measure. It also reacted more sharply to poverty and neighborhood quality. Aid programs that treat symptoms alone may miss the social wounds driving distress.
pmc-13328426:
Emily Denise Fischman and co-authors test a SUMO pathway blocker against the sleeping sickness parasite in a 2026 study. Trypanosoma brucei causes African trypanosomiasis, and current drugs suffer toxicity and creeping resistance. The parasite needs SUMO tagging for cell division and surface switching, so the team applied ML-792, a blocker of its activating enzyme.

The drug cut overall SUMO tagging and nuclear SUMO levels. It slowed parasite growth in proportion to dose, with potency in the micromolar range. It also scrambled cell cycle patterns, leaving abnormal nucleus and kinetoplast pairings. Blocking one enzyme thus jams several vital processes at once. The SUMO pathway earns a place on the target list for safer antitrypanosomal drugs.
pmc-13329326:
Anjana Roy and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a review of tools that assess Agni in Ayurveda. Agni covers digestion and metabolic factors that vary from person to person. Many questionnaires and clinician tools claim to grade its strength, but their quality is unclear.

The review will search several databases and Ayurveda sources for studies in adults aged 18 or older. Two reviewers will screen and extract data, with a third settling disputes. Checks will cover how well each tool measures what it claims, how steady its scores are, and how practical it is in clinics and research. Quality frameworks named in the plan include QUADAS-2 and COSMIN. Results will be summed up in words and tables.
pmc-13330526:
Özge Karabıyık Acar and colleagues report hormone-making cells inside thyroid tissue in a 2026 study. After full parathyroid removal, parathyroid hormone rarely falls to zero, and the source was unclear. The team soaked fresh tissues in saline for 30 minutes and measured hormone in the fluid from thyroid, other tissues, and healthy parathyroid glands.

Groups held 46 thyroid samples, 46 other tissue samples, and 7 parathyroid samples. Thyroid fluid held far more hormone than other tissues, though far less than parathyroid fluid, in the reported values. Staining showed thyroid-like cells bearing hormone granules. The authors propose a new cell population in thyroid tissue as one source of leftover hormone.
pmc-13330626:
Dominic Santoleri and colleagues probe how a common gene variant shifts liver fat and cholesterol in a 2026 mouse study. The variant affects GKRP, a protein that controls glucokinase, the liver enzyme that starts glucose handling. Mouse models swapped in the human variant form or the standard form after removing the mouse gene.

Variant mice held less GKRP and glucokinase protein and showed higher blood cholesterol in the reported results. Removing liver glucokinase alone copied key effects, with more liver cholesterol and fat plus higher fat-making gene activity. Adding a backup enzyme reversed the pattern. Weak glucose handling thus seems to drive the lipid changes, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331226:
Elizabeth Escamilla-Chávez and colleagues present an operative video of neck spine fusion in a 2026 article. A 33-year-old man fell from over 3 metres and suffered many injuries, including a type II odontoid fracture with the peg shifted back by up to 5 mm into the canal. Ligaments at the skull and neck junction had torn, yet the cord stayed unharmed.

Front screw fixing was ruled out by fracture shape and ligament damage. The team used the Goel-Harms method, placing screws in the first and second neck vertebrae from behind. Alignment was restored during surgery without vessel or nerve harm. Afterward the patient stayed neurologically intact, pain eased a lot, and scans showed stable fixing.
pmc-13331826:
Yao Wang and colleagues investigate the protein KIF7 in clear cell kidney cancer in a 2026 study built from tumor data banks, tissue arrays, and cell experiments. KIF7 levels were much higher in tumor tissue than in nearby normal tissue, and high levels tracked with later stage and shorter survival.

In the 786-O cell line, forcing extra KIF7 made cancer cells grow faster, switched on the Wnt and beta-catenin pathway, and raised growth drivers such as c-Myc and c-Jun. High KIF7 also matched heavier immune cell entry into tumors and higher levels of checkpoint molecules PDCD1 and CD160. Drug prediction tools suggested tumors with high KIF7 might respond better to docetaxel and bleomycin. The authors put KIF7 forward as a marker of outlook and a possible treatment target.
pmc-13333426:
Yan Li and co-authors mapped bedside ultrasound uses in feeding critically ill children in a 2026 scoping review. Tube feeding protects outcomes in pediatric intensive care. But judging nutrition, placing tubes, and watching gut function at the bedside are all hard, and ultrasound has crept into each task without shared rules.

Searching eleven English and Chinese databases to 30 November 2025, the review kept 32 studies from 432 hits. Of those, 65.6 percent were published in the last five years and most were prospective cohorts. Ultrasound served three jobs: measuring muscle mass in 20 studies, guiding feeding tube placement in 6, and gauging stomach contents and movement in 6. Technique varied widely in scanning sites, landmarks, and measures, which blocks comparison between studies. The authors call for standard protocols and training frameworks before the tool can settle into routine pediatric critical care nutrition.
pmc-13336226:
Richard Augusto Thomann Beckert and co-authors listened to older adults who had lost a child in a 2026 qualitative study from Brazil. Outliving a child reverses the expected order of life, and the study asked how that grief unfolds and what nursing can learn from it.

Eight older adults, recruited by snowball sampling, gave semi-structured interviews analyzed with the Discourse of the Collective Subject technique. Themes covered how grief for a child differs from other losses, the feelings death triggers, how long they last, what never leaves, and how people cope. Acceptance proved possible, yet longing and absence stayed. Faith and support networks carried much of the coping. The authors argue nurses can play a real supporting role if they understand this particular grief.
pmc-13336426:
Chaoyang Sun and co-authors showed that the microstructure of a zinc implant alloy decides whether bone heals or inflames in a 2026 biomaterials study. Metal implants fail when ion release drives inflammation and bone loss, and galvanic coupling inside the alloy sets that release rate.

In zinc with 0.8 percent magnesium, fine Mg2Zn11 particles act as sacrificial anodes and slow the matrix dissolving, giving a moderate zinc ion flux. In zinc with 0.8 percent iron, coarse FeZn13 phases flip the geometry, multiplying anodic currents a hundredfold and flooding tissue with zinc. The iron alloy drew massive neutrophil recruitment and inflammatory macrophage dominance, ending in poor bone at day 90. The magnesium alloy instead steered immune cells toward regenerative states and collagen-rich bone growth.
pmc-13336626:
Jintong Zhao and colleagues propose a fresh angle on very long-range forecasting in a 2026 methods article. Forecasters often use known helpers such as seasons, yet errors still pile up over thousands of steps. The team shows that, in linked systems, knowing a future effect can steady predictions of its present cause.

Their approach feeds such known future states in as anticipated covariates, a kind of advance helper data. Tests on widely used benchmark sets found much lower errors over ultra-long spans under the right conditions. The idea may help where past data are scarce, costly, or partly hidden. It also invites a rethink of how cause and effect run across time.
pmc-13337126:
Teresa M Thomas and co-authors link a mitochondrial protein to epigenetic stability in Alzheimer's neurons in a 2026 study. CHCHD10 sits inside mitochondria and was tied to other degenerative diseases, but its Alzheimer's role was undefined. Neurons grown directly from patient skin cells keep donor epigenetic marks, making them a faithful test bed.

Alzheimer's neurons showed genome-wide under-methylation like postmortem cortex, and CHCHD10 was reduced across several human datasets. Restoring it cut amyloid-beta and insoluble tau build-up and reversed disease-linked methylation changes at islands, promoters, and control regions. A downstream gene, KATNAL2, carried part of the tau effect. The pathway ties energy failure to epigenetic drift in Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-13337426:
Maha Barbar and co-authors review severe fat spikes in children on leukemia therapy in a 2026 single-center report. At King Hussein Cancer Center, 598 children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia were treated between January 2021 and February 2026. Twelve developed severe triglyceride elevation above 1,000 mg/dL after asparaginase, an incidence of 2% in the cohort.

Most cases, 83% in the series, caused no symptoms and were spotted only by milky blood samples; one child had pancreatitis and one a hyperviscosity syndrome. Median peak triglycerides reached 2,645 mg/dL in the affected group. All received fluids, omega-3 fats, and fibrates, most needed insulin drips, and three underwent plasma exchange. The series maps timing and treatment for a rare but dangerous side effect.
pmc-13339626:
Wei-Kai Shao and Mu-Jeng Cheng build a fragment model for twisted helicene molecules in a 2026 study. Multiple helicenes have huge numbers of mirror and twist variants, and full quantum calculation scales far too steeply. Their model adds up local energy pieces from double fragments instead.

Seven known molecules validated the approach, with energy patterns and true lowest forms matched as reported. A designed giant with 10,944 variants was steered to a symmetric form about 300,000 times faster than full calculation in the reported speedup. Symmetry also raised long-wave optical purity by 82 percent as modeled. Designers gain a fast blueprint for chiral architectures.
pmc-13341426:
Measuring a plant hormone in tough pecan tissue is made practical in a 2026 methods study by Mohadeseh Jahanifard and colleagues. ELISA testing for gibberellic acid is cheap and reliable, but hard, metabolite-rich pecan buds and bark resist standard handling.

Trials varied sample amounts, tissue-to-methanol ratios, and drying methods. Using about 0.0125 g of heat-dried or freeze-dried tissue at a low solvent ratio gave consistently strong readings, and hormone levels stayed stable after long storage at −80 °C. Buds held more gibberellic acid than bark, and bark values predicted bud values well, which helps when bud material is scarce.
pmc-13341526:
Non-motor symptoms foreshadow speech decline in Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 study by Rui Liu and Ciara Leydon. Data came from 417 participants in the Parkinson's Progression Marker Initiative, followed over seven years with speech rated by both patients and examiners.

Baseline REM sleep behavior disorder raised the odds of worse speech at year seven (OR 1.58 for self-rated), as did autonomic dysfunction (OR 1.71). Examiner ratings showed a similar pattern. Since speech loss erodes well-being and self-awareness of decline varies widely, early non-motor clues could prompt timely speech therapy referrals before communication suffers badly.
pmc-13341826:
Who pays when AI products cause harm is compared across Europe and Canada by Jawahitha Sarabdeen in a 2026 legal study. Industries and consumers both want clarity, and the analysis combines a systematic literature review with doctrinal and comparative legal methods.

Proving fault in AI systems is hard, so the study favors strict liability, or a causation presumption that defendants may rebut. That protects users and pushes every party in the chain toward safety. The EU's new directives handle AI liability more completely than Canada's draft law, though gaps remain. Concrete fixes are proposed for Canadian rules on fault, remedies, court roles, and shared liability.
pmc-13342226:
Kathy Liu and colleagues report a 2026 population study of COVID-19 care use and costs in Alberta, Canada. Working from a provincial database, the team asked how age, sex, and deprivation, both social and material, shaped hospital and community care. The adults all had confirmed infection between March 2020 and December 2021.

Older patients and men carried higher total costs, while emergency visits dropped among people over 50. Deprivation raised total spending and emergency and inpatient costs, with material deprivation linked to faster first admission and social deprivation weighing more on outpatient care. The findings show how pandemics load costs unevenly and can guide fairer planning for future outbreaks.
pmc-13343126:
Yipeng Ge and Bilal Irfan write a 2026 commentary on free speech limits inside professional medical bodies and schools. Ge recounts attending the Ontario Medical Association annual meeting on May 7, 2026, where staff asked him to remove an embroidered watermelon pin under new guidance banning displays with messaging.

Ge refused and was escorted out. The authors argue the watermelon, a symbol of Palestinian identity, was singled out while the association speaks freely on other political questions and lobbies government openly. Rules framed as safety and comfort, they contend, can work as selective silencing of Palestinian solidarity. The piece urges medical institutions to face that double standard directly.
pmc-13343226:
Hui Ye and co-authors look for blood markers of postpartum depression in twin pregnancies, in a 2026 retrospective study. Depression after birth harms mothers and children, and immune imbalance is suspected in its roots, yet twin pregnancies had barely been studied, so the team mined routine admission blood counts.

Records covered 846 women who delivered twins at one hospital between 2022 and 2024, with mood screened within four weeks of birth. Symptoms appeared in 145 women, about 17 percent. After full adjustment, higher neutrophil counts and a higher lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio raised the odds, while a lower platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio also tracked with symptoms. Cheap blood markers might flag mothers needing closer mood checks.
pmc-13343526:
Dorota Górniak and co-authors compare survival playbooks of local and worldwide bacteria in Antarctic microbial mats in 2026. Mats dominate land biomass at the poles, and the team asked whether species found only in Antarctica eat and tolerate conditions differently from species that live almost everywhere.

From 43 isolates, 21 strains belonged to 12 endemic species and 22 to 16 cosmopolitan ones. Fingerprint plates showed cosmopolitan strains burned through about half the offered foods, while endemics used only a third, with clear gaps in sugar alcohols, amino acids, and sugar acids. Some cosmopolitan strains paired broad diets with tough tolerance, a mix that could crowd out natives and flatten polar communities.
pmc-13349726:
Vincent Xiao and colleagues question whether model-made exam questions can truly test eye doctors, in a commentary from 2026. A recent pilot had ten eye specialists rate 121 board-style questions, 64 made by ChatGPT-4o and 57 written by people, across five quality areas. Scores looked near identical with most model items fresh against the source bank.

Surface polish is not proof of clinical depth, the authors warn, since rater agreement was only moderate overall and near chance within single areas in the study discussed. Skipping set validation while scaling a flawed format could flood training with pretty questions that fail to measure real competence, a governance worry for medical testing.
pmc-13349826:
Réka Losonczi and a large team studied sex differences in heart damage from the cancer drug trastuzumab in a 2026 rat experiment. Male and female Wistar-Hannover rats received either saline or repeated trastuzumab doses, with heart scans at weeks 12 and 19.

By week 12, treated rats of both sexes showed early diastolic problems, where the heart relaxes poorly. At week 20 the team measured genes and tryptophan breakdown products in heart tissue tied to stress, inflammation, and energy use. Mapping how damage unfolds in each sex may explain why some patients develop lasting heart trouble on trastuzumab and point to markers that give early warning.
pmc-13349926:
Akshita Joshi and a large team reviewed quick smell tests for use during ordinary clinic visits in a 2026 narrative review. Loss of smell can signal brain diseases, infections such as COVID-19, mental illness, and ageing, yet testing is rarely done in routine care.

Well-known tools such as the UPSIT and Sniffin' Sticks are compared with newer rapid screens, child-friendly versions, and tests adapted for different cultures. The review separates quick screening from full diagnostic sets and weighs accuracy, cost, ease of use, and fit for primary care, neurology, and ear, nose, and throat clinics. Making smell checks practical could surface hidden disease earlier.
pmc-13350526:
Jianming Wang and colleagues applied reinforcement learning in 2026 to plan tree thinning in secondary Yunnan pine forests on Cangshan Mountain. These forests often grow in tangled, uneven structures that limit their ecological value, and older optimisation methods were slow or unstable.

Their approach treats each tree as a decision unit and uses a clipped policy algorithm, tuned automatically by Bayesian search, to pick removals. Slopes steeper than 45 degrees were barred from cutting to protect the site. Smarter, site-aware thinning plans could restore forest structure and function without the damage careless logging causes.
pmc-13352626:
Tom J. Smak and co-authors trace how oxygen plus nitrogen oxides cut carbon chains in plain alkanes in 2026. Selective oxidation is hard because carbon-hydrogen bonds are strong and full burning to carbon dioxide is easy. The team used n-decane as a model chain to catch and count short-lived intermediates.

Nitrites, nitrates, alcohols, and ketones appeared along the path, funnelling into shared ketone forms. Those forms became diketones and related compounds, then carboxylic acids. Infrared checks showed polyethylene plastic follows the same key steps. The mapped route gives chemists a base for gentler oxidative recycling of hydrocarbon plastics, aiming at useful acids rather than waste gas.
pmc-13354526:
Ebone E Bady and co-authors studied nerve problems in children with brain tumors in a 2026 report. They looked back at 109 young patients who had weak or lost nerve function linked to their tumor or its care. Most had tumors at the back of the brain, and many of their nerve problems did not go away.

Face weakness and eye movement problems were the most common issues in the group. Only about one in five children was sent to ear, nose, and throat doctors, even though more than half of those not sent never got better. The authors argue that earlier, more routine referrals could help more children regain key functions.
pmc-13355826:
Serdar Charyyev and co-authors present NeRP-MC in 2026, a neural network method to shrink the huge data files used in radiation therapy dose planning. Monte Carlo simulation is the gold standard for dose math, but its particle files can reach gigabytes. Their network learns to predict particle energies from position and direction data for proton beams.

The trained network needs only 600 kilobytes versus three gigabytes for the raw file, and it predicts the energies of 25 million particles in under half a second. Dose patterns in water matched the reference closely, even when trained on twentyfold less data. The authors see gains for speed and storage in clinic planning.
pmc-13356026:
Qian Chen and co-authors present a Smart Data Hub in 2026 to support choices on underground sites for nuclear waste storage in Germany. Picking a disposal site is long and sensitive, and simulation models need data that are open and repeatable. Their hub pairs a dataset with a tool that assembles data packs for a given rock structure.

The dataset draws on 50 published sources covering geology, structure, and rock traits for candidate sites, with uncertainty noted. The assembly tool tags and filters data while keeping it intact. The authors argue this gives model-based decisions a reliable, clear data base for a process that must look thousands of years ahead.
pmc-13358826:
Molly Tokaz and co-authors compare two platinum drugs after lung cancer surgery in a 2026 study. For early-stage non-small cell lung cancer removed by surgery, added chemotherapy lowers the risk of return. Cisplatin is the classic choice but is harsh on kidneys and ears. Carboplatin is gentler and often swapped in, though its real-world results were unclear.

Using national data on veterans treated from 2006 to 2020, the team balanced the two groups on key traits and compared survival, cancer return, kidney harm, and hospital stays. Such real-world proof matters because trial patients are often fitter than the people doctors treat every day.
pmc-13359826:
Wei Li and Xi-Ming Yuan report a cell finding on artery disease in a 2026 paper. Inside artery plaques, macrophages gorge on fats. Some oxidized cholesterol forms, called 7-oxysterols, push these cells toward death and stir oxidative stress. The team asked what happens to CD163, a surface protein on one macrophage type thought to steady plaques.

They exposed lab-grown macrophages to a plaque-like mix of the two oxysterols. Surface CD163 fell as the dose rose, and the fall tracked closely with more cell death and more oxidative stress. The authors suggest this surface protein may help macrophages survive in plaques, and its loss may mark growing plaque danger.
pmc-13359926:
Markus Schärer and co-authors sort recurrence patterns in a rare cancer in a 2026 study. Soft tissue sarcomas can come back where they started, spread to distant sites, or do both. Studies usually treat these as separate outcomes, which can hide meaningful patterns. The team instead grouped 668 patients by the full pattern of what actually happened.

Four groups emerged: just over half had no event, about a quarter spread only, and the rest split between local return only and both together. Local return paired with spread behaved aggressively and came early, while local return alone came later and tied more to local treatment. The phenotypes should sharpen future risk models.
pmc-13361626:
Abdulrahman Hamad Aldousari and co-authors pooled trials of esketamine for gallbladder surgery pain in a 2026 analysis. Keyhole gallbladder removal is the standard cure for gallbladder disease, but it often leaves strong pain after surgery. Opioids remain the main treatment, yet they bring nausea and breathing problems. Esketamine blocks a pain-related receptor and might ease pain with fewer opioid side effects.

The team searched five databases through August 2025 for randomized trials of esketamine given around surgery. They combined results on pain scores, blood pressure and heart stability, recovery, and safety. Pooling small trials gives a clearer verdict on whether the drug helps and harms. Surgeons and anesthetists weighing opioid-sparing plans can use these pooled findings to decide where esketamine fits.
pmc-13362726:
Marco Infante and a large team present a 2026 guidance article on iron deficiency linked to the new wave of weight and diabetes drugs. These incretin-based drugs, such as GLP-1 agonists and tirzepatide, cut appetite and food intake, which can quietly drain iron and other nutrients. The article reviews early reports, explains how low intake, gut side effects, and slower stomach emptying may combine, and sets out practical steps for doctors.

The authors note that iron deficiency still looks uncommon on these drugs, but it can progress to anemia if missed. They propose screening habits, diet advice, and treatment options tuned to patients on long-term therapy. Some proposed links, such as vitamin B2 shortage and gut microbe shifts, remain theories that need direct study.
pmc-13363826:
Chenghai Shan and colleagues present a 2026 study comparing four onion varieties with yellow, red, and white bulbs to learn why their quality differs. The team measured bulb size, nutrients, scent compounds, antioxidant strength, and gene activity in parallel. The yellow type gave the biggest bulbs and top phenolic levels, marking it as a strong processing pick.

One red type packed pigment genes that deepen its color, while the other red type led on sweetness-linked scents and antioxidant power, suiting fresh eating and health foods. The white type tasted mild but trailed on yield and protective compounds, fitting raw salads best. The authors frame the results as breeding and marketing guidance by use.
pmc-13365726:
Mingzhe Wu and co-workers map in 2026 how a guard gene reins in sugar flow in cervix cancer cells. The guard, named LKB1, runs low in tumor flesh next to near well flesh. It steers which form of a sugar burn enzyme the cell makes, by a splice choice in its code.

More guard cuts the harsh enzyme form, a growth cue, and the sugar gate on the cell skin. Less enzyme or cue also cuts sugar take in. The guard works through a known cell fuel path. The chain marks fresh aims to starve these tumors.
pmc-13366926:
Sun and colleagues examine the lethal tug-of-war inside elderly, very ill patients whose immune systems are both aging and overreacting, in 2026 ICU research. Aging weakens immune defenses, a process called immunosenescence, yet infection can trigger hyperinflammation, an excessive inflammatory surge. The study enrolled very ill patients with multiple simultaneous infections, admitted between February 2023 and September 2025, and modeled which blood measures predicted death when these opposing forces collide.

The team screened candidate variables, then built a model using elastic net regression, a method that shrinks weak predictors to zero, with ten-fold cross-validation. Low total protein and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, a quotient of two white cell counts, drew focus as death signals. Viral triple infection was forced into the model as a suspected worsener of the immune imbalance. Checking used 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Sun argues fatal results reflect the imbalance itself, not either force alone.
pmc-13370826:
John Choe and co-workers find in 2026 the blood rank of a sun vitamin form that ties to a set drop in a gland hormone gone wild in kidney ill. The gland ill rides weak vitamin work in mid kidney loss. Old sound ranks for the vitamin do not fit this ill.

Pool trial data on a slow release form lets them map dose to reply. A rank near the mid eighties ties to a near third drop in the hormone. High ranks show no ill shift in bone marks. The rank gives care teams a clear aim for this drug.
pmc-13375826:
Jonghoon Chang and co-authors ask if long eye face pain fits a pain group in a 2026 review. Ten long pain ills are known to stack in one person and share brain-based paths. Long eye pain, past three months, is most put down to dry eye alone.

The review sets eye pain next to the group on counts, risks, paths, tests, and care. Eye pain shares much: it is common, hits women more, grows with age, and stacks with the group. The team says some eye pain may be a lost limb of that group. That shift would change tests and care for a pain long brushed off.
pmc-13376326:
Alice Caulfield and co-authors give ten hands-on tips to set up a mind-drug study in a 2026 paper. Such drugs show hope for hard mind ills, but they sit in the top drug ban class in many lands. That rank brings thick rules and high costs to any trial.

The tips span plan, law, and drug source steps. They draw on the team's own non-ward work in the United Kingdom, with notes on what shifts in next lands. Lead checks, safe source, and dose craft lead the list. New teams can save months by the map of snags the team hit first.
pmc-13377126:
Arthur Lemson and co-authors tried a death risk score in Dutch lung patients in a 2026 study. The score was built in South Korea for a slow germ lung ill that is not TB. Five plain facts feed it: weight, age, lung holes, a blood mark, and sex.

The Dutch set held 183 adults seen from 2008 to 2019, most on germ drugs. More than half died in the watch years. The score split 118 folk in low, mid, and high risk sets. How true the score rang far from its home was the ask. A score that holds abroad can travel to new clinics with trust.
pmc-13380126:
Angie Katherine Osorio and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a benign lump under the shoulder blade that can be mistaken for cancer. The condition, called elastofibroma dorsi, is uncommon, so no standard surgical approach has been agreed. Their patient was a woman whose tissue tests confirmed the diagnosis.

She was treated with an operation that removed the lump for examination, with a drain placed to collect fluid afterwards. The team followed her progress for two months after surgery. The report sets out their hospital's approach and compares it with published work. The authors hope wider awareness will help clinicians recognise this harmless growth and avoid treating it as something more sinister.
pmc-13381026:
Asmae Baaziz and Asmaa Mdaghri Alaoui present a 2026 case report from Morocco of an extremely rare inherited brain development disorder linked to a gene called TMX2. The condition causes severe learning disability, a small head, stiffness, epilepsy, and abnormal folding of the brain surface. Their patient was a 13-month-old boy whose parents are cousins.

The baby had severe delays, very weak trunk control, no head control, and a head that grew too slowly. Epilepsy began at seven months. Brain imaging showed abnormal folding on both sides at the front. The examination also found joined toes on both feet, a feature not previously reported with this disorder, which widens its known picture.
pmc-13383826:
Caroline E. Caplan and colleagues simulate space weathering on ice-coated silicon in a 2026 lab study. Airless bodies face electron bombardment, and ice-rich shadowed spots on the Moon and Mercury are prime sites. Earlier work hinted that electrons drive odd oxygen exchange between ice and the surface below at very low temperatures.

Fine infrared mapping showed new silicon-oxygen bonds formed where electrons struck the ice layer. The amount of surface oxidation depended on electron energy, ice amount, and timing of ice placement. Electron images confirmed thicker oxide in zones of strongest interaction, suggesting cosmic rays may reshape cold dust grains more than once thought.
pmc-13385426:
Sumaiyah Z. Shaha and colleagues identify a protein variant that helps placental surface cells fuse in 2026 work. The placenta's outer exchange layer forms when precursor cells merge into one giant shared cell. A Hippo pathway factor normally keeps those precursors in a stem-like state, but its controls were murky.

A newly described form of the protein aPKC, named aPKC-zeta III, runs high in both precursors and the fused layer. It wins a binding spot away from a Hippo kinase, which switches the stemness factor off and lets fusion proceed. The authors cast the variant as a key timing switch for early placental growth.
pmc-13386526:
Tribani Boruah and colleagues scale up an electrochemical reduction by numbering up flow channels in 2026 work. Their reactor runs 16 parallel channels across eight modules with two-sided cathodes, reaching up to 9.2 grams per hour at the 100 gram scale. Residence time stayed at one minute without fresh tuning, they report.

Eighteen examples covered chalcones, ring-bearing enones, esters, ketones, and acids, with broad tolerance for added groups. Average productivity rose 75-fold over the batch method across the set tested. The authors present the platform as a cost-effective route from lab grams toward pilot-scale electrochemical hydrogenation.
pmc-13387426:
Pavel Holeka, Jan Trlica, and Filip Studnicka report a combined transplant and ligament rebuild in a young man's knee in a 2026 case report. The 22-year-old had pain, swelling episodes, and limits after two earlier operations, including a failed ligament rebuild. Scans and scope checks showed severe loss of both menisci plus ligament insufficiency.

One operation delivered fresh-frozen grafts for both menisci and a revision ligament graft from his own kneecap tendon. At six months the knee was stable with motion from 0 to 130 degrees and high function scores. No swelling or graft problems appeared, which supports the joint-preserving route.
pmc-13387626:
Olga Vera-Lastra and colleagues describe an autoimmune syndrome after cosmetic filler and its dissolving enzyme in a 2026 case report. A 35-year-old woman had hyaluronic acid lip augmentation, then developed body-wide symptoms fitting the adjuvant-induced syndrome ASIA. Hyaluronidase given for stubborn symptoms was followed by worsening, not relief.

Features included dryness symptoms, Raynaud's phenomenon, fogged thinking, deep fatigue, and skin that grew lax and over-stretchy. That skin change matched acquired cutis laxa, an unusual turn the authors highlight. High-dose steroids and other drugs brought no clear gain, which argues for early recognition of such reactions.
pmc-13388526:
Elisabet Gomis-Lleal and co-authors systematically review, in 2026, why a serious leak can form after total removal of the larynx. The leak, called a pharyngocutaneous fistula, is the most common major problem after this surgery and can greatly slow recovery.

The review covers cohort studies published from 2010 to 2024 that each included at least 25 adults. Prior radiation, low blood albumin, a breathing tube placed before surgery, and closure without extra flap tissue were the main risks found. Care without surgery healed about seven in ten cases, while flap repair healed about nine in ten. Surgeons and nurses get a graded summary of which risks carry strong proof and which still need better study.
pmc-13390526:
Julia Foldi leads a 2026 prospective study tracking tumour DNA in blood during chemotherapy given before breast cancer surgery. Clearing all invasive cancer by surgery strongly predicts lower relapse risk, and blood tumour DNA may signal that response earlier.

The MONITOR-Breast study enrolled 154 patients across breast cancer subtypes and sampled blood at high frequency using an ultrasensitive residual disease test built from each patient's whole tumour genome. Earlier studies sampled less often with less sensitive tests. Oncologists gain a detailed picture of how blood signals rise and fall during treatment, a step toward using blood tests to adjust therapy before surgery rather than waiting for pathology results.
pmc-13392626:
Una Milovanovic and four colleagues assembled an illustrated guide to infections of the hand, organised by how deep each infection sits. Material comes from the archive of a certified hand surgeon and ranges from surface problems seen daily to deep infections that can threaten the limb. Speed matters here, since the hand's tight compartments let infection spread fast and stiffen fingers if care lags.

Each condition gets its typical look, the tests and scans that help, the germs most often responsible, and first steps in treatment, backed by clinical photographs and imaging. The layout is meant for use at the bedside. It helps staff in emergency, primary, and surgical care judge urgency and pick starting antibiotics. It also spots patients who need a hand specialist or an operation without delay.
pmc-13392826:
Jinquan Sun, Jiayong Cui, Tianlei Qiu, and Guoshuang Shen studied a long non-coding RNA called STEAP3-AS1, a molecule copied from the opposite strand of the STEAP3 gene. The team asked whether it shapes breast cancer behaviour. Database mining and nine paired patient samples both pointed the same way: the RNA runs low in tumour tissue compared with healthy breast. Levels also varied across hormone-defined cancer subtypes.

The RNA also teamed up with its partner gene STEAP3, and together they suppressed migration and invasion further. The authors claim the first evidence that this RNA acts as a tumour brake in breast cancer, and propose it as a lead for future treatment design.
pmc-13393626:
Ercan Mevliyaoğulları analysed a breeder's own registry for Gloster canaries. The fancy breed pairs crested Corona birds with plain-headed Consorts. He asked whether which parent carries the crest changes hatching success or chick type. Twenty pairs at one hobby facility in Adana, Türkiye, were followed through four breeding cycles each. The pairs split evenly between the two directions. They covered two hundred fifty-four eggs on commercial seed and egg food.

Hatchability did not differ significantly by mating direction, nor did the split of crested to plain chicks, which landed almost exactly even overall. What did move hatchability was time: success slid steadily from over ninety percent in the first cycle to about two thirds by the fourth. The author cautions that one facility's retrospective records, kept untouched as recorded, limit how far the findings travel.
pmc-13393826:
Mphatso D Phiri leads a fourteen-author survey of tuberculosis exposure in Blantyre, Malawi, measuring immune reactivity to the TB bacterium in adolescents and adults to see where the sexes diverge. Households were sampled randomly from building footprint data across thirty-three peri-urban neighbourhoods, and two thousand eight hundred thirty-three residents aged ten to forty gave blood for a standard reactivity assay. Bayesian models estimated prevalence by age and sex alongside other risk factors.

About eighteen percent tested positive overall, implying an annual infection risk just under one percent. Boys and girls matched in the teens, and men and women matched in their thirties, but men in their twenties ran clearly higher than women, with male conversion risk peaking at twenty-one. Smoking and drinking, both commoner in men, fed into the gap. The authors frame young adult men as a priority group for TB control.
pmc-13394626:
Tania Warnakulasuriya, Zaid Bahi, and Rohit Ramchandra review, in 2026, how steady pump flow may affect kidneys in heart failure care. Heart pumps called LVADs keep blood moving, but many give smooth flow instead of the natural pulse. Pulse loss can shift nerve signals that raise stress activity and can change nitric oxide release. The review asks what that means for kidney work.

Pulsed flow seems to calm stress nerve activity in lab and clinic reports. Proof that kidneys then work better is weak, though. Most studies were small, looked back at old data, and used rough kidney measures. The authors call for sharper tests of kidney parts in future work.
pmc-13394726:
Masamitsu Kido and co-authors chart, in 2026, ten years of rectal prolapse surgery across Japan. Prolapse lets the rectum slip down and harms daily life.
