Women had surgery far more often than men, and rates peaked in the late eighties. Overall and classic surgery fell over the decade, while keyhole surgery rose. Spring and winter brought more operations than summer, and counts dipped as weather warmed. The authors offer the map for planning surgical care.
pmc-13395426:
Kiera McDuff and a large team recount, in 2026, how bots and fake replies swamped their Long COVID survey. The web survey ran in four countries with people living with the condition. Two rounds of replies were planned one week apart. Fake floods hit the first launch, forcing a pause.

The team built screens for fakes, killed tainted links, and relaunched with new outreach and design. Of thousands of first-round replies, fewer than one in five were kept. The second round kept about half. Tricks that helped included hiding the payment offer, skipping open social media, and checking reply speed and place. The authors share a playbook for survey defence.
pmc-13395826:
Kimlin Ashing and a large team build, in 2026, a survivorship care toolkit shaped for Black men after prostate cancer. Black men carry the heaviest load of this cancer of any group. The team reviewed care guidance, built consensus with stakeholders, and interviewed Black survivors in depth. Twenty-two survivors then reviewed and tailored the kit.

The kit grows a standard roadmap with family history, care team contacts, and follow-up plans. It adds symptom care, quality of life, major other illnesses, and resources that fit Black survivors' lives. Survivors rated it credible and useful for talks with doctors. The authors pitch it as a tool to lift activation and follow-up care.
pmc-13396326:
Malin Schulze and co-authors validated a sensor-based motor test for hereditary spastic paraplegia, a group of inherited disorders that stiffen the legs and can quietly affect the arms too. Their 2026 study argues that simple clinic scores miss mild arm problems and early disease.

Forty-one patients with varied genetic types, averaging 48 years old, performed rapid foot tapping, alternating hand movements, and finger tapping against a precise force sensor. Their results were set against 48 matched healthy controls and against the standard spastic paraplegia rating scale and patient reports. Sensitive digital measures like these could make future treatment trials able to spot small changes.
pmc-13396426:
Sofia Tuttle and co-authors asked whether the season in which a medical student does an emergency medicine sub-internship changes how the student fares. Their 2026 study looks at 84 students bound for emergency medicine who completed the four-week rotation between 2021 and 2024.

Students were scored on shift evaluations, rated from inadequate to outstanding, and on a national specialty exam scored out of 100, and both fed the final grade. The team compared the count and level of evaluations, exam scores, and grades across rotation timing. The question matters because students cluster in summer to win recommendation letters before residency applications, and crowding or off-season timing might quietly help or hurt.
pmc-13396726:
Zhen-Sheng Ma and co-authors show how the supposedly good cholesterol from people with diabetes can turn harmful to blood vessel linings, in a 2026 cell study. Healthy HDL protects the endothelium, but in type 2 diabetes the same particles become dysfunctional and impair it instead.

Human vein cells were bathed in HDL from healthy donors or from diabetic patients. The diabetic version raised iron levels, fat oxidation damage, and superoxide inside the cells while cutting nitric oxide, the vessel-relaxing signal. The damage ran through ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, switched on by a protein called NCOA4 that frees iron from its stores.
pmc-13397326:
Cheng Lu and co-authors borrowed a trick from proteins to build flatter, stiffer light-absorbing molecules for medical imaging and treatment, in a 2026 paper. In β-sheet proteins, branched side chains steer the backbone into interlocked patterns; the authors copy that steering with branched chains on synthetic dye molecules.

The target agents work in the second near-infrared window, light that penetrates tissue well, and they can both image and heat tumors. Two pairs of isomers, linear and branched, were made and crystallized. The branched versions locked flat through directed contacts between sulfur, oxygen, and fluorine atoms, gaining the rigidity and light harvesting that loose molecules lose.
pmc-13398126:
Lydia E Kitelinger and co-authors test whether a tumour's instant response to sound-wave destruction predicts immune awakening inside it. Their 2026 study uses boiling histotripsy, focused ultrasound that shreds tissue mechanically without heat or radiation, in melanoma. Checkpoint drugs free the immune system against cancer, yet a stubborn share of patients gains nothing from them.

When the treatment stalled tumour growth right away, antigen-presenting cells grew scarcer inside the tumour but carried more tumour material each. Immune activation then stood out in one dendritic cell branch, the cDC1 subset prized for rallying killer T cells. Live imaging scores during treatment also tracked the response, raising the hope of reading success while the patient is still on the table.
pmc-13398726:
Yeo and Ryan systematically review, in 2026, whether functional imaging can protect the thinking brain during radiation therapy for glioma, brain tumors where dose must be balanced against cognition. Searching three databases under PRISMA guidelines for studies to December 2024, they found five eligible papers published between 2019 and 2023. The set held two retrospective cohorts, one pilot study, one cross-sectional study, and one theoretical study, of moderate quality overall.

Across them, adding functional MRI information to planning let physicists cut dose to cognition-critical networks, including the default mode network, without compromising tumor coverage. Default-mode-avoidance plans reduced the mean dose to those regions by 20 percent and maximum dose by 12 percent in the analysis. The plans carried an estimated 20 to 23 percent reduction in memory loss risk. The authors describe a shift toward functional-avoidance planning, while cautioning that small, mostly retrospective studies with little prospective cognitive validation limit the evidence.
pmc-13399526:
Takuma Koinuma, Manato Yoshida, and Manabu Akazawa used claims data in a 2026 cohort study. They tested whether the conditions that make doctors choose SGLT2 inhibitor drugs also change the drugs' infection risk. These drugs protect the heart and kidneys, so guidelines steer them toward patients with cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease. Yet sugar spilling into urine has long raised infection fears in those sicker patients.

The analysis covered people aged 65 and older starting an SGLT2 inhibitor (66,968) or a DPP-4 inhibitor as the comparison drug (170,678). Infection rates were higher in SGLT2 users who carried the guideline conditions, 2.04 percent against 0.84 percent in those without. Against the comparison drug, the hazard ratios sat below one in both strata, at 0.80 for patients with the conditions and 0.51 for patients without. Starting these drugs did not raise infection risk in either group, supporting guideline-based use in high-risk patients.
pmc-13399726:
Foldager and team review, in 2026, results and complications of hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement syndrome, the painful hip condition caused by abnormal bone contact. Searching five databases and excluding dysplasia and severe arthritis, they pooled 42 studies of 5,885 operated hips. They graded evidence certainty with the GRADE approach and bias with a Cochrane tool for non-randomized studies.

Major complications were uncommon on average: 2.1 percent of hips converted to total hip replacement, 5.2 percent needed revision surgery, and 3.8 percent had nerve paresthesia, though ranges across studies were wide. Patient-reported results improved meaningfully, with mean gains from baseline of 9.4 to 35.0 points for pain and 15.0 to 45.5 points for sports activity on hundred-point scales. Despite the encouraging averages, the evidence quality was rated very low overall. The authors advise care in reading the benefits until stronger studies arrive.
pmc-13399826:
Valeria Vismara and colleagues describe a minimally invasive reconstruction of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament, the elbow's key restraint against posterolateral rotatory instability, in a 2026 technical note. This approach works through small incisions and lays the graft on the bone surface instead.

With the patient face-up and the arm on a hand table under X-ray control, two short incisions expose the lateral humeral column and the ligament's ulnar footprint. The joint capsule stays closed and the common extensor origin stays attached. A tendon graft is fixed with knotless suture anchors in an onlay fashion, hugging the bone along the ligament's natural path. They present the technique as a way to keep reconstruction's durability while trimming the collateral damage of getting there.
pmc-13399926:
Hiroko Setoyama and colleagues examined whether a combined hepatitis C test could plug a leak in Japan's care pathway, in this 2026 evaluation from Kumamoto Prefecture. The Elecsys HCV Duo assay detects both antibody and core antigen from one blood draw, offering same-visit triage. The survey confirmed the leak: nonspecialist departments performed 86.6 percent of in-hospital antibody testing. Yet only 22.7 percent of antibody-positive people went on to RNA confirmation. Against RNA results, the antigen half of the Duo assay was highly specific at 99.8 percent but only 62.8 percent sensitive. Its detection rose steeply with viral load, from zero below a low threshold to 86.2 percent at the highest loads. The authors propose the Duo test as a triage gate: a positive antigen result fast-tracks patients to specialists.
pmc-13400626:
Jule Romea Lammers and co-authors test, in 2026, touch perception in teenage girls with anorexia nervosa, a condition where body size is persistently overestimated. Whether faulty touch processing feeds that distorted body image was unclear. The study paired behavior tests with brain recordings.

Thirty-six patients and 41 matched healthy peers took part. Touch detection thresholds were normal in the patient group, but counting rare touch signals and telling stimuli apart went worse. Brain responses, measured by combined electric and magnetic recordings, separated rare from standard stimuli equally in both groups. Overall activity in two rear brain areas tied to body representation ran lower in patients. The authors infer the deficit lies in integrating touch into a body picture, not in sensing it.
pmc-13400726:
Thomas D Pollard explains, in 2026, a surprise about how muscle actin filaments grow at their slow end. Actin strands add and lose units at both ends, but the pointed end in muscle was thought to be capped shut by another protein. Two new studies overturn that picture, identifying a protein called leiomodin 2 as the first known builder at the pointed end.

Pollard traces the puzzle from early observations that pointed ends in living muscle do change length, through the biophysics and structural work that caught leiomodin in the act. He discusses what kind of machinery could add units at a capped end and lists the questions now open. The discovery, he argues, will reshape thinking on muscle filament length control.
pmc-13401126:
Aki Katamine and colleagues compare, in 2026, two diabetes drugs in the same class for their effects on eye and kidney complications in Japanese patients. Liraglutide is injected daily and dulaglutide weekly. Both lower blood sugar, but whether they differ on the microvascular complications that drive blindness and dialysis was unclear at these local doses.

The study followed 341 patients who started one drug or the other between 2015 and 2020, using statistical weighting to balance the groups. Over roughly four years, risks of new or worsening eye disease and of reduced kidney filtration did not differ between drugs. Dulaglutide showed a lower rate of worsening urine protein, though its adjusted risk was statistically similar.
pmc-13401326:
Malikah Saba wrote a 2026 case report of endophthalmitis, a severe infection inside the eye, that cost a sedated intensive care patient his eye. The man, a Caucasian in his fifties, was admitted after a motor vehicle collision and could not report vision symptoms because of sedation.

Redness spread around his right eye without any identified eye injury or wider signs of infection. A CT scan showed orbital cellulitis with probable endophthalmitis and a dislocated lens. Urgent eye specialist care, antibiotics given body-wide and injected into the eye, and orbital decompression all failed to halt the disease. The cornea perforated, and the eye was removed. Early lens dislocation looked like a poor prognostic sign. Saba stresses watchful eye checks and fast specialist involvement in sedated patients.
pmc-13402226:
Mohammadi studies, in 2026, life expectancy across Asian Muslim-majority countries side by side, asking how far income and health systems explain the gaps. Using World Bank data and other global databases, the study groups countries by income level and contrasts mortality, child health, and fertility patterns across the region's very different economies.

High-income Gulf states, named as Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, and Kuwait, show the region's highest life expectancy. They have lower mortality and better child health, credited to advanced health systems and strong economies. At the other end, Afghanistan, Yemen, and Pakistan record lower life expectancy, higher mortality, and higher fertility, driven by poverty, instability, and thin health care access. Middle-income countries sit between, with slowly improving numbers. The author concludes economic status tracks life expectancy strongly and urges targeted health policy, wider care access, and development to close the regional gaps.
pmc-13402326:
Hayoung Song and colleagues used brain scanning to catch the moment of insight, when a viewer suddenly grasps how two story events cause each other. Volunteers watched a TV episode cut into scrambled order inside an fMRI scanner, pressed a button at each aha moment, and explained their thinking aloud. More than 40 percent of those explanations pointed back to an earlier event causally tied to the current one.

At those moments, brain patterns for the earlier event lit up again across the cortex, a replay the authors call reinstatement. That replay came about two seconds before the button press and drove a sudden shift in wider brain patterns, as if the mental model of the story had been rewritten. Distant brain areas also held similar patterns for causally linked events, beyond what shared words or images explain. Making sense, the study suggests, means fetching causes, then updating the story.
pmc-13402626:
Xu and co-authors build, in 2026, a Janus metafiber system that gives fiber-bundle endoscopes both full-color 2D vision and 3D depth sensing in a single round trip of light. Fiber bundles gather intensity images but not depth. The depth mode showed a 60-degree field of view with beam spread under 2 degrees, about 1.5 degrees in the refined tests, and depth accuracy better than 2 centimeters. Time-division capture, alternating single-wavelength array scanning with polychromatic illumination, kept the two channels apart and preserved image quality under noise. Combining data streams produced depth-resolved color images with edge detection. The authors target real-time medical diagnostics, LiDAR, and inspection inside engines and pipelines.
pmc-13402926:
Ting Chen and co-authors chart three decades of epilepsy change worldwide from 1990 to 2021, with China as the worked example of a country mid-transition. Population growth and aging push patient counts up even as age-standardized death rates fall with better drug access. A stubborn treatment gap, above all in poorer countries, still decides who gets anti-seizure medicines at all.

Rich countries now wrestle mainly with epilepsy in old age and its companions; poorer ones still fight preventable causes such as birth injury and brain infection. China carries both loads at once, plus sharp regional and urban-rural divides, and stroke-driven epilepsy in its elderly is swelling as stroke tops its disability tables. The authors use the Chinese path to argue integrated strategies must match each setting epidemiological moment.
pmc-13403026:
Amtul Saleem Asfa and colleagues screen preterm and low birth weight babies at corrected term age for osteopenia, the metabolic bone disease of prematurity. Babies born before 34 weeks or under 1500 grams miss the late-pregnancy mineral surge and face feeding hurdles that starve growing bone. At a hospital in Warangal, India, 110 such infants admitted between September 2022 and April 2024 were assessed with clinical, biochemical, and X-ray data.

Twenty-two babies, a prevalence of 20 percent, met the diagnosis. Lower birth weight and gestational age, being small for gestational age, longer breathing support and tube feeding courses, extended caffeine use, and delayed start of gut feeding all tracked with disease. The authors argue screening at corrected term, weighted toward the sickest and latest-fed infants, can catch weak bones before fractures announce them.
pmc-13403526:
Piotr Stendera and Jolanta Kostrzewa-Janicka checked in 2026 how well dental torque wrenches keep their accuracy after heavy use and cleaning. Right tightening force keeps implant screws firm without cracking them. They tested 22 wrenches of three common designs, before cleaning and after 50 and 100 steam cycles.

Spring-type tools started least exact, most of all at low force settings. After repeated cycles, toggle-type tools drifted the least from their set values. Spring types lost the most exactness over time. Overall shifts stayed modest, yet the authors favor the toggle design for clinics that reprocess tools often.
pmc-13403726:
Adnan Ahmad and a broad team reported in 2026 a metal-free powder that makes hydrogen peroxide from water, oxygen, and light. The paired atoms spread charge unevenly, which keeps light-made charges apart longer. Oxygen also sticks and reacts more readily at those sites. Output followed the clean two-step oxygen path. Yields beat versions with lone atoms of either kind. The design may guide other light-driven chemical tools that need no metals.
pmc-13404826:
Mobeen Tabassum and co-authors survey feeding of babies at a hospital serving a poor area of Rawalpindi, Pakistan, in 2026. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first months protects infants, yet many families mix in formula or animal milk. The team asked which factors line up with exclusive breastfeeding.

Questionnaires covered 385 infants born between 34 and 42 weeks of pregnancy. Just over half, 206 babies or 53.5 percent in the reported figures, were exclusively breastfed, while about a third received mixed feeding. Exclusive breastfeeding varied with age, birth weight, delivery mode and nursery admission. Timing of the first feed, pre-milk feeds and vaccination status also showed links.
pmc-13405126:
Dulce E Alarcón-Yaquetto and colleagues review how social position changes the cost of treating type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 systematic review. Income, schooling, work, place and ethnicity shape both who develops diabetes and what care costs. Few studies had gathered the cost side of that story.

Five databases were searched for peer-reviewed studies reporting treatment costs by social factors. Nineteen articles from several countries met the criteria. Costs were compared between the bottom and top of each social gradient where the data allowed. Rural versus urban living and ethnic group formed separate comparisons. The review shows where diabetes spending falls hardest, informing fairer funding choices.
pmc-13406426:
Katarina Tomelić Ercegović and colleagues test school doctor talks for children with high cholesterol, in a 2026 trial. Children aged six to seven with raised cholesterol joined, bar those with a family pattern of the fault. Talks aimed at food, play and time spent sitting.

Cholesterol drifted down in the talked-to group, a good trend that fell short of clear proof in the reported tests. Mediterranean-style eating rose, and some play and sitting measures moved the right way. School health teams can lift family know-how through such talks, the authors say. Bigger trials with longer checks and fuller fat panels are needed to confirm any real gain.
pmc-13407226:
Yuying Wang and Xueming Lu, in 2026, used brain scanning to test why living things are spotted so fast. Volunteers viewed animate and inanimate items, four subcategories each, flashed for 33 milliseconds or shown for 500 milliseconds while performing an unrelated noise-spotting task. pmc-13407726:
Boyu Xie and Qing Wen systematically review, in 2026, sniffing out cancer through the volatile chemicals a body releases. Such compounds sit in urine or cell cultures. Twenty-nine studies qualified. Prostate cancer profiles leaned toward reduced organic acids and alcohols, while bladder and kidney cancers more often showed raised ketones and aldehydes. Four compounds, including hexanal and phenol, recurred across cancer types, and 28 volatiles were shared between urine and cell models, seven moving in the same direction in both. Accuracy for separating patients from healthy controls was generally good, though methods varied widely between laboratories.
pmc-13407826:
Ruidan Li and co-authors design, in 2026, an artificial enzyme built around iridium and manganese clusters to make radiotherapy more lethal to tumours. That immune awakening, the design intends, turns a local radiation treatment into a body-wide response, reversing the suppressive tumour environment. Combined with checkpoint-blockade immunotherapy in the reported work, the approach aims to prevent the spread and return of malignant tumours, the outcomes that usually defeat treatment.
pmc-13408226:

pmc-13408926:
Sen Wang and colleagues stack and shear a common polymer gel in 2026 until its molecules line up almost as neatly as those in natural tendon. The authors offer the process as a general route to load-bearing gels for machines, bioelectronics, and thermal management.
pmc-13409826:
Mykola Patyka and colleagues report in 2026 on three local strains of a bacteria used to kill mosquito larvae. The strains, named Bti 33, 87/1, and 7-1/3, came from Ukrainian ecosystems. Trials then pitted the liquid mixes against lab-raised Aedes aegypti and against wild mosquito groups outdoors. Killing power stayed high in both settings, and the liquid mixes kept well over time. The team sees these home-grown strains as a base for greener larvicide products made near where they will be used.
pmc-13411326:

Rwanda's vaccine coverage and Mexico's fast-track referral scheme show what joined-up delivery achieves. Too many national plans, though, lack budgets, equity goals, and accountability. Fragile coordination, not missing knowledge, is the core failure the authors name, and fixing systems precedes scaling any single service.
pmc-13411626:

pmc-13411826:

Named gene switches per cell type, from muscle builders to liver regulators, give breeders a mechanistic shortlist beyond raw markers.
pmc-13411926:

Women made up about two thirds of the group, and most patients had the generalized form. The middle wait for a diagnosis was eleven months, with nearly half waiting a year or longer. About 14 percent had disease that resisted standard drugs, and crises were most common in that group. The authors press for faster recognition and better steroid-sparing care.
pmc-13413026:
Maria Rincon Nigro and co-authors investigate in 2026 why a promising antileishmanial drug, OJT007, reaches the blood poorly when swallowed. Yet rats pre-treated with the acid blocker absorbed about 40 percent less drug, the opposite of the team's guess. pmc-13413226:

Self-assessed ability rose significantly in every domain, interest in the specialty climbed, and satisfaction ran high across the group surveyed. A third of participants later chose otolaryngology as their specialty during follow-up. The authors offer the model for resource-limited schools.
pmc-13413726:
Ajeet P Maurya and co-authors pair a hard case with a sweep of past work in 2026 on fixing visceral artery false aneurysms through a scope steered by sound scans. These bulges follow swelling or injury to gut arteries. Tube-based repair through blood vessels is the norm when the path allows. The sweep found 30 studies with 122 patients treated this scope-based way. Glue with coil was the most used mix, in 57.4 percent of cases. Pooled success reached 94.25 percent, with side effects near 11.5 percent and fresh bleeding the chief one. The authors keep the method as a backup plan.
pmc-13413826:
Guanghui Li and colleagues use made-up data in 2026 to sharpen strength forecasts for cemented sand and gravel, a dam-building mix. Testing each recipe in the lab is slow and dear. The pair explained 98.97 percent of strength spread, ahead of either method alone. Forecast errors fell with the added data, which the authors offer as a way to cut lab work.
pmc-13415126:
Yangwei Deng and co-authors design a long acting dexamethasone prodrug for joint pain in osteoarthritis, reporting in 2026. Their carrier is a four-armed polyethylene glycol scaffold, a star shaped polymer. One version carried four dexamethasone molecules, another carried eight, linked by bonds that break in acid.

The four-drug version dissolved well yet never gelled. The eight-drug version thickened with warmth and formed a gel, and a little ethanol made it injectable. In a rat style mouse model of joint pain, one injection into the joint eased pain quickly. Relief lasted up to 28 days, far longer than a plain steroid shot usually manages.
pmc-13415826:
Youqiang Huang and colleagues observe tunable chiral spin textures in a layered magnet using nonlinear optics, in 2026. Chiral textures such as spin spirals and skyrmions could power compact, low energy memory, yet few host materials exist. Their material, CrPS4, is a van der Waals magnet whose layers stack weakly.

Changing magnetic field and temperature reshaped the textures, driven by spin couplings within and between layers. The textures answered with strong chiral third order optical signals, showing light can read these magnetic states sensitively. Layered magnets may thus serve reconfigurable spin photonics, where light, charge, and spin meet in one platform.
pmc-13416126:
Somasekhar and co-authors describe, in 2026, resistance to the rice root-knot nematode in Aganni, an Indian indica rice landrace. The worm pest cuts rice yields by 16 to 32 percent and can destroy up to 87 percent of a crop in severe attacks. Screening 25 indica lines by their root gall index, the team found one resistant line, two partly resistant, and the rest susceptible or worse.

Aganni stood out with a gall index between 0.80 and 0.85, and its resistance held across seasons and setups. Attraction assays showed fewer nematodes homing to Aganni roots than to the susceptible cultivar TN1, a pre-infection defense. Worms that did enter penetrated, developed, and reproduced significantly less, a post-infection defense in studies. Infected Aganni roots fired higher activity of antioxidant defense enzymes, ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and superoxide dismutase. The authors recommend Aganni as breeding stock for nematode management.
pmc-13416626:
Micha Jongejan and co-authors compare survival in older kidney failure patients who chose dialysis or conservative care, sorted by whether dialysis would have suited them, in 2026. One center followed patients aged sixty-five and up who recorded a treatment decision between 2017 and 2024. Conservative care means full medical and symptom support without dialysis.

Median survival was fifty-three months for dialysis choosers, thirty-two months for conservative patients judged suitable for dialysis, and eighteen months for those judged less suitable. About thirteen percent of dialysis choosers later switched to conservative care. Splitting conservative patients by suitability changes survival comparisons meaningfully.
pmc-13417026:
A Randall Hughes and colleagues ask how plant sourcing choices shape salt marsh restoration, in a 2026 genetics study. Restored marshes often differ from natural ones, and the source of planting stock may be one reason. Two dominant marsh grasses were sampled from local wild stands, seedlings grown from their seed, and commercial nursery stock.

Wild stands differed only weakly from each other in genetic makeup. Seed grown plants differed more, and nursery plants differed most while also holding higher diversity. Since plant genetics can affect marsh function and resilience, sourcing deserves explicit planning, the authors argue, rather than being left to supply and price alone.
pmc-13419226:
Giuliana Nardacchione and colleagues test adults with developmental dyslexia on an artificial grammar task to sort out which memory system falters. One theory blames the brain system that learns habits and sequences, while rival reviews blame other systems or shared pattern learning. The task asks people to judge new strings of letters built by hidden rules.

Adults with dyslexia leaned more on how common small letter pairs were, using surface frequency to guide their answers on fresh items. That reliance points to statistical cue use covering for a weaker rule-learning route. Earlier clashes in the field may stem from studies mixing several learning parts in one task. Cleaner tasks like this one can help schools and clinics pin down what reading support should target.
pmc-13419426:
Madeline T. Gemoules and colleagues test a commercial panel that names bacteria in sputum quickly, asking whether its results actually change antibiotic care. The study covers 189 sputum samples from ward patients outside intensive care who were suspected of lower airway infection. Culture remains the standard route, yet it is slow, so broad drugs often run on guesswork.

Changes that doctors made were compared with changes that the results made possible in theory, at two points in the workup. Only 48.7 percent of possible changes were acted on after panel results, while 87.8 percent were acted on after standard culture results in the same review. That action gap, not test speed, looks like the barrier. The authors call for work on why clinicians hesitate to use rapid panel answers.
pmc-13420126:
Homero Contreras-Salinas and colleagues scan the United States drug safety reporting system for harms tied to bevacizumab injected into the eye. The drug was approved for cancer yet is used widely off-label for retinal vessel diseases at a fraction of rival drugs' cost. Trial proof for the eye use is thin, so spontaneous reports carry much of the safety picture.

The set held 1495 case reports covering 5232 adverse events in the database pull. Some 114 event terms stood out statistically, split among expected harms, want of effect, and surprises in the reported shares. A side-by-side risk comparison against a licensed rival drug adds context to the counts. Eye specialists get a signal map to weigh against the drug's cost edge.
pmc-13420326:
Ayşe Sinan and colleagues test how fermentation time and curing change sucuk döner kebab, a spiced meat product, during cold storage. Starter culture fermentation, at 24 and 72 hours in the design, was crossed with cured and uncured recipes. The team tracked leftover nitrite, chemistry, aroma compounds, germ counts, and taste panels in chilled and frozen storage.

Uncured fermented batches lost the most weight in cooking, while their cured semi-fermented matches lost the least in the reported comparisons. Taste panels favored the uncured semi-fermented batches most for overall liking. Fermentation itself, whatever its length or curing partner, proved central to shelf life, quality, and safety in the results. Makers get a recipe map that trades tradition, safety margins, and flavor against each other in plain terms.
pmc-13420426:
Qian Zhang and colleagues ask whether rotating shift work and low exercise together raise fatty liver risk, using a national United States survey from 2017 to 2018. Liver fat was read by an ultrasound-based stiffness device rather than by symptoms, giving a firm case line. The analysis held 653 participants with full shift, activity, and liver data.

Floating shifts raised fatty liver odds to 1.40 in the adjusted model reported, with a p value of 0.019 beside it in the same results. Exercise leaned protective but fell just short of the usual proof line. Among cases, defined by a liver fat score at or above 248 in the device's units, floating shifts were far more common than among controls. Work scheduling emerges as a liver health issue, not only a sleep issue.
pmc-13421326:
Darren Lee leads a large team reporting, in 2026, the first comprehensive account of BRAF mutations in acute myeloid leukaemia. Changes in the pathway BRAF belongs to are common in this leukaemia. They usually hit the genes NRAS and KRAS. BRAF itself is changed rarely, and it has been linked to poor outcomes.

Among 5,779 fully profiled patients at two major American cancer centres, about one percent carried BRAF mutations, mostly outside the well-known V600 hotspot and often in leukaemia arising from prior marrow disorders. Single-cell profiling showed mutation-specific patterns of partner mutations and cell identity. Survival was poor on current treatments, including venetoclax-based regimens. Drug sensitivity data, the authors argue, point toward tailored options for this small subgroup.
pmc-13424526:
Li and colleagues report a 2026 study of a blood ratio that pairs inflammation with a protective fat in critically ill heart patients. The ratio divides monocyte count by HDL cholesterol. Using United States intensive care databases, the team followed 3,004 adults with coronary heart disease and tracked deaths over one year.

Patients in the highest third of the ratio were sicker and needed more treatment. Their one-year survival was lower than the lowest third's, at roughly seven in ten versus eight in ten patients alive. The link rose in a straight, dose-like pattern and held after the team adjusted for age, other illnesses, and treatments. Each added unit of the ratio came with clearly higher death risk. Both parts come from routine blood tests, so the ratio could flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13424726:
Anastasiya Kuznyetsova and David A. Hood review how lysosomes, the cell's recycling centres, adapt to exercise in skeletal muscle. Mitochondrial adaptation to training is famous; lysosomes clear the worn-out mitochondria and other debris, yet their own training response has been underappreciated until recently, the authors argue.

Every single bout of exercise, recent work shows, starts fresh lysosome production, driven by gene switches TFEB and TFE3 moving into the nucleus and turning on recycling programmes. The same switches support a pick-and-deliver form of cleanup and the rebuilding of spent lysosomes. Repeated bouts therefore remodel the whole disposal system alongside the power plants it services. The review gathers the pathways and their open questions for muscle health.
pmc-13425026:
Anna Cetera and colleagues used scalp brain recordings to read which kind of grasp a person plans before the hand even moves. Volunteers prepared either a precision pinch, a full power grip, or no grasp, while the team recorded brain waves.

Slow brain waves, in the 0.5 to 8 hertz range, carried grasp clues laid down during planning and kept through movement. A classifier using those waves told precision from power grasps with about 75 to 78 percent accuracy. That beat the older movement-signal method, which managed about 61 percent on the same task. Features came from front and side brain areas during planning, shifting to movement areas during execution, Cetera reports.
pmc-13425526:
Dae Ho Kim and colleagues describe two Sarcoscypha fungi from Korea in a 2026 taxonomic article, including one species new to science. Sarcoscypha orientalis resembles S. occidentalis but differs by having completely stalkless fruiting cups. Genetic analyses using ITS, LSU, and RPB2 sequences split earlier S. occidentalis records into United States and East Asian lineages.

Korean material fell in the East Asian lineage, supporting its recognition as a separate species on both form and DNA evidence. Remaining specimens proved to be S. vassiljevae, recorded in Korea for the first time, expanding the known national list for this cup fungus genus.
pmc-13425626:
Sakamoto-Iwata and colleagues report 2026 results from a Japanese registry of thirty-seven centers. It covers drug therapy around balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a catheter procedure that opens lung arteries narrowed by old clots. The registry tracked patients with inoperable chronic clot-related lung hypertension registered between 2018 and 2023, covering 557 patients before the procedure and 966 after it.

About seventy percent received drug therapy before the procedure, and those patients started with worse circulation measures. Three-year survival did not differ between untreated, single-drug, and combination-drug groups, all at ninety-four percent or higher. After the procedure, twenty percent had their drugs reduced. That group had lower artery pressure but also a lower cardiac index, a measure of pumping output, at last follow-up. The authors advise care when trimming drugs even after pressures normalize.
pmc-13426026:
Raju Sapkota and colleagues surveyed people with diabetes at eye clinics in Trinidad and Tobago about what they know, feel, and do. The team also checked clinical records, including eye damage from diabetes, to see how personal traits link with knowledge and health.

Among 194 patients, about 43 percent had diabetic eye disease and about 6 percent had sight-threatening disease. Over a third did not know a diabetic eye exam differs from a normal glasses test. Higher fasting blood sugar and schooling below secondary level each predicted eye disease on their own. Women and younger patients felt less able to discuss diabetes openly, so Sapkota urges teaching shaped to each group.
pmc-13426426:
Yusuke Murakami and colleagues built a microscope that images living cells by their chemical fingerprints, without dyes or labels. The tool reads how molecules vibrate when lit, a signal called Raman scattering, boosted by electronic resonance for weak targets.

Unlike older narrow-band versions, the new microscope captures the whole fingerprint range of vibrations at once. It filmed low-abundance cytochromes, the energy proteins inside cells, alongside common fats, proteins, and DNA material in living human kidney cells. Applied to mouse tissue, it mapped where cytochromes gather in the brain cortex, the ventricle wall, and the liver. Murakami presents the method as a route to label-free tissue checks from single cells to whole slides.
pmc-13427526:
Zihan Guo and colleagues compared four long-acting white-cell growth factors head to head in breast cancer chemotherapy in a 2026 prospective observational cohort study in Shanghai, China. Long-acting granulocyte colony-stimulating factors are standard protection against chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, yet comparative data among products were limited. Patients at high risk of fever with low counts received pegfilgrastim, mecapegfilgrastim, telpegfilgrastim, or efbemalenograstim alfa once per cycle by clinical choice.

The main outcome was severe grade 3 or 4 neutropenia across cycles and follow-up, with bone pain tracked as the signature side effect. Direct comparison helps Chinese oncology centers choose among domestically available long-acting options.
pmc-13427926:
Marta Codes and colleagues review, in a 2026 study, how implanted brain electrodes steer treatment for epilepsy that drugs cannot control. The method, called SEEG, threads fine electrodes into the brain to find where seizures start. Records covered 71 patients monitored between 2016 and 2025, with 958 electrodes placed in total. Recordings confirmed the team's starting suspicion in about 85 percent of cases.

Based on the findings, about half the patients went on to surgery that removes the seizure zone. A heat treatment delivered through the same electrodes helped about three quarters of treated patients at one year, though full seizure freedom was uncommon. Responses to that heat step then guided later choices. Serious lasting harm was rare, near 1 percent. Clinicians gain a staged framework rather than a single yes-or-no test.
pmc-13428026:
Liu and colleagues report a 2026 case of familial chylomicronemia syndrome in an infant, a rare inherited disorder where the blood cannot clear dietary fat, leaving triglyceride levels dangerously high. The baby, a girl admitted at forty-one days old, was diagnosed by genetic testing that found two faulty copies of the lipoprotein lipase gene, the main fat-clearing enzyme.

Treatment centered on a strict low-fat diet supplemented with medium-chain triglycerides, fats that bypass the broken clearing pathway. Over one year of follow-up, her triglyceride levels improved markedly. She also showed catch-up growth, closing the gap toward normal infant size. The authors stress that early genetic diagnosis matters because diet started in infancy can control the disorder and help prevent its feared complication, repeated pancreas inflammation.
pmc-13428126:
Mondaza-Hernandez and colleagues published a 2026 study on drug response markers in sarcoma. Soft tissue sarcoma covers many rare cancers with few good drug options. Pazopanib is a standard second drug, yet patients respond in uneven ways. The team compared tumor samples taken before and after pazopanib treatment.

Gene profiling found 38 genes whose activity changed after treatment ended. One gene, SERPINE1, rose more than fourfold and tracked with poorer survival. Lab tests in sarcoma cell lines backed the gene findings with protein checks. The drug also shifted immune-related cells within tumors in their analysis. The authors frame SERPINE1 as a lead for bigger validation studies ahead. Patient selection for pazopanib could sharpen if the marker holds up.
pmc-13428426:
Christoph Beger and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 paper, a software suite that helps medical teams define patient types precisely and find them in data. Phenotyping, describing the observable traits that define a condition, is often done by hand and varies between groups. Their TOP framework lets users define traits formally, organize them into a structured hierarchy, and build disease models. A sample case built around a liver failure score shows the machinery in action.

Queries generated by the suite can pull matching patients from records automatically. Built-in testing checks that definitions behave as intended. Eleven users rated the experience, scoring appeal and practical quality clearly on the positive side of the scale. The authors claim gains in speed, scale, and reproducibility for studies that depend on exact patient definitions, a need precision medicine keeps sharpening.
pmc-13428626:
Qihua Qiu and Jaesang Sung check, in a 2026 study, whether laws raising the tobacco purchase age to 21 change young adults' body weight. Tobacco 21 laws cut youth smoking by blocking initiation, and quitting smoking often brings weight gain, which raised the question. The team used national behavior survey data from 2009 to 2019 for 18 to 20 year olds. A difference-in-differences design compared states as the laws rolled out at staggered times.

Average weight and overweight rates barely moved overall. Obesity did dip slightly, driven by small losses among those just above the obesity line. The dip appeared in the first year after adoption, then faded. Effects concentrated among never smokers, which fits prevention rather than quitting as the channel. Reported exercise rose and diets improved in the same window, suggesting wider lifestyle ripples.
pmc-13429126:
Yi Jiao Angelina Tian and colleagues sift, in a 2026 scoping review, which qualities in the doctor-patient relationship actually move patients to follow treatment. Sticking with treatment saves lives and money, and good relationships are often credited. The team searched three databases for empirical studies from 2015 to early 2025 that tied a specific relational quality to adherence. Forty-eight studies qualified across many designs and settings.

Six qualities recurred: communication, shared decision-making, trust, empathy, continuity of care, and agreement between doctor and patient on the plan. Communication led the list, especially what is said, how it is said, and how often. Few studies defined or measured these qualities the same way, which the authors call the field's main gap. Digital care and subspecialization may also be thinning the very relationships that adherence depends on.
pmc-13429226:
Tuğba Yanık-Yalçın and co-authors distill, in a 2026 consensus report, what Türkiye's infection control leaders see as their system's weak points. The material comes from the seventh national symposium on healthcare-associated infections, whose recorded sessions were transcribed and thematically analyzed. Participants led infection prevention programs across the country. Antibiotic resistance frames the whole discussion, since resistant infections now kill millions globally each year.

Five barrier themes recurred: reporting pressure that bends the data, habits and culture that resist change, thin training and staffing, patchy standardization, and committee decisions that stall before reaching the ward. Suggested fixes include visible leadership backing, simpler data systems, and behavior-change strategies built to last. The report reads as an insider map of why good rules fail in practice, drawn from the people charged with enforcing them.
pmc-13430526:
Juan Mendoza Turmero and co-authors made tiny bone-like mineral particles in 2026 with the help of high-pitched sound waves, a route they frame as kind to the environment. The team varied how long the sound ran, from a quarter hour to a full hour. They also varied the liquid mix, pairing water with one of three other liquids.

Tests of shape and makeup showed a form of the mineral much like the one in real bone, with size and shape tied to the liquid used. All batches held up well under heat and gave strong yields. Blood tests showed low harm for one mix, with no block to clot cell action. One mix cut the growth of a common germ film the most, which hints at use in bone repair materials.
pmc-13431026:
Wei Ding and colleagues tested whether a heart ultrasound measure can foretell serious heart events in people on long-term kidney dialysis. The measure, peak strain dispersion, gauges how unevenly the heart's main chamber squeezes across its walls.

The team matched 336 dialysis patients into high and low measure groups using a cut-off set before the study. Over a median of about 47 months, major heart events struck about 38 percent of the high group versus about 20 percent of the low group. High readings also doubled the risk of heart death and raised overall death risk after adjustments. Ding suggests adding the measure to routine heart checks for dialysis patients, pending wider tests.
pmc-13431426:
Priyanka Kumari Nahak wrote a 2026 letter that questions a pooled review of exercise therapy for forward head posture in people with neck pain. The letter praises the review team for gathering proof on a shared and growing problem, and for hewing to set reporting rules. Posture of this kind links to pain, lost function, and poorer daily life.

One worry targets who got into the pooled counts. The review said it would bar studies that paired exercise with other care, yet several pooled studies set exercise against active care such as standard therapy or posture lessons. The pooled figures thus mix unlike contests. A second worry notes very wide spread in results across studies for head angle, pain, and neck function. The letter warns that such spread can bend what the pooled figures truly mean.
pmc-13434226:
Mohan Ajmeera, P Chiranjeevi, and A Krishna Mohan present TriAttnNet in 2026, a vision model that spots cotton pests and sorts leaf disease from photos. Small data sets, uneven class counts, and repeated traits make the task hard in the field. Their pipeline cleans images first and then adds made up images to widen training.

A segmentation step marks the leaf area of interest before sorting begins. The main model weighs space, channel, and context cues at once. Reported accuracy reached 98.66 percent, above two strong rival models named in the study. Farm advisers get a fast aid, though field trials beyond test images still matter most.
pmc-13434426:
Chuan Li and coauthors build a water based battery that still works at deep cold in 2026. Dual ion designs store charge in graphite at high voltage, yet they once needed costly, thick salt mixes that fail when cold. A gel rich in polar molecules replaces the thick mix here.

The gel holds only dilute salts yet stays stable past a wide voltage span at minus 40 degrees. High voltage scans wake the graphite to take in the charge carrying ions. Cells gave high plateaus at minus 20 and minus 40 degrees. Cold stores and polar sites gain a safer battery option.
pmc-13435726:
Rainer Gosert and a large team compare two shop bought antibody tests for RSV in 2026. Blood from 462 people spans healthy adults, pregnant women, children, and transplant patients with vaccine shots. Both kits hunt total IgG and IgA against the virus.

Agreement on IgG calls ran high at 83.8 percent. One kit still read higher values and more positives across the board. Both kits tracked the sharper pre fusion antibody well, most in children. IgA showed rarely and matched less well. The kits are not swaps for each other, the team warns. Clinics must stick with one kit when tracking change.
pmc-13436526:
Pausas, Valbuena, and Beltrán-Marcos report how fire reached beech forest in Spain, a damp, shady woodland long seen as a fire barrier. Beech canopies shade out undergrowth, and high altitude summer fires were once rare. During a fifteen day heatwave in summer 2025, lightning lit the Barniedo fire in León. It burned 19,100 hectares across shrubland, oak, and beech. Their 2026 report reads satellite severity maps and field signs to judge the damage.

Fire raced through shrubland as crown fire, then slowed to a creeping litter fire inside beech stands. The barrier effect is real but not absolute. About a third of the beech was untouched or barely scorched, with nearly all trees surviving. Another third burned as a low intensity, high severity ground fire that killed most trees. The last third came out mixed. Fire regimes, the authors warn, are climbing into forests new to fire.
pmc-13436926:
Verónica Fuentes-Santamaría, Carmen María Díaz García, and Juan Carlos Alvarado review the research linking hearing loss with a higher risk of dementia, including Alzheimer disease. Their 2026 critical review weighs what is known, what stays unclear, and how doctors should read the link in daily care. Studies show risk rising as hearing gets worse, yet a direct cause has not been proven.

Several paths may connect the two conditions, the authors explain. The brain may lose input, reorganize itself, and work harder to follow speech. Lonely and withdrawn daily life may add further harm, since hearing loss often cuts people off from others. Problems with central hearing may also signal early weakness in the brain itself. Hearing tests for older adults and hearing aids may help, the review concludes, though firm proof that treatment protects memory is still missing.
pmc-13437526:
Shen Jiang, Teng Zhang, and Xiaona Gu tested a new rinse for skin burns from metallic sodium, a chemical that reacts fiercely with water and leaves strong alkali in wounds. Their 2026 study made a wash from glycine and a chelating salt, then tested it in sixty rats. The five groups were no rinse, plain water, boric acid, a commercial fluid, and the new wash. Each wound was rinsed for fifteen minutes starting three minutes after exposure.

The new wash pulled wound alkalinity down fast, reaching near-neutral levels by rinsing's end. By day fourteen, those wounds had healed more than the no-rinse, water, and boric acid groups. Markers of vessel growth and repair ran higher, two harsh inflammatory signals fell, and a calming signal rose highest. The authors present the wash as a promising emergency rinse, while noting direct proof of sodium removal is still missing.
pmc-13437926:
Stahl and colleagues test an idea about malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, aggressive cancers arising in people with neurofibromatosis type 1. Many of these tumors lose a gene silencing complex called PRC2. Earlier work hinted the cells survive only by methylating their DNA heavily, so removing methylation might kill them. Their 2026 study maps DNA methylation and gene activity in tumor lines and engineered human Schwann cells with and without PRC2. It then applies two methylation blocking drugs.

Losing PRC2 did not change global DNA methylation at all, undercutting the premise. Both drugs stripped methylation, yet they split in effect. Azacitidine killed tumor cells directly and stirred RNA processing genes. Decitabine caused no direct killing and stirred immune response genes instead. Methylation loss alone does not kill these tumor cells. The authors suggest pairing such drugs with other treatments rather than relying on them alone.
pmc-13438426:
Ashley Blawas and colleagues strapped heart monitors to blue and humpback whales to learn how the heart keeps up with lunge feeding. A rorqual whale surges open-mouthed into prey, then slows to filter tons of water through its baleen while gliding. Diving animals usually brake the heart to save oxygen, and how that brake bends during such bursts was unknown. Their 2026 study read heart rate across whole feeding dives.

Heart rates stayed high through the lunge and, strikingly, held up during the filtering glide that follows, keeping blood flowing to muscles largely stopped. The pattern resembles a sprinter more than a saver: the lunge seems to run partly on oxygen-free energy, building a debt filtering time only partly repays. The authors read this cardiac flexibility as the unlock for the rorqual style. Their tags turn a long theoretical debate about dive heart control into measured fact.
pmc-13439026:
Kate M Bermingham and colleagues present a 2026 report on building and testing a digital food questionnaire for everyday eating habits. Their PREDICT questionnaire holds 265 food items and is filled in online by each person. Diet tools often miss foods people eat now, so the team drew items from two older questionnaires plus cohort data from the United States and the United Kingdom.

Over one month, 68 people completed the new questionnaire and six 24-hour recalls for comparison. Agreement was fair to good, with food group links ranging from weak for legumes to strong for meat. Most people fell in the same or a nearby quarter rank for diet quality on both tools. The authors conclude that the new tool gives a usable picture of modern diets for large nutrition studies.
pmc-13440726:
Sabrina Ee-Ying Ong and colleagues pool trials of therapies meant to repair social functioning in traumatised teenagers, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. Posttraumatic stress symptoms often sour friendships, family ties, and trust, yet therapy research usually grades symptom relief alone. Searches found seventeen studies yielding thirty-five effect sizes on interpersonal functioning. Intervention type, delivery mode, and session count were tested as possible moderators of benefit.

Gains right after treatment were small but reliable across studies. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy produced the largest effect of any approach. Formats mixing solo sessions with joint or group work beat group-only delivery. At three months, the pooled effect grew to medium size on the few available measures. More sessions did not change immediate gains, though they tracked with stronger follow-up results. The authors ask for trials that target social mechanisms directly and track them longer.
pmc-13441826:
Ping Li and colleagues pool studies on a nutrition-and-inflammation score as a survival predictor for lung cancer patients on immune checkpoint drugs, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. The prognostic nutritional index blends albumin and lymphocyte counts from routine blood work. Fourteen observational studies covering 2,106 patients with non-small cell lung cancer treated with PD-1 or PD-L1 blockers were pooled with standard quality grading.

Patients with higher scores at baseline lived markedly longer overall and went longer without progression. The pattern held across study regions, spanning China, Turkey, Japan, and the United Kingdom, and across the score cutoffs used. Survival pooling showed heavy statistical heterogeneity, yet sensitivity checks kept the result standing. Signs of publication bias appeared, and correction for missing studies barely moved the estimate. The authors nominate the index as a cheap candidate marker for immunotherapy prognosis.
pmc-13442426:
Erin Karissa and colleagues map where microbe hunters have found actinomycetes across Indonesia in a 2026 review. These thread-like microbes make many drug-like compounds, yet most past finds in the island nation came from plain soil. The review builds a family tree from gene reads for 152 strains drawn from soils, caves, hot areas, mangroves, seas, and plants.

Most strains fell in one genus, Streptomyces, long known as a rich source of new compounds. Just 44 microbe products from the country have firm or likely structures so far, a small count next to world reports. The authors note that few strains get full DNA reads and public deposits. They urge wider hunts in odd habitats, paired with gene work, to lift both name accuracy and drug finds.
pmc-13443026:
Ruben Munoz-Cabrera and colleagues map smart computer tools onto HIV care tasks in a 2026 review. Virus care now spans test, drug choice, and long watch phases, each with rich but messy data. Their review covered more than 50 studies from 2017 to November 2025, sorted by care scope, data type, source, and tool type.

The map pairs each clinic task with the tool class that fits it best, from plain math models to neural nets and text tools. Drug care has tamed the virus for many, yet gaps in speed and reach keep tools welcome. Source banks and their limits get blunt notes for each task. The authors aim the frame at clinicians who must pick tools without deep tech training. They stress fit to task over raw model power.
pmc-13443626:
Yi-Xuan Wang and colleagues join whole-genome reads with blood chemical scans in up to 199,138 UK Biobank members in a 2026 study. Blood metabolites mark how genes shape health, yet array-based gene work missed much of their code. The team mapped gene control of 313 blood chemicals at full genome depth.

Single-variant hunts found 36,105 solo signals, with a 22.20 percent share new to science in their count. Fine maps pinned 12,361 likely cause links with sharper aim than array work. Rare variant group tests added 1,527 gene-trait pairs. Twin checks with disease genes gave 245 likely cause links, such as omega-3 fats with gallstone risk. Protein picks with matched effects named 410 drug target leads, all shared in an open web resource.
pmc-13443926:
Hussam Osman reviews smart computer tools in blood lab diagnosis in a 2026 paper. Blood work leans on hand scope reads and expert eyes, which vary between labs and tire with load. The review sweeps four databases for tools that read cell shapes, flow data, chromosome maps, and gene marks.

Deep learning nets scored well at cell shape reads, from blood smears to marrow slides, and caught faint odd marks. Flow tools sped gate work and flagged rare events. Gene tools aided chromosome sorts and variant calls, while triage tools helped plan care steps. Blocks span messy data, thin proof, cost, and rule gaps, with African labs in sharp focus. The author urges shared data and staged proof before wide trust.
pmc-13446326:
Valérie Dormal and colleagues test strawberry leaf extract in older adults who feel their memory slipping, in a 2026 randomized trial with a placebo arm and blinded dosing. Plant compounds called ellagitannins, rich in strawberry leaves, show guard effects on the brain in lab work. The trial asked whether the extract lifts memory and eases felt stress in daily life.

Treated adults beat the placebo group on a paired-associates learning test, a standard probe of episode memory. Gains also showed in word memory and working memory tasks. After twelve weeks the treated group reported lower felt stress than at the start. The extract was safe and well borne in this group, and the authors frame it as a gentle option for aging minds.
pmc-13447226:
Junjie Zhong leads a team studying an ovary response index in older fertility patients in a 2026 review of treatment cycles in Yulin, China. The index combines eggs collected and drug dose to show how sensitively ovaries respond. Women aged thirty-five and older often respond poorly, so a simple guide to likely outcomes would help counselling.

More than a thousand fresh embryo transfer cycles from 2021 to 2023 were split into low, middle and high index thirds. Higher index patients needed less drug, produced more eggs and had more good embryos, with higher pregnancy test rates. Live birth rates did not differ across the groups, however. Once age and a hormone marker of egg supply were taken into account, the index no longer predicted pregnancy on its own.
pmc-13447826:
Xavier Bosch-Capblanch leads a team mapping stakeholder positions around introducing the RTS,S malaria vaccine in Ghana in a 2026 study. New health technologies fail without the right actors engaged at the right stage, from research through regulation to delivery. A partnership framework supplied the stages, and members of a research consortium reported where they and others sit along that chain.

Thirty-one stakeholders answered a questionnaire, with a workshop held to validate the map. Most involvement clustered near service delivery, the final stage, rather than earlier research and regulatory steps. A small number of actors held the highest interest and influence over introduction. High vaccine demand beside thin domestic research capacity mirrors wider African patterns, the authors note, and broader inclusion plus stronger upstream capacity would firm the path for future technologies.
pmc-13448026:
Sen Wang and colleagues build a machine learning model to predict kidney injury after off-pump heart bypass surgery in a 2026 study. Kidney injury complicates roughly a quarter of heart operations and raises death risk and cost. Off-pump bypass, done without a heart-lung machine, still carries substantial risk, so early warning from routine data could guide protective care.

Records for nine hundred thirty-eight patients treated between mid 2023 and early 2025 were analysed, and about twenty-two percent developed kidney injury. Features drawn from before surgery plus time-series signals during surgery fed several models. A gradient boosting model won on held-out validation with very strong discrimination. Explanation analysis ranked a kidney filtration marker first and a heart strain marker second among predictors, giving clinicians a ranked risk picture.
pmc-13448126:
Nishimura presents a 2026 commentary on a nationwide study of repeat lumbar surgery after spinal fusion in patients with Parkinson disease. Parkinson's brings stiff posture, weak back muscles, bone thinning, and balance problems, all hostile to fusion surgery. The commented study used matched nationwide data to compare later surgery rates, a design the commentary examines for what it can and cannot prove.

The commentary's value lies in framing: which risks belong to the disease, which to surgical choice, and where matched data blur the two. Surgeons counseling Parkinson's patients need exactly that separation before quoting reoperation odds, and patients deserve prognosis built on their disease's mechanics, not generic fusion statistics.
pmc-13448826:
Darren Gray and a large team report in 2026 a village-level trial in Central Java, Indonesia, testing whether better latrines plus hygiene education can curb intestinal worm infections. Eight village clusters with 2,155 participants took part between October 2016 and October 2017. Intervention villages got mass deworming drugs, an improved pit latrine called the BALatrine, and community hygiene teaching, while control villages received the drugs alone.

Stool samples checked twelve months later showed infection starting near 13 percent in both arms. The combined intervention cut the odds of any worm infection sharply, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.22. Protection reached full effectiveness against roundworm and 95 percent against hookworm, though the drop in whipworm did not reach statistical significance. The authors argue sanitation and education deserve a central place beside drug campaigns.
pmc-13449526:
Nurul Adilah-Amrannudin and co-authors investigate in 2026 insecticide resistance in the mosquito Aedes albopictus across northern Peninsular Malaysia, where spray programs are losing their bite. Alongside the known F1534L change, the team found new mutations, A1022S and A1022P, E1041K, P1585R, and F1695L, scattered across the channel. Docking showed the new variants alter how pyrethroids grip the channel, tying genotype to the survival phenotype and giving control programs a molecular watch list.
pmc-13452226:
Liu and colleagues built in 2026 a neural network, MD-Mamba, that classifies breast cancer tissue images into four classes from normal to invasive cancer. Standard image networks see only small neighborhoods at once and can miss the broad tissue patterns pathologists rely on. Their design joins a state-space model, which reads long-range order cheaply, with widened convolutions that view the tissue at several scales at once.

A two-path attention stage then spotlights diagnostic regions and reweights features, which also makes the model's choices easier to inspect. On the BACH benchmark of four hundred microscopy images, the model reached accuracy above ninety-six percent and classified every malignant image correctly in its test run. Part-removal studies showed each block of the design adds to the score.
pmc-13452326:
Pileggi and colleagues published a 2026 study on how stomach bypass surgery rewires women's muscles. Roux-en-Y bypass shrinks the stomach and reroutes food to aid weight loss. The team tracked 41 women before surgery and one year afterward. They read gene tags and gene activity in thigh muscle samples.

Over 8,000 gene regions changed their chemical tags after the surgery. More than 2,000 genes also changed how strongly they switched on. Muscle-building and protein-making genes turned up, aiding strength and repair. Energy-factory genes eased down even as those factories grew in number. Pre-surgery muscle traits partly predicted who lost the most weight. Weight loss and fat loss were marked across the full group. Muscle samples came from the thigh muscle of each participant studied.
pmc-13453026:
Kim surveyed Seoul-area baby boomers in 2026 on a Korean policy that would build retirement communities offering housing and care in one place, often outside big cities. South Korea became a super-aged society in late 2024, and the policy hopes to draw city retirees to smaller regions. The plan rested on an old web survey that missed offline elders, so fresh face-to-face data were gathered.

Willingness to join came in high, at about four in five respondents. Most wanted to stay within an hour of the capital and near medical care. Low-rise, mid-size apartments were favored, as were mixed rental and owned units. Respondents were mostly educated and middle class, which Kim reads as a sign that support should reach beyond low-income groups.
pmc-13453726:
Yuanyang Ye and four co-authors report a brain tumor that hid behind a large bleed and was first read as a stroke from high blood pressure. Their 2026 case report follows a 60 year old man whose CT scan showed an 87.1 millilitre bleed deep in the right side of his brain. Surgeons drained the blood, and he went home with a pressure related diagnosis.

Two months later he returned with a bulging skull flap and rising pressure, yet scans showed only a fluid filled cyst. Three spinal taps then told the true story: the fluid teemed with odd cells bearing cancer marks, and its chemistry ran far from normal. Tissue proof later confirmed a grade IV glioblastoma that had spread along the brain's lining. The authors urge spinal fluid cell checks when a bleed behaves oddly.
pmc-13453826:
Aida Sehle and Joachim Liepert test a gait training aid that triggers the leg's flexor reflex with electric pulses in people years past a stroke. The reflex bends the hip, knee, and ankle together, which can help a stiff leg swing through. Their 2026 pilot covers five patients a mean of 3.8 years after stroke, in 15 training sessions over five weeks.

Walking tests ran with and without the pulses, at two baselines, right after training, and at 3 and 12 months. Both the ten metre walk and the two minute walk improved after training, and the gains still showed at three months. Walking with the reflex on also beat walking with it off at the checks. Users rated the device highly, and blinded video review saw safer, faster gait. The authors call for a randomized trial to split training gains from device gains.
pmc-13454026:
Yanting Shi and five co-authors report Sweet syndrome, a painful skin flare of fever and tender plaques, arising in a woman whose ulcerative colitis seemed quiet. Their 2026 case report follows a 60 year old woman on anti TNF therapy whose bowel scope had suggested remission. A skin biopsy showed the dense neutrophil crowd typical of the syndrome, and infection tests came back clean.

A fresh colonoscopy then told another story: the bowel was in fact actively inflamed, which likely drove the skin flare. The anti TNF drug infliximab failed, so the team switched to upadacitinib, a JAK inhibitor, at 45 milligrams a day. Pain eased within a week and the plaque healed fully by week eight, with the bowel healed at follow up. A lower dose then held both conditions in remission.
pmc-13454226:
Shanshan Chen and eight co-authors describe staged nursing care for a 13 year old girl with the worst grade of mouth sores after a stem cell transplant. The girl, treated for transfusion dependent thalassemia, developed sores on day six that reached grade 4 by day seventeen, with bleeding, a locked jaw, and no ability to eat. Her blood counts were wiped out and platelet transfusions kept failing.

The nursing path split care into phases, mixing constant checks with behavior tools such as tell show do coaching and music distraction. Caregiver help made mouth rinsing and ultraviolet treatment possible despite severe pain. The sores eased to grade 1 by discharge at day 32 and cleared by day 84, while pain fell from 8 to 0. Anxiety and nutrition risk scores also improved. The authors note that many measures ran at once, so no single one can take credit.
pmc-13454726:
Agata Bronisławska and six colleagues review, in 2026, macrohormones, oversized hormone complexes that fool laboratory tests. A macrohormone forms when a normal hormone sticks to an antibody, creating a molecule too large to act yet still counted by assays. The result can be a false high reading in a healthy person.

The best-known case involves prolactin, and a simple chemical settling test can unmask it. Reports now cover many other hormones, from thyroid and growth signals to insulin and calcitonin. Each can send doctors toward scans and drugs a patient never needed. The authors urge testing for macrohormones whenever symptoms and lab values disagree. That single check, they argue, can prevent overdiagnosis and spare patients needless treatment.
pmc-13454826:
Bayar A. Qasim and five colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, a twelve-year-old girl whose knock-knees traced back to a hormone disorder, not a bone problem. Overactive parathyroid glands are rare in children. Her legs bent further despite corrective surgery and supplements, and she had earlier suffered high calcium during a pancreas attack.

Blood tests showed calcium far above normal and parathyroid hormone at roughly fifteen times healthy levels, with very low vitamin D. Neck imaging found a small tumor on one gland, and X-rays showed cystic, soap-bubble lesions in her bones. Tissue checks confirmed the classic bone disease of hormone excess. Burning the tumor away with a radiofrequency needle normalized her calcium and hormone levels. Her lesions nearly vanished on follow-up scans, and the leg bend improved markedly. The authors urge hormone checks before bone surgery in such children.
pmc-13456526:
Bevens and co-authors study the teamwork behind universal depression screening in this 2026 qualitative study inside a large pediatric hospital network. Eight focus groups gathered 37 nurses, physicians, and behavioral health staff from participating units. Six barriers and five proposed solutions emerged, organized along the care cascade from screening through assessment to planning what happens after a positive result. Staff flagged screening questionnaire wording that fits younger and neurodivergent patients poorly, rigid separation between medical and mental health roles, and missing infrastructure for follow-up referrals. Their fixes include adapting the language, cross-training staff, and creating dedicated follow-up roles.
pmc-13457126:
Marco Öchsner and six colleagues test, in a 2026 imaging study, one brain tumor model that keeps working when a key scan type is missing. Glioblastoma outlining software usually expects a full MRI set, including the FLAIR sequence that lights up swelling. Real clinics sometimes lack it. The team trained a standard segmentation network while randomly blanking the FLAIR channel, a trick called targeted dropout.

With the full scan set, the dropout model matched the ordinary one, scoring about 95 percent overlap with expert outlines. When FLAIR was removed at test time, the ordinary model sagged to about 81 percent, while the dropout model held near 93 percent. Whole-tumor volume error shrank from a forty-six milliliter miss to under one. A separate model trained only on three sequences did just as well, though. The authors credit adapting to fewer inputs, by dropout or by design, as the real fix.
pmc-13457226: High-level water sport athletes — competition and training loads, in a scoping review of monitoring methodology. Claire Nancy Walker, Michael Lambert, Karen Estelle Welman, and others scope the literature. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is sports monitoring. It scopes paddlers' training loads.
pmc-13457526:
Ruoxi Yang and co-authors ran a head-to-head comparison of two imaging scans for finding and staging pancreatic cancer. Their 2026 prospective study scanned 97 patients suspected of having the disease with both a newer tracer scan, FAPI PET/CT, and the standard FDG PET/CT scan. The FAPI scan targets a protein abundant around pancreatic tumors. Of the group, 88 patients were confirmed to have pancreatic cancer by pathology or follow-up imaging.

Using it changed the recorded stage of seven patients and altered treatment plans for six, including patients moved from surgery to non-surgical care.
pmc-13458826:
Javier Melchor Duart Clemente and three colleagues wrote this 2026 letter on complications of ACDF. The operation, anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, removes damaged neck discs and fuses the spine bones with plates. They respond to a paper by Mundis comparing one long plate against several segmental plates in long neck fusions. The letter pushes the biomechanical side of the argument further.

Mundis proposed that a single long plate is less stiff, especially in rotation. Stress then piles up at the lowest segment, raising failure risk there. The letter writers agree this distal instability helps explain failed fusion at that level. They add points the original paper left aside. Plate design matters, because dynamic plates that allow slight movement share load differently from rigid ones. Shorter plates generally behave better, too. Weighing the mechanical environment, they argue, could prevent complications rather than merely explain them.
pmc-13459426:

Their 2026 review covered seventy two patients operated on for trimalleolar fractures between 2017 and 2022. Patients were split by whether the posterior malleolar fragment covered under or over a quarter of the joint surface. Other foot scores and pain ratings did not differ between the fragment groups, however. Against healthy controls, both patient groups walked with clearly impaired speed, step timing, step length, and cadence. Gait stayed abnormal regardless of fragment size.
pmc-13460226:
Jiayi Xu and co-authors map in 2026 research linking idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with interleukins, a family of immune signaling proteins. Interest in this pairing has grown because some interleukin pathways drive scarring while others might be druggable. Searching two databases, the team gathered 832 papers and fifteen clinical studies, then charted themes, cited links, and keyword bursts with mapping software spanning 1999 to 2025.

Mechanism studies and treatment strategy work dominate the themes, and bursting keywords include the antifibrotic drug pirfenidone alongside diagnosis and fibrosis itself. The authors present interleukins as promising markers and offer their map to guide lab checks and patient grouping for future trials.
pmc-13460526:
Katie Louise Saxby and colleagues tested in 2026 whether metformin, the common diabetes drug, actually protects against abdominal aortic aneurysm, a dangerous ballooning of the main artery. People reporting metformin use had roughly half the aneurysm risk of others. The genetic analysis agreed, estimating about a forty-three percent risk reduction for an effect equal to a prescribed dose, and the signal appeared only for metformin's own targets. The authors call for clinical trials of the drug in aneurysm patients.
pmc-13460726:
Nezahat Merve Ata Soylu leads a Turkish team that studied in 2026 whether ordinary blood count markers can flag children likely to suffer preoperative anxiety or emergence agitation. Their prospective study enrolled 350 children aged five to twelve, rating anxiety in the waiting room and agitation in recovery with standard scales, alongside pain scores timed after surgery.
